job-1:1:4.summary: God repeats that Job is “true, blameless, God-fearing, keeping away from every evil.”
job-1:1:4.why: Confirms Job's character in God's words.

job-1:1:7.summary: God's description of Job as “blameless, true, God-fearing, keeping away from every evil deed” repeats this verse.

job-1:1:0.summary: James cites “Job's endurance” and the Lord's merciful outcome.
job-1:1:0.why: New Testament use of Job's example.

job-1:1:2.summary: Job named with Noah and Daniel as righteous men.
job-1:1:2.why: Shows Job as a byword for righteousness.

job-1:1:3.summary: “Reverence for God is wisdom, and abstaining from evils” mirrors Job being God-fearing and keeping away from evil.
job-1:1:3.why: Defines the virtues ascribed to Job.

job-1:1:6.summary: Job says he guarded God's ways and will not turn aside; general integrity theme.

job-1:1:8.summary: Abram told to “be blameless”; shared word only.

job-1:1:9.summary: Abraham shown to “fear God”; shared virtue only.

job-1:1:10.summary: “The fear of the Lord hates” evil ways; general link of fearing God and shunning evil.

job-1:1:11.summary: Zechariah and Elizabeth were “righteous…walking blamelessly”; similar virtue description.

job-1:1:13.summary: Hezekiah walked “in truth” and did good; general integrity theme.

job-1:1:14.summary: Saints Jeremiah's list here shows no Uz or Ausitis; no link to Job's land.
job-1:1:14.why: Place-name link absent in Greek text.

job-1:1:15.summary: Saints reads “dwelling upon the land,” without Uz; no link to Ausitis.
job-1:1:15.why: Place-name link absent in Greek text.

job-1:1:16.summary: “Turn away from evil and do good”; shared virtue only.

job-1:1:17.summary: Job's long oath of innocence (truncated) elaborates his blamelessness and avoidance of evil.
job-1:1:17.why: Job's own defense of his integrity.

job-1:1:18.summary: Hezekiah “did what was good and right”; general piety theme.
job-1:1:18.why: Loose parallel of an upright man.

job-1:1:19.summary: Genealogy names “Os,” possibly the eponym of Ausitis; tie is uncertain from shown text.
job-1:1:19.why: Possible origin of Job's land's name.

job-1:1:20.summary: Men “who fear God, righteous men”; shared virtue terms only.

job-1:1:21.summary: Shown text lists Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad; no Uz or Ausitis appears.

job-1:1:22.summary: Names “Uz the firstborn”; Ausitis may derive from Uz, but Saints Job does not say Uz.

job-1:1:23.summary: Edomite genealogy names “Uz”; the link to Ausitis is plausible but not explicit.

job-1:2:1.summary: Sons as “the Lord's inheritance”; general blessing-of-children theme.

job-1:2:2.summary: Job asks his friends to be silent; nothing to do with his children.

job-1:2:3.summary: Saints Esther mentions wealth and glory but not sons; no real link to Job's children.
job-1:2:3.why: Greek text lacks the assumed link.

job-1:2:4.summary: Sons “like newly planted olive trees” around the table; general blessing of children.
job-1:2:4.why: Children as blessing on the God-fearer.

job-1:2:5.summary: God blessed them and they multiplied; general blessing theme.

job-1:3:1.summary: Mentions “the sons of the east”; loosely related to Job's standing “among those from the sunrise.”

job-1:3:2.summary: “The Lord's blessing…makes rich”; general wealth-as-blessing theme.

job-1:3:3.summary: Saints reads “all ancient people,” not sons of the east; no link to Job's eminence.
job-1:3:3.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:3:4.summary: Job recalls he “sat as ruler” like a king, reflecting his noble standing.
job-1:3:4.why: Job's own memory of his eminence.

job-1:3:5.summary: Balaam came “from the eastern mountains”; loose eastern-region link.

job-1:3:6.summary: Abram had sheep, donkeys, slaves and camels; similar inventory of pastoral wealth.

job-1:3:7.summary: Abram's acquired possessions; general wealth theme.

job-1:3:8.summary: Jacob went “into the land of the east”; loose eastern-region link.

job-1:3:9.summary: Job recalls powerful men falling silent and calling him blessed, showing his former eminence.

job-1:3:10.summary: Abram and Lot's possessions were many; general wealth theme.

job-1:3:11.summary: “The man was very great: he had three thousand sheep” uses the same pattern of greatness measured in flocks.
job-1:3:11.why: Parallel description of a wealthy herdsman.

job-1:3:12.summary: Mesha's tribute in lambs and rams; general large-flocks theme.

job-1:3:13.summary: Abraham sent sons “into the land of the east”; loose eastern link.

job-1:3:14.summary: Hezekiah's great stock of sheep and cattle; general wealth theme.

job-1:3:15.summary: Large counts of sheep, cattle and donkeys; only numerical livestock listing.

job-1:3:16.summary: Shechemites covet livestock; no real link beyond the word livestock.

job-1:3:17.summary: Eastern invaders' innumerable camels; loose eastern-camels link.

job-1:3:18.summary: Uzziah had many herds; general wealth theme.

job-1:3:19.summary: “Sons of the east” with countless camels; loose eastern link.

job-1:3:20.summary: Mentions “the sons of the east”; loose regional link only.

job-1:4:0.summary: “Let brotherly love remain”; general sibling harmony theme.

job-1:4:1.summary: Good “for brothers to dwell together”; general sibling harmony theme.

job-1:5:1.summary: Noah offered “whole burnt offerings”; general righteous sacrifice theme.

job-1:5:2.summary: Samuel “consecrated Jesse and his sons” for sacrifice, like Job purifying his sons before offerings.
job-1:5:2.why: Parallel purification of sons for sacrifice.

job-1:5:3.summary: Praying “at every time…for all the saints”; general persistent intercession.

job-1:5:4.summary: Jacob has his household “purify yourselves” before making an altar, as Job purifies his children.
job-1:5:4.why: Patriarch purifying his household for worship.

job-1:5:5.summary: Bildad says “if your sons sinned,” recalling the very sons for whom Job sacrificed.
job-1:5:5.why: Later reference to Job's sons' possible sin.

job-1:5:6.summary: The “blessed” God euphemism is absent from Saints Job 1:5, which reads “evil thoughts toward God.”
job-1:5:6.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:5:7.summary: “Perhaps the intention of your heart may be forgiven”; similar concern with hidden heart sin.

job-1:5:8.summary: The “blessed” God euphemism does not appear in Saints Job 1:5.
job-1:5:8.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:5:9.summary: Abraham “rose in the morning” for a burnt offering; similar early-rising sacrifice.

job-1:5:10.summary: God examines hearts; general theme of hidden heart sin.

job-1:5:11.summary: God will reveal “the purposes of hearts”; general hidden-thought theme.

job-1:5:12.summary: “Day and night” crying for justice has no real tie to Job's continual sacrifices.

job-1:5:13.summary: “Wash your heart clean of evil”; general inner purification theme.
job-1:5:13.why: Loose parallel of purifying from evil thoughts.

job-1:5:14.summary: “All our days” of holiness shares only a general idea of continual devotion.

job-1:5:15.summary: Paul's purification with an offering “for each one of them” loosely resembles Job's offering per child.

job-1:5:16.summary: Pilgrims “purify themselves” before Passover; general purification theme.

job-1:5:17.summary: “Purify them today and tomorrow”; shared purification wording, different setting.

job-1:5:18.summary: “Evil reasonings” come from the heart; general inner-sin theme.

job-1:5:19.summary: Advice to work with strength before Hades; no real link to Job's sacrifices.

job-1:5:20.summary: The devil claims Job “will curse Thee,” echoing Job's worry about his sons' attitude toward God.
job-1:5:20.why: Ironic link of feared and alleged sin.

job-1:5:21.summary: A question about the godless man's freedom before God; no real link.

job-1:5:22.summary: Jethro offered “whole burnt offerings”; general patriarchal sacrifice.

job-1:5:23.summary: Shown text is truncated before the wife's words; no visible link to Job 1:5.
job-1:5:23.why: No visible link in shown text.

job-1:5:24.summary: About the sea beast's terror; no link to Job's sacrifices.

job-1:5:25.summary: Burnt offering of a calf “to make atonement”; general sacrificial background.

job-1:5:26.summary: “In the morning” the psalmist stands before God; shared morning devotion only.

job-1:5:27.summary: People “continually set his heart upon evil”; shares evil-heart and continual ideas.

job-1:5:28.summary: Priests “purified the people”; general purification theme.

job-1:5:29.summary: A man cursed the Name and was stoned (truncated); general theme of cursing God.
job-1:5:29.why: Shows the gravity of reviling God.

job-1:5:30.summary: Young men offered burnt offerings and calves; general sacrifice theme.

job-1:5:31.summary: Paul's godly jealousy for his converts' purity; loosely parallels Job's concern for his children.

job-1:5:32.summary: Twelve stones “according to the number” of tribes; shared counting phrase only.
job-1:5:32.why: Loose parallel of offerings by number.

job-1:6:0.summary: Second heavenly council: “the angels of God came to stand before the Lord, and the devil came among them.”

job-1:6:1.summary: God's “angels” praising at creation are the same heavenly beings who stand before the Lord here.
job-1:6:1.why: Identifies the heavenly court in Job.

job-1:6:3.summary: The Devil is the “accuser…accusing them before our God,” as here he appears before the Lord.
job-1:6:3.why: Shows the devil's role as accuser.

job-1:6:5.summary: Saints Job reads “angels of God,” not “sons of God,” so the phrase link to the giants passage is absent.
job-1:6:5.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:6:6.summary: “The devil stood in Israel” as an adversary, the same figure appearing before the Lord here.
job-1:6:6.why: Another Old Testament appearance of the devil.

job-1:6:7.summary: “One of you is a devil”; only the word devil is shared.

job-1:6:8.summary: Angels “continually see the face of My Father”; general angels-before-God theme.

job-1:6:9.summary: “His angels…doing His word”; general angelic-service theme.

job-1:6:10.summary: “Sons of God” in Genesis is not matched by Saints Job's “angels of God.”
job-1:6:10.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:6:11.summary: Adam called “of God” in a genealogy; no link to angels before the Lord.

job-1:6:12.summary: Shares the phrase “an angel of God,” but in the fiery furnace context.

job-1:7:2.summary: An unclean spirit “passes through waterless places”; loosely parallels the devil roaming.

job-1:7:3.summary: “The devil came down to you” on earth, with fury, matches the devil going around the earth.
job-1:7:3.why: Shows the devil's activity on earth.

job-1:7:4.summary: Satan goes out to the “four corners of the earth”; loose roaming theme.

job-1:7:5.summary: The Devil “thrown to the earth”; identifies him but not his roaming.

job-1:7:6.summary: Those sent “to travel around the earth” report “we have traveled around all the earth,” like the devil's report.
job-1:7:6.why: Same idiom of heavenly patrol of earth.

job-1:7:7.summary: Elisha asks “From where, Gehazi?”; shared question only.
job-1:7:7.why: Loose parallel of a master's question.

job-1:7:8.summary: Horses “travel around the earth” at God's command, the same patrol idiom as the devil's answer.
job-1:7:8.why: Same image of patrolling the earth.

job-1:8:0.summary: God repeats nearly verbatim: “Have you then paid attention to My servant Job?…no man like him.”

job-1:8:2.summary: “The fear of the Lord hates” evil; general link of fearing God and avoiding evil.

job-1:8:3.summary: God's “My servant Moses” commendation parallels “My servant Job”; general divine praise.

job-1:8:4.summary: “No king like him” for Josiah; shared incomparability formula.

job-1:8:5.summary: “Stop your evil deeds”; shared avoidance of evil only.

job-1:8:6.summary: The Lord “will not reject the innocent”; general innocence theme.
job-1:8:6.why: Bildad on God and the blameless.
job-1:8:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-1:8:7.summary: Job says he guarded God's ways; general integrity theme.

job-1:8:8.summary: Moses meek “beyond all the men upon the earth”; similar incomparability formula.

job-1:8:9.summary: Good things for “those who walk in innocence”; general theme.

job-1:8:10.summary: God again calls him “My servant Job” and vindicates him.
job-1:8:10.why: Frames the book's beginning and end.

job-1:8:11.summary: “The righteous are mocked”; general suffering-of-the-righteous theme.
job-1:8:11.why: Job's view of the righteous suffering.

job-1:8:12.summary: “Jacob is My servant”; shared title only.

job-1:8:13.summary: “True people” and the faithful holding their way; general integrity theme.

job-1:8:14.summary: “Do you not even fear God” from the thief; only incidental fear-of-God wording.

job-1:8:15.summary: Solomon “wiser than all people”; similar incomparability, different quality.

job-1:8:16.summary: “I will be blameless with Him”; shared word blameless.

job-1:8:17.summary: Saints lacks the Hebrew set-his-heart phrase; no link to paying attention to Job.
job-1:8:17.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:8:18.summary: Job calls himself “a righteous and blameless man” become a mockery, echoing God's verdict.

job-1:8:19.summary: Do not turn aside, “My servant” Moses; general obedience theme.

job-1:8:20.summary: “Set in your heart” what is shown loosely resembles paying attention in one's mind.

job-1:8:22.summary: The lawless has “no fear of God”; contrast with God-fearing Job.

job-1:8:23.summary: Nathanael “in whom there is no deceit”; similar commendation of integrity.

job-1:8:24.summary: Nehemiah acted rightly “because of the fear of God”; general theme.

job-1:8:25.summary: “Turn aside from evil and do good”; shared avoidance of evil.

job-1:8:26.summary: “Turn aside from evil and do good”; shared avoidance of evil.

job-1:9:0.summary: Gaining the world but losing one's life has no real tie to the devil's charge.

job-1:9:1.summary: “Godliness is beneficial”; touches the gain-from-piety question loosely.

job-1:9:2.summary: “Godliness with contentment is great gain”; loose piety-and-gain theme.

job-1:9:4.summary: The wicked ask “what benefit is there” in serving the Mighty One, the same question of piety for profit.
job-1:9:4.why: Same debate about motives for serving God.

job-1:9:5.summary: Shares “for nothing,” about kindling God's altar; different context.

job-1:9:6.summary: Job accepts good and bad from God and does not sin, refuting the claim he serves for gain.

job-1:10:0.summary: An angel “will encamp around those who fear Him,” like God fencing in the God-fearing Job.
job-1:10:0.why: Same image of protection around the God-fearer.

job-1:10:1.summary: God as “a wall of fire around” Jerusalem; general protection image.

job-1:10:2.summary: Believers “guarded by the power of God”; general protection theme.

job-1:10:3.summary: Blessings on “the herds of your cattle, and the flocks” for obedience parallel God blessing Job's works and livestock.

job-1:10:4.summary: “The Lord's blessing…makes rich”; general wealth-as-blessing theme.

job-1:10:5.summary: Whoever “touches you” touches God's eye; general protection theme.
job-1:10:5.why: Loose parallel of God guarding His own.

job-1:10:6.summary: Job denies rejoicing in “much wealth”; loose link to his blessed wealth.

job-1:10:7.summary: “He blessed them…and He did not diminish their livestock” parallels God blessing Job and multiplying his livestock.

job-1:10:8.summary: “I shield you” to Abram; general protection theme.

job-1:10:9.summary: “Direct the works of our hands”; shared phrase “works of our hands.”

job-1:10:10.summary: God will “bless you, and multiply you” and bless “the herds of your cattle,” matching Job's blessed livestock.

job-1:10:11.summary: God will “remove its fence”; shared fence image, different context.

job-1:10:12.summary: “The Lord blessed him” in harvest; general blessing theme.

job-1:10:13.summary: The one who fears the Lord is blessed in labor and household; general theme.

job-1:10:14.summary: “The Lord blessed Job's latter things,” doubling his livestock.
job-1:10:14.why: Restoration of the blessing here described.

job-1:10:15.summary: Men “like a wall around us” protecting flocks; similar protective image.
job-1:10:15.why: Loose parallel of a protective hedge.

job-1:10:16.summary: Jacob became wealthy with much livestock; general wealth theme.

job-1:10:17.summary: “I put a fence around it”; shared fence image for a vineyard.

job-1:10:18.summary: “Shelter from the God of old”; general protection theme.

job-1:10:19.summary: God “blessed you” with blessings of heaven and earth; general blessing theme.

job-1:10:20.summary: God increasing His greatness and restoring the psalmist; no real link to Job's hedge or wealth.

job-1:10:21.summary: “The Lord has blessed you” and increased Laban's flocks; general blessing-of-increase theme.

job-1:10:22.summary: Lists Job's livestock, the possessions the devil says God has multiplied.

job-1:10:24.summary: “Accept the works of his hands” shares the phrase but in Levi's blessing.

job-1:10:25.summary: “Thou wilt bless the righteous” and crown with favor; general blessing-and-protection theme.
job-1:10:25.why: Loose parallel of blessing the righteous.

job-1:10:26.summary: God's blessing “was upon all that he had, in the house and in the field,” like Job's blessing on all he has.

job-1:10:27.summary: “Why didst Thou tear down her fence”; shared fence image, removal of protection.

job-1:11:1.summary: Job says “the Lord's hand…touched me,” the very touch the devil asked for.

job-1:11:2.summary: People “blasphemed the God of heaven” because of pains; contrasting response to suffering.

job-1:11:3.summary: People “blasphemed the name of God” under plagues; general theme.

job-1:11:4.summary: People “blasphemed God because of the plague”; general theme.

job-1:11:5.summary: “The one who serves God is futile”; loose link to serving God for advantage.

job-1:11:6.summary: Whoever “touches you” touches God's eye; shared touch idea only.
job-1:11:6.why: Loose parallel of touching God's own.

job-1:11:7.summary: Job responds “blessed be the name of the Lord,” refuting the claim he would curse God.

job-1:11:8.summary: Job feared his sons had “evil thoughts toward God,” ironically the sin the devil predicts of Job.

job-1:11:9.summary: God's response: “everything he has I give into your hand, but do not touch him.”

job-1:11:10.summary: Job's wife begins urging him (truncated); shown text does not include cursing.

job-1:11:11.summary: The Lord “brought His hand against them and struck them”; general hand-of-judgment image.
job-1:11:11.why: Loose parallel of God's striking hand.

job-1:11:12.summary: Eliphaz says pain “touched you”; shares the touch wording.
job-1:11:12.why: Later reference to Job being touched.

job-1:11:13.summary: “Do not touch My anointed ones”; shared touch idea only.

job-1:11:14.summary: Abimelech forbids touching Isaac; only the word touch is shared.

job-1:11:15.summary: Hungry people “speak evil of the ruler”; suffering leading to cursing.

job-1:12:1.summary: “A messenger of Satan, to strike me” is allowed for Paul; loose permitted-affliction theme.

job-1:12:2.summary: The Father giving all things into the Son's hand has no real tie to the devil's permission.
job-1:12:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-1:12:3.summary: God “will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear,” as He limits the devil: “do not touch him.”

job-1:12:4.summary: Authority “given you from above”; general theme of permitted power.

job-1:12:5.summary: God sending Israel away in wrath; no link to the devil's limited permission.

job-1:12:7.summary: Jesus “permitted” the demons; general permitted-evil theme.

job-1:12:8.summary: Human thought acknowledging God; no real link in Saints wording.
job-1:12:8.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:12:9.summary: “He is in your hands”; shared handing-over formula, unrelated setting.

job-1:12:10.summary: “Your slave woman is in your hands”; shared handing-over formula.

job-1:12:11.summary: The Lord put a lying spirit in prophets; loose theme of spirits acting under God's permission.

job-1:13:0.summary: Drinking and “that day come upon you suddenly”; loose theme of sudden disaster during feasting.

job-1:13:1.summary: “You do not know what the coming day will bear”; general unexpected-day theme.

job-1:13:2.summary: Eating and drinking “until the day” destruction came; sudden calamity amid feasting.

job-1:13:3.summary: People trapped “at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly”; general theme.

job-1:13:4.summary: “Eat, drink, be glad” before sudden death; loose sudden-calamity theme.

job-1:14:0.summary: A messenger reports slaughter and “both your sons are dead,” the same disaster-report pattern Job hears.

job-1:14:1.summary: “Announcer to meet announcer” loosely resembles successive messengers.

job-1:14:2.summary: “A messenger came to David”; shared messenger formula.

job-1:15:0.summary: Saints Job 1:15 reads “raiders,” not Sabeans; the Sheba genealogy link is absent.
job-1:15:0.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:1.summary: Sabeans are not named in Saints Job 1:15, which says “The raiders.”
job-1:15:1.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:2.summary: The Seboin have no link to Saints Job's unnamed “raiders.”
job-1:15:2.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:3.summary: Sheba in a genealogy; Saints Job 1:15 names no Sabeans.
job-1:15:3.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:4.summary: Shown Saints text names no Sabeans, and Job 1:15 says only “raiders.”
job-1:15:4.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:5.summary: Men “out of the wilderness” at a feast; no Sabean link in either Saints text.
job-1:15:5.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:6.summary: Repeats the refrain “I alone was saved and came to report to you.”

job-1:15:7.summary: Saba bringing gifts; Saints Job 1:15 names no Sabeans.
job-1:15:7.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:8.summary: Sheba in a genealogy; no link to Saints Job's “raiders.”
job-1:15:8.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:15:9.summary: One son “was saved” and told David of the slaughter; similar lone-survivor report.

job-1:16:1.summary: The Lord rained “fire…out of the heaven” on Sodom, matching “fire fell from heaven.”
job-1:16:1.why: Same image of destructive heavenly fire.

job-1:16:2.summary: “Fire came out from the Lord and consumed them,” like fire that “consumed the shepherds.”

job-1:16:3.summary: “Fire from the Lord fell from heaven and consumed,” nearly identical wording.
job-1:16:3.why: Same phrasing of fire from heaven.

job-1:16:4.summary: Fire from the Lord consumed the offering; divine fire, but not destructive calamity.
job-1:16:4.why: Divine fire in a different sense.

job-1:16:5.summary: The beast makes “fire come down from heaven”; shared image in a deceptive sign.
job-1:16:5.why: Fire from heaven by an evil agent.

job-1:16:7.summary: “Fire from the Lord blazed among them and consumed” part of the camp, like the fire consuming flocks and shepherds.

job-1:16:8.summary: Judgment “by fire” devouring; general fire-judgment theme.

job-1:16:9.summary: Thunder, hail and fire in Egypt; general fire-plague theme.
job-1:16:9.why: Loose parallel of fire from the sky.

job-1:16:10.summary: “Fire came down from heaven and consumed” the captains and men, closely matching the messenger's report.

job-1:16:11.summary: Terror from the Lord in a camp; no fire or similar wording.

job-1:17:0.summary: Saints Job 1:17 says “horsemen,” not Chaldeans; the place link is absent.
job-1:17:0.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:17:1.summary: Chaldean warriors are not named in Saints Job 1:17, which reads “horsemen.”
job-1:17:1.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:17:2.summary: Chaldeans' land; Saints Job 1:17 names only “horsemen.”
job-1:17:2.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:17:3.summary: Country of the Chaldeans; no link to Saints Job's “horsemen.”
job-1:17:3.why: Greek wording lacks the assumed link.

job-1:17:5.summary: A man “come safely away” from a camp to report disaster; similar survivor-messenger pattern.

job-1:18:0.summary: Introduces the daily drinking feasts of Job’s sons with their three sisters, the setting of the disaster reported in Job 1:18.
job-1:18:0.why: Shows the family feast as the scene of the catastrophe.

job-1:18:1.summary: Same scene in nearly the same words: Job’s sons and daughters “drinking” in the house of “their elder brother.”
job-1:18:1.why: Sets up the fourth messenger’s report.

job-1:18:2.summary: A lament of unparalleled pain sent by the Lord; only a general link to Job’s mounting calamities.

job-1:18:3.summary: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous” speaks generally to a righteous man’s suffering, not this report.

job-1:18:4.summary: One event comes to righteous and ungodly alike; a general theme loosely applicable to Job’s losses.
job-1:18:4.why: Raises the question of undeserved disaster.

job-1:18:5.summary: A king’s son killed during a wine feast; loose parallel to Job’s children dying while drinking.
job-1:18:5.why: Another feast that ends in death.

job-1:18:6.summary: Job later wishes his pains could be weighed; general response to the calamities, not the report itself.
job-1:18:6.why: Job’s own later reflection on his grief.

job-1:18:7.summary: Bildad refers to Job’s sons and suggests their death was punishment for sin.
job-1:18:7.why: Shows how the friends interpret the children’s death.

job-1:18:8.summary: A scourge passing “morning after morning” suggests repeated blows, only loosely like successive reports.

job-1:18:9.summary: The wicked man’s sons are “for slaughter”; general theme of children perishing.

job-1:18:10.summary: “Announcer to meet announcer” pictures one messenger after another bringing disaster news, like Job’s successive messengers.
job-1:18:10.why: Distinctive image of relay messengers of calamity.

job-1:18:11.summary: Job laments God stripping his glory and hope; general reflection on loss.
job-1:18:11.why: Job’s later interpretation of his ruin.

job-1:18:12.summary: A series of divine afflictions in succession (shown text truncated); only loosely like Job’s serial disasters.

job-1:18:13.summary: God’s hand heavy on Job’s groaning; general suffering theme.
job-1:18:13.why: Job’s later sense of God’s pressure.

job-1:18:14.summary: “Fall upon fall” describes blows in succession, loosely matching the stream of disasters.

job-1:19:0.summary: Jacob bereaved of children says “All these things have come upon me”; general parallel of a bereaved father.

job-1:19:1.summary: “Ruler of the authority of the air” is not linked to the wilderness wind in the text shown.
job-1:19:1.why: Speculative link to Satan behind the wind.

job-1:19:2.summary: David’s lament for Absalom shows a father’s grief at a child’s death; no specific link to the house collapse.
job-1:19:2.why: Parental grief at death of children.

job-1:19:3.summary: “The house fell upon” those inside, killing them, as with Job’s children.
job-1:19:3.why: Vivid parallel of a fatal house collapse.

job-1:19:4.summary: Jacob receives the report of his son’s death; loose parallel to Job hearing of his children.
job-1:19:4.why: Father receiving news of child’s death.

job-1:19:5.summary: A “spirit” from the wilderness, but the Greek wording speaks of wandering, not a destructive wind.
job-1:19:5.why: Only a verbal echo of wind from the wilderness.

job-1:19:6.summary: Islanders read a snakebite as divine justice; the source makes no such judgment.
job-1:19:6.why: Assumed theme of disaster as punishment.

job-1:19:7.summary: A tower that fell and killed eighteen, not as greater sinners; loosely parallels the fatal collapse.
job-1:19:7.why: Disaster is not proof of guilt.

job-1:19:8.summary: A wall fell on the survivors in Aphek; a collapse killing many, otherwise unrelated.

job-1:19:9.summary: Winds “struck that house, and it fell,” closely echoing the wind that struck Job’s house.
job-1:19:9.why: Same image of wind-struck house falling.

job-1:20:0.summary: Humbling oneself under God’s hand; general link to Job’s humble worship.

job-1:20:1.summary: David lies on the ground over his dying child; the shown text is truncated before his rising to worship, paralleling Job.
job-1:20:1.why: Worship in the face of a child’s death.

job-1:20:2.summary: Jacob “tore his garments” mourning his son, the same mourning gesture as Job.
job-1:20:2.why: Classic mourning rite for lost children.

job-1:20:3.summary: Reuben “tore his garments”; shared gesture only, different situation.

job-1:20:5.summary: Jesus falls on His face and submits to the Father’s will; general parallel of prostrate submission.

job-1:20:6.summary: Moses fasting forty days in intercession; no shown mention of falling down, mourning, or loss.

job-1:20:7.summary: Israel “fell face down” and “worshiped”; shared posture but a joyful setting.

job-1:21:2.summary: Giving thanks in everything; general parallel to blessing God amid loss.

job-1:21:3.summary: Every good gift is from above; loosely echoes “the Lord gave.”
job-1:21:3.why: God as giver of all good.

job-1:21:4.summary: Job again accepts both good and bad from the Lord’s hand, and “did not sin” with his lips.
job-1:21:4.why: Job’s second statement of the same faith.

job-1:21:5.summary: At death a person “will not take everything” with him, like leaving naked as one came.
job-1:21:5.why: Nothing is carried out of life.

job-1:21:6.summary: Always giving thanks for all things; general link to blessing God in loss.

job-1:21:7.summary: Dust returns to the earth and spirit to God who gave it, echoing return at death and “the Lord gave.”
job-1:21:7.why: Return of life to its source.

job-1:21:8.summary: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich,” matching the Lord who gives and takes away.

job-1:21:9.summary: Return to the earth from which you were taken, matching departing naked back “there.”
job-1:21:9.why: Human origin and return to earth.

job-1:21:10.summary: God makes peace and creates calamities; general sovereignty over good and ill.
job-1:21:10.why: God behind both blessing and calamity.

job-1:21:11.summary: Calamities and good both come from the Most High; general sovereignty theme, closer to Job 2:10.

job-1:21:12.summary: God gave Jacob over to plunder because of sin; shares God taking away but adds a sin rationale.

job-1:21:13.summary: The master may do as he wishes with what is his; loosely parallels God’s right to give and take.

job-1:21:14.summary: Silent acceptance because God did it; general submission theme.

job-1:21:15.summary: The Lord’s name will be glorious; only a general praise of the divine name.

job-1:21:16.summary: Eli accepts judgment: “He is the Lord. He will do what is good before Him,” like Job’s “as it seemed good to the Lord.”
job-1:21:16.why: Parallel resigned acceptance of God’s will.

job-1:21:17.summary: What God’s hand determined beforehand happened; general providence theme.

job-1:21:18.summary: “I will bless the Lord at every time” echoes Job’s blessing of the Lord’s name in loss.

job-1:21:19.summary: Joseph sees God’s purpose in his loss; general providence theme.

job-1:21:20.summary: David accepts humiliation, hoping the Lord will repay with good; loose submission theme.

job-1:21:21.summary: The turn of events came from the Lord; general divine causation.

job-1:21:22.summary: Hezekiah calls the Lord’s word of judgment “good”; loose acceptance theme.

job-1:21:23.summary: The adversary predicted Job would curse God if his possessions were touched; Job instead blesses the Lord’s name.

job-1:21:24.summary: God withholds the fruit of the womb; God gives and withholds children, a loose link.

job-1:21:25.summary: Wealth and possessions are God’s gift; general link to “the Lord gave.”

job-1:21:26.summary: No calamity in a city the Lord has not done; general divine causation of disaster.

job-1:21:27.summary: A lament accusing God of rejecting His anointed (truncated); contrasts with Job’s blessing response.

job-1:21:28.summary: Every human is born the same way, crying at first breath; echoes coming “naked from my mother’s womb.”

job-1:21:29.summary: “One entrance into life, and the same departure” matches Job’s naked coming and going.
job-1:21:29.why: Birth and death as common lot.

job-1:22:0.summary: Blessing for one who endures trial; general endurance theme fitting Job.

job-1:22:2.summary: Faith tested like gold by fire; general testing theme.

job-1:22:3.summary: Endurance makes one complete; general endurance theme.

job-1:22:4.summary: Not answering back to God; loosely matches Job not charging God with folly.

job-1:22:5.summary: Elihu on insulting kings and rulers; no real link to Job’s sinless response.

job-1:22:6.summary: Later Job places a hand over his mouth after reproving the Lord; loose contrast with early blamelessness.

job-1:22:7.summary: Elihu insists on not acting ungodly before the Lord; only general theme of not wronging God.

job-1:1:12.summary: Proverbs 16:6 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-1:1:12.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-1:1:12.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-2:1:1.summary: Angels as “ministering spirits” relates to God's angels standing before Him.

job-2:1:2.summary: Gabriel “stands before God,” as the angels came “to stand before the Lord.”
job-2:1:2.why: Same picture of angels before God.

job-2:1:3.summary: Seraphim “stood around” the enthroned Lord, another view of the heavenly court.

job-2:2:0.summary: “The devil walks about” seeking prey, as the devil was “walking through” the world.
job-2:2:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-2:2:2.summary: “The ruler of the world” relates to the devil's range over the world.
job-2:2:2.why: General view of the devil's domain.

job-2:2:3.summary: “Where have you come from?” is the same question, asked of Hagar.

job-2:2:4.summary: “The god of this age” relates loosely to the devil's worldwide activity.
job-2:2:4.why: General view of the devil's domain.

job-2:3:8.summary: Job is “true, blameless, righteous, and God-fearing, keeping away from every evil,” the same description.

job-2:3:0.summary: Job says God multiplied his injuries “without cause,” matching “for nothing.”

job-2:3:2.summary: Blessing on one who “endures a trial” relates to Job holding to innocence.

job-2:3:3.summary: Job vows, “I will not give up my innocence,” confirming “He still holds to innocence.”

job-2:3:4.summary: Paths that “turn aside from evils” relate to keeping away from every evil.

job-2:3:5.summary: Faith “tested by fire” relates to Job's tested integrity.

job-2:3:6.summary: Paul pressing on toward perfection has no specific link to God's praise of Job.

job-2:3:7.summary: Suffering not due to sin parallels Job's innocent suffering.

job-2:3:9.summary: God rejecting the sacrifices of the impious has no specific link here.

job-2:3:10.summary: God restores after suffering, loosely relating to Job's tested faithfulness.

job-2:3:11.summary: Job doubts that being “blameless” will help him, a link on the word blameless.

job-2:3:12.summary: Joab's refusal to destroy relies on the Hebrew “swallow up,” with no real link here.
job-2:3:12.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-2:3:13.summary: “Guard innocence” shares the word innocence as a value.

job-2:3:14.summary: Righteousness guarding “the innocent” relates loosely to Job's innocence.

job-2:3:15.summary: Job blesses the Lord and “did not sin at all,” the proof that he still holds to innocence.
job-2:3:15.why: Shows the basis of God's praise.

job-2:3:16.summary: Noah is “righteous” and “blameless,” the same exemplary description.
job-2:3:16.why: Noah and Job as righteous models.

job-2:3:17.summary: The devil's claim that Job would curse God is the challenge God refers to here.

job-2:3:18.summary: Job resolves to plead before God even while subdued, persevering in integrity.

job-2:3:19.summary: The righteous escaping while the impious is handed over loosely relates to Job's case.

job-2:3:20.summary: One who walks uprightly “fears the Lord,” loosely matching Job's description.

job-2:3:21.summary: God sustains the psalmist “because of innocence,” sharing the word innocence.

job-2:3:22.summary: “I walked in my innocence” shares the word innocence.

job-2:4:0.summary: Paul gladly loses all things for Christ, the opposite of the devil's cynical claim.

job-2:4:1.summary: “Is life not more than food” relates loosely to valuing life above possessions.

job-2:4:3.summary: Ten men offer their stores to save their lives, illustrating paying anything for life.
job-2:4:3.why: Example of trading goods for life.

job-2:4:4.summary: Esther pleads for her life, loosely relating to valuing one's life.
job-2:4:4.why: Loose example of pleading for life.

job-2:4:5.summary: Throwing cargo overboard to survive illustrates giving up goods for life.
job-2:4:5.why: Example of trading goods for life.

job-2:4:6.summary: Casting away silver and gold idols in terror is only loosely related.

job-2:5:1.summary: The law on one “who curses God” relates to the devil's prediction that Job will curse.

job-2:5:2.summary: Job's “flesh decayed” and “bones,” and “the Lord's hand ... touched me,” fulfill this request.
job-2:5:2.why: Shows the outcome of the devil's request.

job-2:5:3.summary: Job's concern that his sons had evil thoughts toward God relates to cursing God.

job-2:5:4.summary: Wasting from “the strength of Thy hand” loosely parallels God's hand touching the body.
job-2:5:4.why: General image of God's hand afflicting.

job-2:5:5.summary: Job's wife begins to question his persistence; the shown text is cut off before her words.
job-2:5:5.why: Points toward the temptation to curse.

job-2:5:6.summary: God's heavy hand and aging bones loosely parallel touching bones and flesh.
job-2:5:6.why: General image of God's hand afflicting.

job-2:5:7.summary: The hungry “speak evil” of rulers and idols, a loose parallel to cursing under pressure.

job-2:5:8.summary: God's hand pressed on the psalmist with “no healing in my flesh” and no peace for “my bones.”
job-2:5:8.why: Same hand, flesh and bones affliction.

job-2:5:9.summary: David asks God's “hand” to be upon him, a loosely similar phrase.

job-2:6:0.summary: God does not allow testing “beyond what you can bear,” as He limits the devil to sparing Job's life.

job-2:6:1.summary: “Satan demanded to have you all,” like the devil requesting power over Job.
job-2:6:1.why: Satan asks leave to test the faithful.

job-2:6:3.summary: The devil will test believers for a limited time, like his limited power over Job.

job-2:6:4.summary: God setting bounds for the sea loosely parallels limiting the devil.

job-2:6:5.summary: Demons act only when Jesus “permitted them,” like the devil acting by God's leave.

job-2:6:6.summary: The devil bound by an angel shows God's control over him.

job-2:6:7.summary: God stilling the sea has no specific link to limiting the devil here.

job-2:6:8.summary: Satan “loosed” for a time loosely parallels being handed power within limits.

job-2:7:1.summary: “My skin has darkened greatly” describes the effect of the ulcer on Job's body.
job-2:7:1.why: Job's own description of his disease.

job-2:7:2.summary: “From feet to head” matches the ulcer “from his feet to his head.”

job-2:7:3.summary: “The Egyptian ulcer” and “grievous scab” match Job's “grievous ulcer.”
job-2:7:3.why: Ties Job's disease to covenant curses.

job-2:7:4.summary: Job's body “fouled with the decay of worms” and discharge describes the ulcer's effect.
job-2:7:4.why: Job's own description of his disease.

job-2:7:5.summary: A spirit says “I will go out” from God's council with permission to harm, as the devil went out.

job-2:7:6.summary: Job's bones “burned” by night describe his bodily torment.
job-2:7:6.why: Job's own description of his disease.

job-2:7:7.summary: Boils with blisters break out on all Egypt, a parallel plague of skin sores.

job-2:7:8.summary: People blaspheme God because of “their sores,” unlike Job who did not curse.
job-2:7:8.why: Contrast with Job's response to sores.

job-2:7:9.summary: The Hebrew link is a scab on the head; here God merely humbles and uncovers Zion's daughters.
job-2:7:9.why: Link depends on the Hebrew reading.

job-2:8:0.summary: Job sits on the dung heap here and later regards himself as “earth and ashes”; both picture his abasement, though the setting differs.
job-2:8:0.why: Frames the start and end of Job's humiliation.

job-2:8:1.summary: The king of Nineveh “sat in ashes”; Job sits on a dung heap, a related but different image of abasement.

job-2:8:2.summary: Mourners “spread ashes beneath them”; Job sits on a dung heap, only a general shared image of mourning abasement.

job-2:8:3.summary: Repentance “in sackcloth and ashes” shares only a general mourning image; the Saints text of Job has a dung heap, not ashes.

job-2:8:4.summary: Lazarus “covered with sores” lies outside a gateway, echoing sore-afflicted Job sitting outside the city.
job-2:8:4.why: Similar picture of an afflicted outcast.

job-2:8:5.summary: The psalmist's “bruises stank and rotted” loosely parallels Job scraping off his discharge.
job-2:8:5.why: Another description of festering bodily affliction.

job-2:8:6.summary: Tamar puts ashes on her head in grief; the Saints text of Job mentions no ashes, only a potsherd and dung heap.
job-2:8:6.why: No specific link in the texts.

job-2:8:7.summary: “No healing in my flesh” loosely matches Job's diseased body, but is a general lament.

job-2:8:8.summary: Job later describes being disowned by household and kin, loosely matching his isolation outside the city.

job-2:8:9.summary: Jeremiah calls for sackcloth and ashes; the Saints text of Job has a dung heap, not ashes or mourning rites.
job-2:8:9.why: Link depends on the Hebrew “ashes” reading.

job-2:8:10.summary: “Glory instead of ashes” for Zion's mourners has no real tie to Job's potsherd and dung heap in this text.
job-2:8:10.why: Link depends on a word absent here.

job-2:9:0.summary: The wife's challenge follows the adversary's prediction that Job will “curse Thee”; the shown words only begin her speech.
job-2:9:0.why: Shows the test the wife's words press.

job-2:9:2.summary: Complaint that serving God is “futile” loosely resembles the wife's impatience with Job's persistence.
job-2:9:2.why: Similar doubt about the value of faithfulness.

job-2:9:3.summary: “Why should I wait for the Lord any longer?” loosely echoes the wife's “How long will you persist.”

job-2:9:4.summary: The wicked's “What benefit is there” in serving God loosely resembles the wife's challenge to Job's persistence.

job-2:9:5.summary: Solomon's wives turned his heart from God; Job's wife urges him to give up, a loose theme of spousal influence.
job-2:9:5.why: Contrasts a man who yielded to his wives.

job-2:9:6.summary: The adversary's claim that Job will “curse Thee” is the test the wife's words press, but her shown words do not say this.

job-2:9:7.summary: Eve giving fruit to her husband is a loose parallel to a wife urging her husband toward wrong.

job-2:9:8.summary: Adam blaming “the woman” loosely parallels a wife's role in temptation; no shared wording.

job-2:10:0.summary: Blessing on the man “who endures a trial” fits Job's acceptance of bad things, but only thematically.
job-2:10:0.why: New Testament teaching on enduring trials.

job-2:10:1.summary: “Will not calamities and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” closely echoes receiving good and bad from the Lord.
job-2:10:1.why: Same theology of accepting both good and ill from God.

job-2:10:3.summary: “Persevere in affliction” matches Job's endurance only in general terms.

job-2:10:4.summary: James explicitly cites “Job's endurance” as an example of suffering patiently, as Job does here.
job-2:10:4.why: New Testament commentary on this very episode.

job-2:10:5.summary: Submitting to the Father's discipline loosely parallels accepting bad things from the Lord's hand.

job-2:10:6.summary: Jesus rebukes Peter for human thinking that would avoid suffering, loosely like Job rebuking his wife.
job-2:10:6.why: Similar rebuke of a close one's counsel.

job-2:10:7.summary: “The cup that the Father has given Me—shall I not drink it?” parallels “shall we not bear the bad things?” from God.
job-2:10:7.why: Christ's acceptance of suffering mirrors Job's.

job-2:10:8.summary: Accountability for words loosely relates to Job not sinning “with his lips.”
job-2:10:8.why: Teaching on the weight of speech.

job-2:10:9.summary: David's confession that he “acted very foolishly” shares only the idea of folly with Job's rebuke.

job-2:10:10.summary: “So as not to sin with my tongue” closely echoes Job not sinning “with his lips.”
job-2:10:10.why: Same ideal of guarded speech under trial.

job-2:10:11.summary: Adam was condemned for listening to his wife; Job refuses his wife's counsel, a loose contrast.

job-2:10:12.summary: “Like one of the foolish men” echoes “like one of the foolish women,” but the contexts are unrelated.

job-2:10:13.summary: One who “does not stumble in speech” is complete, loosely matching Job not sinning with his lips.
job-2:10:13.why: Links Job's blamelessness to controlled speech.

job-2:10:14.summary: “Good things and bad … are from the Lord” states the same principle Job voices.
job-2:10:14.why: Wisdom literature echo of Job's confession.

job-2:11:0.summary: “Weep with those who weep” fits the friends' coming to comfort only in general terms.

job-2:11:1.summary: Job's kin “heard everything that had happened to him and came to him” and consoled him, framing the book like the friends here.
job-2:11:1.why: Matching consolation scenes at the book's start and end.

job-2:11:2.summary: In this text Job laments that mercy and the Lord's care overlooked him; nothing mentions friends or comfort.
job-2:11:2.why: Greek wording lacks the friend link.

job-2:11:3.summary: Shuah, son of Abraham and Keturah, is the likely namesake of Bildad's people, the Shuhites.

job-2:11:4.summary: A friend useful “in times of need” fits the friends' visit only in general terms.

job-2:11:5.summary: Teman is named as a place of wisdom, the homeland of Eliphaz king of the Temanites.
job-2:11:5.why: Background on Eliphaz's renowned wise homeland.

job-2:11:6.summary: Members suffering together loosely parallels friends coming to share Job's suffering.

job-2:11:7.summary: Edomite chiefs include sons of Eliphaz, with Teman and Sophar, names matching Eliphaz the Temanite and Zophar.

job-2:11:8.summary: Jacob's children “came to comfort him,” a similar phrase in an unrelated mourning scene.

job-2:11:9.summary: Job appeals to these same “friends” for mercy because the Lord's hand touched him.
job-2:11:9.why: Shows what Job hoped for from the friends.

job-2:11:10.summary: Jews came to Martha and Mary “to console them,” a similar comforting visit in another story.

job-2:11:11.summary: “Sons of Eliphaz were Teman … Sophar” links the names Eliphaz, Teman and Zophar to Edom.

job-2:11:12.summary: Job mentions “the roads of the Temanites,” sharing only the place name with Eliphaz's people.

job-2:11:14.summary: Keturah's son appears as “Soe” here, so the Saints wording only faintly suggests the Shuhites.

job-2:11:15.summary: Remembering the mistreated as if sharing their body loosely fits the friends' visit.

job-2:11:16.summary: A nearby friend in misfortune loosely parallels friends coming to Job.

job-2:11:17.summary: “Who will grieve with you … Who will comfort you?” shares the comfort theme only generally.

job-2:11:18.summary: Job's supplication and tears before the Lord mention no friends in this Greek-based wording.
job-2:11:18.why: Link relies on Hebrew “my friends” reading.
job-2:11:18.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-2:11:19.summary: Job calls these would-be comforters “unjust physicians,” contrasting their stated aim to comfort him.
job-2:11:19.why: Shows how the friends' comfort failed.

job-2:11:20.summary: Introduces a speech by “Bildad the Shuhite,” one of the three friends named here.

job-2:11:21.summary: Introduces another speech by “Bildad the Shuhite,” one of the friends named here.

job-2:11:22.summary: Introduces a speech by “Eliphaz the Temanite,” one of the friends named here.

job-2:11:25.summary: Those Job loved rose against him, a loose foreshadowing of the friends turning accusers.
job-2:11:25.why: Contrasts friends' arrival with later hostility.

job-2:12:0.summary: Elders put “dust on their heads” and sit in silence, matching the friends' earth-sprinkling and silent sitting.

job-2:12:1.summary: Mourners “raise a cry … cry bitterly” and “put earth on their head,” as the friends do.

job-2:12:2.summary: Israel assembles in sackcloth, a general mourning rite without the shared gestures here.

job-2:12:3.summary: Joshua “tore his clothes” and the elders “put dust on their heads,” the same gestures as the friends.

job-2:12:5.summary: “Raised their voices and wept” shares only the weeping aloud.

job-2:12:6.summary: Disfigured Nazirites were “unrecognized,” as the friends did not recognize the afflicted Job.

job-2:12:7.summary: Mordecai “tore his clothes … sprinkled himself with ashes” and cried loudly, matching the friends' rites.

job-2:12:8.summary: “Is this Naomi?” shows an afflicted person barely recognized, loosely like Job's friends.
job-2:12:8.why: Similar shock at a changed sufferer.

job-2:12:9.summary: “Did not acknowledge me” concerns rejection, not physical non-recognition, a loose echo.
job-2:12:9.why: Loose echo of not being recognized.

job-2:12:10.summary: Esau “cried with a great and exceedingly bitter cry,” sharing only the loud weeping.

job-2:12:11.summary: “Raised their voice and wept” shares only weeping aloud.

job-2:12:12.summary: Mourners “threw dust upon their heads and cried, weeping,” the same gestures as the friends.

job-2:12:13.summary: “Raised their voices, and wept” shares only loud weeping.

job-2:12:14.summary: “Raised their voices and wept” shares only loud weeping.

job-2:13:0.summary: Joseph mourned his father “seven days,” the same seven-day mourning period as the friends' sitting.
job-2:13:0.why: Shows the customary seven days of mourning.

job-2:13:1.summary: Nehemiah “sat down and wept, and mourned for days,” a general parallel to sitting in grief.

job-2:13:3.summary: Being “dashed to the ground” in judgment does not match the friends sitting silently with Job.
job-2:13:3.why: Greek wording lacks the sitting image.

job-2:13:4.summary: Ezra tore his garments and “sat quietly” in grief, like the friends' silent sitting.

job-2:13:5.summary: Eliphaz's first words follow the silence, but the verse itself does not mention it.

job-2:13:6.summary: Creation's “Day” and “Night” share only incidental words with “seven days and seven nights.”

job-2:13:7.summary: “I was troubled and did not speak” loosely echoes silence before great affliction.

job-2:13:8.summary: Creation's second day has no link beyond the word “day.”

job-2:13:9.summary: Babylon told to “sit on the ground”; the Saints text says the friends sat beside Job, not on the ground.

job-2:11:24.summary: Proverbs 18:24 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-2:11:24.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-2:11:24.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-3:1:1.summary: Moses speaking rashly with his lips when embittered loosely parallels Job's outburst.

job-3:1:2.summary: Silence broken as the heart grows hot and “I spoke with my tongue” parallels Job opening his mouth.

job-3:1:3.summary: Job 3:3 gives the content of the curse: “May the day perish on which I was born.”

job-3:1:4.summary: Elihu says Job “vainly opens his mouth,” echoing Job opening his mouth.

job-3:1:5.summary: Satan predicts Job will curse God; Job instead curses his day.

job-3:1:6.summary: Job earlier “did not sin at all,” contrasting with his now cursing his day.

job-3:1:7.summary: Job did not sin with his lips despite his wife's urging, contrasting with his cursing the day.

job-3:1:8.summary: Satan predicts Job “will curse Thee”; Job curses his day, not God.

job-3:2:0.summary: A speech-introducing “saying” in Judges is only an incidental formula match.

job-3:3:1.summary: Job asks why he was brought from the womb, repeating his wish never to have been born.

job-3:3:2.summary: Jeremiah's “Woe to me, mother!” laments his birth, paralleling Job cursing his birthday.

job-3:4:0.summary: The plague of “darkness, gloom” over Egypt shares the darkness image Job invokes.

job-3:4:1.summary: “A day of darkness and gloom” matches Job's wish that the day be darkness.

job-3:4:2.summary: Days without sun or stars in a storm share only absence of light with Job 3:4.

job-3:4:3.summary: The beast's kingdom darkened shares only darkness with Job's curse.

job-3:4:4.summary: Darkness at the crucifixion shares only darkness with Job's curse.

job-3:4:5.summary: The Lord's day “is darkness, not light” echoes “may that day be darkness… no brightness.”

job-3:4:6.summary: God's eyes always on the land contrasts with Job's wish that God not seek out that day.

job-3:5:4.summary: “Darkness and death's shadow” is the same pairing as in Job 3:5.

job-3:5:9.summary: God brings people out of “darkness and death's shadow,” the very pair Job invokes.

job-3:5:1.summary: Job 28:3 pairs “darkness and a shadow of death,” the same terms as 3:5.

job-3:5:2.summary: Walking in “death's shadow” shares the phrase but with trust, unlike Job's curse.

job-3:5:3.summary: The Saints Jeremiah text describes a waterless land without “death's shadow,” losing the link.

job-3:5:5.summary: Those in “darkness… shadow of death” see a great light, sharing Job's pairing.

job-3:5:6.summary: Waiting for light “and there is death's shadow… darkness” echoes Job 3:5 and 3:9.

job-3:5:7.summary: Sinai with “darkness, gloom, tempest” shares darkness and gloom with Job 3:5.

job-3:5:8.summary: Heaven growing dark in judgment loosely matches Job's wish for darkness.

job-3:5:10.summary: A “day of cloud and gloom” shares gloom vocabulary with Job 3:5.

job-3:5:11.summary: The “gates of death” relate to death's realm but lack the darkness pairing.

job-3:5:12.summary: “A shadow lies upon my eyelids” echoes shadow imagery; the Saints text drops “of death.”
job-3:5:12.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-3:5:13.summary: Job 24:17 repeats “shadow of death,” the term Job invokes on his day.

job-3:5:14.summary: “Sitting in darkness… shadow of death” shares Job's pairing, answered by light.

job-3:5:15.summary: “Darkness and death's shadow” is the same pair, here dispelled by divine light.

job-3:5:16.summary: “Death's shadow covered us” matches Job's wish that death's shadow take possession.

job-3:5:17.summary: “A day of darkness and gloom” matches Job's darkness and gloom on the day.

job-3:5:18.summary: Amos turning feasts to mourning lacks the darkness imagery of Job 3:5 in this verse.

job-3:5:19.summary: Sinai's “gloom and darkness and storm” shares gloom and darkness vocabulary.

job-3:5:20.summary: God “turning death's shadow into morning” reverses Job's wish for death's shadow over the day.
job-3:5:20.why: God reverses the darkness Job invokes.

job-3:5:21.summary: The Saints Ezekiel text lacks the cloudy-day imagery, sharing only “day.”

job-3:7:0.summary: Babylon's desolation without inhabitants loosely echoes a joyless, barren night.

job-3:7:1.summary: God stops “the sound of those rejoicing and… glad,” as Job wishes no gladness or joy on that night.

job-3:7:2.summary: No more music or bridal voices in Babylon parallels the absence of joy Job wishes.

job-3:7:3.summary: “The joy of tambourines has ceased” echoes Job's wish that no joy come.

job-3:8:0.summary: The “dragon” God asks about relates to the “great sea creature” Job names.
job-3:8:0.why: Same sea monster motif in Job.

job-3:8:1.summary: God's challenge about the monster prepared for Him loosely relates to subduing the great sea creature.

job-3:8:2.summary: Laments over Josiah depend on the Hebrew mourning sense, absent from Saints Job 3:8.
job-3:8:2.why: Greek text lacks the mourning link.

job-3:8:3.summary: Children's songs and laments have no link to cursing the day in Saints Job 3:8.
job-3:8:3.why: Greek text lacks the mourning link.

job-3:8:4.summary: Mourners at Jairus's house do not relate to cursing the day or the sea creature.
job-3:8:4.why: Greek text lacks the mourning link.

job-3:8:5.summary: Amos's “skilled in wailing” assumes a Hebrew reading not in the Saints Job text.
job-3:8:5.why: Greek text lacks the mourning link.

job-3:8:6.summary: Skilled lamenting women rely on the Hebrew sense; Saints Job speaks of cursers and a sea creature.
job-3:8:6.why: Greek text lacks the mourning link.

job-3:8:7.summary: Fear at the sea creature's turning relates to the great creature Job mentions.

job-3:9:0.summary: The creature's eyes look like “the dawn-bearer,” echoing the “morning star rising” Job wishes unseen.

job-3:9:1.summary: “You will wait for light, and there is death's shadow” matches Job's night waiting and not coming to light.

job-3:9:2.summary: Job waited for good and met evil, loosely like waiting for light that does not come.

job-3:9:3.summary: Waiting for peace and healing but finding none loosely echoes waiting for light in vain.

job-3:10:0.summary: The Lord “shut every womb,” sharing the image of a closed womb Job wishes for.

job-3:10:2.summary: A stillborn child is better off and has more rest, echoing Job's wish the womb had closed.
job-3:10:2.why: Better never to have been born.

job-3:10:3.summary: Job's weariness and bitterness of soul relate to the pain he wishes removed.

job-3:10:4.summary: Job wishes his pains weighed, relating to pain in his eyes.

job-3:10:5.summary: The Lord “opened her womb” shares the womb-opening image Job laments.

job-3:10:6.summary: God's hand heavy on Job's groaning relates loosely to his pain.

job-3:10:7.summary: The Lord “had closed her womb” shares the closed-womb image.

job-3:10:8.summary: Advice to remove anger and evil does not relate to Job's birth lament.

job-3:10:9.summary: Job asks why God brought him from the womb rather than taking him “from the womb to the tomb.”
job-3:10:9.why: Job's recurring wish not to be born.

job-3:11:1.summary: God carrying Israel “from the belly” contrasts with Job's wish to perish from the belly.
job-3:11:1.why: God's care from birth versus Job's lament.

job-3:11:2.summary: Jeremiah laments his mother bore him, paralleling Job's wish to have died at birth.

job-3:11:3.summary: God's care in forming the psalmist in the womb contrasts with Job's wish to have died there.
job-3:11:3.why: Contrast of womb as divine care.

job-3:11:4.summary: Hosea's “childless womb and dry breasts” loosely relates to Job's womb and breasts lament.

job-3:11:5.summary: God drew the psalmist “from the belly” as hope, contrasting with Job's lament.

job-3:11:6.summary: The Saints psalm verse has melting wax, lacking the stillbirth image, so only “not see the sun” is loose.

job-3:11:7.summary: Supported by God “from the womb” contrasts with Job's wish to have died there.

job-3:12:1.summary: Bearing “upon my knees” illustrates the receiving knees Job mentions.

job-3:12:2.summary: Children born on Joseph's thighs illustrates receiving a newborn on one's lap.

job-3:12:3.summary: An infant uncared for at birth contrasts with the knees and breasts that received Job.

job-3:13:0.summary: The wicked “fell asleep in the rest of Hades,” matching Job's death as sleep and rest.

job-3:13:1.summary: No deed or knowledge in Hades loosely relates to the quiet of death Job imagines.

job-3:13:3.summary: Job's “I will depart into the earth… I am no more” relates to his imagined rest in death.

job-3:13:4.summary: Job's statement of inner knowledge has no link to resting in death.

job-3:13:5.summary: Going down to Hades never to return relates to Job's imagined death.

job-3:13:6.summary: Job's land of everlasting darkness describes the death he would have entered.

job-3:13:7.summary: “Hades is my house… my bedding is spread” echoes lying down in death.

job-3:13:8.summary: The stillborn child “has more rest,” echoing Job's wish he would have rested.

job-3:13:9.summary: A man dying comfortable and prosperous does not match Job's imagined rest in death.

job-3:14:0.summary: Job 15:28 speaks of deserted cities and houses; the Greek of Job 3:14 has kings “who exulted in swords,” not rebuilt ruins.
job-3:14:0.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

job-3:14:2.summary: Both picture the powerful brought down in death, with death shepherding people into Hades.

job-3:14:3.summary: Psalm asks who can escape death; Job 3:14 imagines kings lying in death, a general mortality theme.

job-3:14:4.summary: Ezekiel's “people of old” in the depths of the earth loosely parallels joining past kings in death.
job-3:14:4.why: Underworld company of the ancient dead.

job-3:14:5.summary: No authority over the day of death; Job pictures rulers who also died, a general theme.

job-3:14:6.summary: Both mention “counselors” and the earth's rulers, but Job 12:17 is about God humbling them, not death.
job-3:14:6.why: Same class of figures in Job.

job-3:14:7.summary: Solomon “slept with his fathers” illustrates a king in death, only a general example.

job-3:14:8.summary: Isaiah's house-to-house greed has no real link to kings who “exulted in swords.”
job-3:14:8.why: No shared element in the Greek.

job-3:14:9.summary: Rebuilding ancient deserted places assumes the Hebrew “rebuilt ruins,” absent from this Greek reading.
job-3:14:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-3:14:10.summary: Job later says earth is “the house of every mortal,” echoing that even kings end in death.
job-3:14:10.why: Job's recurring view of death as common.

job-3:14:11.summary: Tyre's trade list (truncated) has nothing on kings or counselors in death.

job-3:14:12.summary: Those boasting in wealth and strength perish together, loosely like mighty kings who die.
job-3:14:12.why: Wealth and might cannot redeem from death.

job-3:14:13.summary: David “lay down with his fathers,” a generic instance of a king in death.

job-3:15:0.summary: “Silver and gold” will not rescue on the day of wrath; Job's rulers with gold also died.
job-3:15:0.why: Wealth's futility before death or judgment.

job-3:15:1.summary: Solomon made gold and silver common, an example of rulers rich in gold.

job-3:15:2.summary: Job 22:25 uses silver as an image of refining, unrelated to rulers' hoarded wealth.

job-3:15:3.summary: God “pours dishonor upon rulers,” loosely connecting to rulers brought low.

job-3:15:4.summary: Balaam's “house full of silver and gold” echoes houses filled with silver, in an unrelated context.
job-3:15:4.why: Shared image of a house full of silver.

job-3:15:5.summary: Job 27:16–17 pictures one who gathers silver and gold yet loses it, matching rulers who filled houses with silver.
job-3:15:5.why: Job's theme of hoarded wealth not lasting.

job-3:15:6.summary: Tyre “stored silver like dust and gathered gold,” a similar image of amassed wealth.

job-3:15:7.summary: Land “filled with silver and gold” echoes houses filled with silver.

job-3:16:0.summary: Those who “did not see the sun” parallel infants “who never saw light,” though the psalm lacks the stillbirth image here.

job-3:16:2.summary: Paul calls himself “one untimely born,” the same image as Job's “miscarriage.”
job-3:16:2.why: Paul's self-description echoes this rare image.

job-3:17:0.summary: The dead “rest from their labours,” echoing Job's “those worn out in body rested.”
job-3:17:0.why: Death as rest from toil, transformed in Christ.

job-3:17:1.summary: Descending together to Hades loosely parallels the shared place of the dead in Job 3.

job-3:17:2.summary: Hebrews' “rest” is God's promised rest, only loosely related to rest in death.

job-3:17:3.summary: A “Sabbath rest” for God's people echoes the rest motif only generally.

job-3:17:4.summary: The righteous taken from injustice to burial in peace parallels death as rest from the ungodly.

job-3:17:5.summary: Job wishes to be hidden in Hades until wrath ceases, a related view of death as refuge.
job-3:17:5.why: Job's wish for Hades as shelter.

job-3:17:6.summary: Fear not those who kill the body has no specific link to rest in death in Job 3:17.

job-3:17:7.summary: Fearing God over killers of the body does not connect to the rest of the dead.

job-3:17:8.summary: “Relief” for the afflicted while God repays afflicters loosely parallels rest for the worn out.

job-3:17:9.summary: The psalmist longs to “fly away and rest,” a general longing for rest.

job-3:17:10.summary: Lot tormented by lawless deeds loosely relates to the ungodly kindling anger, with no shared rest motif.

job-3:18:1.summary: God gives rest from harsh slavery and “the taskmaster rested,” paralleling freedom from the tax collector's voice.
job-3:18:1.why: Oppressor silenced, the oppressed at rest.

job-3:18:2.summary: Israel's scribes under Pharaoh's harsh demands illustrate oppressive exactors, loosely like the tax collector (range truncated).

job-3:18:3.summary: Jabin's oppression of Israel has no specific link to the dead not hearing an exactor's voice.

job-3:18:4.summary: Pharaoh's taskmasters imposing quotas are loosely like the oppressive exactor whose voice the dead escape.

job-3:19:0.summary: “Earth is the house of every mortal” matches small and great sharing the same place in death.
job-3:19:0.why: Job's own statement of death's universality.

job-3:19:1.summary: No one has authority over the day of death, a broad parallel to death equalizing all.

job-3:19:2.summary: Dust returning to earth reflects the common end of all people, generally.

job-3:19:3.summary: The human going “to his everlasting home” loosely parallels the place where small and great are.

job-3:19:4.summary: “Rich and poor together” in a psalm about death parallels “small and great are there.”

job-3:19:5.summary: Wise and foolish die and “perish together,” wealth unable to redeem, like small and great together in death.

job-3:19:6.summary: The rich man's glory does not descend with him into Hades; loosely about death erasing rank (truncated).

job-3:19:7.summary: All people die once, a general statement of mortality.

job-3:19:8.summary: Rich man and poor man both die, but their fates differ, unlike Job's leveling picture.

job-3:20:1.summary: Job asks release of his soul and calls his life empty, the same weariness with life as 3:20.

job-3:20:2.summary: Hannah's “anguish of soul” parallels “souls in pain,” in a different situation.

job-3:20:3.summary: Wine given “to those in pain” uses similar wording but a different concern.

job-3:20:4.summary: Job asks to be wounded but not destroyed completely, related only broadly to life in pain.

job-3:20:5.summary: Elihu says God rescues the soul so life may praise Him “in light,” answering Job's question about light and life.

job-3:20:6.summary: Infants “who never saw light” in the same speech contrast with light given to the bitter.

job-3:20:7.summary: The Shunammite's “soul is in pain” echoes “souls in pain” verbally only.

job-3:20:8.summary: “My life will see light” answers Job's complaint that light and life are given to sufferers.

job-3:20:9.summary: “Death is better than a bitter life” matches light given “to those in bitterness” who prefer death.

job-3:21:0.summary: People “will seek death and will certainly not find it,” closely echoing longing for death without obtaining it.

job-3:21:1.summary: Searching “like treasures” is the same simile as digging for death “as for treasures.”

job-3:21:2.summary: Jonah says “It is better for me to die than to live,” a sufferer longing for death.

job-3:21:3.summary: Elijah asks the Lord to take his life, a parallel longing for death.

job-3:21:4.summary: Moses asks God to slay him rather than see misery, longing for death amid suffering.
job-3:21:4.why: Death sought as escape from misery.

job-3:21:6.summary: “O death, how good is your sentence” to the needy, echoing longing for death.
job-3:21:6.why: Wisdom view of death as welcome.

job-3:23:0.summary: “I have been walled in all around” matches God having “shut him in.”
job-3:23:0.why: Job's repeated image of being hemmed in.

job-3:23:2.summary: Isaiah's “way was hidden from God” relies on Hebrew Job's hidden way, absent from this Greek verse.

job-3:23:3.summary: God did “not enclose me” in enemies' hands, the opposite of being shut in.

job-3:23:4.summary: “If He shuts people in, who will open?” echoes God having shut him in.
job-3:23:4.why: Same idea of God's confining power.

job-3:23:5.summary: “I was handed over and did not go out” resembles confinement, loosely.

job-3:23:6.summary: Being encircled by those lying in wait loosely resembles being shut in.

job-3:23:7.summary: God blocking her way with thorns is a related image of divine confinement.

job-3:23:9.summary: The Lord “raised His stronghold against me” parallels God having shut Job in.
job-3:23:9.why: Job attributes his confinement to God.

job-3:24:0.summary: Eating ashes as bread and mixing drink with weeping parallels sighing before food and weeping.

job-3:24:2.summary: “Bread of tears” matches sighing in place of food and weeping.

job-3:24:3.summary: “Roared from the groaning of my heart” parallels sighing, without the food image.

job-3:24:4.summary: A sufferer unable to receive food is loosely like sighing before food.

job-3:24:5.summary: Crying out all day long is a general lament parallel.

job-3:24:6.summary: Crying by day and night to God is a general lament parallel.

job-3:24:7.summary: Job unable to swallow saliva in pain loosely parallels sighing before food.

job-3:24:8.summary: Isaiah's bear and dove traveling together lacks the moaning or sighing in this Greek reading.

job-3:24:9.summary: Job sees “my food as a stench,” the same aversion to food amid grief.

job-3:24:10.summary: “I will cry and call out” is a general lament parallel to weeping.

job-3:25:0.summary: Job's anxious sacrifices “perhaps my sons have conceived evil” may illustrate the fear he had beforehand.

job-3:25:1.summary: Pains returning and hope vanishing loosely parallel feared calamity arriving.

job-3:25:2.summary: “Fear of the Lord gripped me” shares fear wording but a different sense.

job-3:26:0.summary: Frightening dreams deny Job rest, loosely matching “no rest.”

job-3:26:1.summary: “Constraint comes upon him” loosely parallels wrath coming upon Job.

job-3:26:2.summary: Prayer to bring the soul out of distress is a general response to trouble.

job-4:1:0.summary: Job’s opening lament is the speech Eliphaz now answers.

job-4:1:1.summary: “Then Bildad the Shuhite replied” uses the same speech formula.

job-4:1:2.summary: “Eliphaz the Temanite” reappears when God restores him through Job.

job-4:1:5.summary: “Then Job replied” is the same formula for Job’s answer to Eliphaz.

job-4:1:6.summary: Eliphaz is introduced as one of Job’s three friends who came to comfort him.

job-4:2:0.summary: Elihu is “full of words” and must speak; loosely like the force of words.

job-4:2:1.summary: “Cannot keep from speaking” relies on the Hebrew; this verse asks who can endure Job’s words.

job-4:2:2.summary: God holding back fury has no link to Eliphaz’s question.

job-4:2:3.summary: Paul’s grieving letter relies on the Hebrew “be grieved” absent here.
job-4:2:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-4:2:4.summary: Jeremiah unable to hold back God’s word relies on the Hebrew sense absent here.

job-4:2:5.summary: Paul’s sorrowful letter has no specific link to this verse.

job-4:3:1.summary: Peter is told to “strengthen your brothers,” loosely like Job encouraging the weak; the shared idea is general.
job-4:3:1.why: Shows strengthening others as a calling.

job-4:3:2.summary: The Greek-based verse speaks of righteous lips knowing “lofty things,” not of admonishing or strengthening others.
job-4:3:2.why: No real link in this wording.

job-4:3:3.summary: Job speaks of “strength in my mouth,” faintly recalling his former words of encouragement, but the link is indirect.
job-4:3:3.why: Job's own view of his speech.

job-4:3:4.summary: Hebrews calls readers to straighten “drooping hands” and “weakened knees,” the same paired image as Job 4:3–4.
job-4:3:4.why: Same image of strengthening the faint.

job-4:3:5.summary: Moses is told to “strengthen” and “encourage” Joshua; shared vocabulary of encouragement, different setting.

job-4:3:6.summary: Paul urges speech that builds up hearers, a general parallel to Job's encouraging words.
job-4:3:6.why: Speech meant to build others up.

job-4:3:7.summary: An angel strengthening Jesus shares only the idea of strengthening, with no link to Job's admonition of many.

job-4:3:8.summary: A proverb about sweet speech and the wise being called worthless has no specific tie to Job's encouragement.

job-4:3:9.summary: Wise lips “bound to discernment” is a general wisdom saying with no specific connection to strengthening the weak.

job-4:3:10.summary: Abraham commanding his household shares only the idea of instruction, not encouraging the weak.

job-4:3:11.summary: The servant receives “a tongue of instruction” for the right word; the Greek lacks the Hebrew's sustaining of the weary.

job-4:3:12.summary: False prophets “strengthened the lawless person’s hands,” an inverted use of Job's idiom of strengthening hands.

job-4:3:13.summary: Gracious, seasoned speech is a general teaching with no specific link to strengthening weak hands.

job-4:3:14.summary: God turned the king “to strengthen their hands,” the same idiom in an unrelated temple-building context.

job-4:4:0.summary: Wise tongues “heal,” loosely like Job raising the weak with words.

job-4:4:1.summary: Paul's call to “admonish,” “comfort the fainthearted” and “hold fast to the weak” closely mirrors Job's ministry of words.
job-4:4:1.why: New Testament form of the same care.

job-4:4:3.summary: The Lord “raises up” those who fall, as Job “raised up the weak”; the same action attributed to God.
job-4:4:3.why: Job imitated God's support of the falling.

job-4:4:4.summary: Isaiah's “limp hands and paralyzed knees” and “give encouragement” echo Job's strengthening of hands and knees.

job-4:4:5.summary: The shown Greek-based text of Belshazzar's fear lacks the knees image the English label assumes.

job-4:4:6.summary: Paul urges comforting a sorrowing man, a general parallel to encouraging the weak.

job-4:4:7.summary: “Good words” bring “healing,” loosely like Job's words raising the weak.

job-4:4:8.summary: God “comforts the lowly,” a general theme of comfort rather than a specific echo.

job-4:5:0.summary: Job says the Lord’s hand “touched me,” matching Eliphaz's claim that pain has “touched” him.
job-4:5:0.why: Job's own view of the same blow.

job-4:5:1.summary: Paul does “not lose heart” though wasting away, contrasting with Job's agitation; only a general theme.

job-4:5:2.summary: Job's lament that what he feared “came upon me” is what Eliphaz now answers with pain having “come upon you.”
job-4:5:2.why: The speech Eliphaz is responding to.

job-4:5:3.summary: The fragment speaks of a “day of affliction, until he fails,” loosely like collapsing under trouble.

job-4:5:4.summary: The devil asks God to “touch everything he has,” the testing behind the pain that has “touched” Job.
job-4:5:4.why: Reveals the hidden cause of the touch.

job-4:5:5.summary: Hebrews warns against “fainting in your souls,” a general parallel to Job's agitation.

job-4:5:6.summary: Hebrews says not to “faint when reproved,” loosely parallel to Job's distress under suffering.

job-4:5:7.summary: Job laments that mercy has disowned him; it reflects his agitation but shares no specific wording.

job-4:5:8.summary: The devil asks God to “touch his bones and his flesh,” the bodily affliction Eliphaz says has “touched” Job.

job-4:5:9.summary: Paul does “not lose heart,” only a general contrast with Job's agitation.

job-4:6:0.summary: The Lord over “all your ways” supports the foot; loosely related to trusting God in one's way.

job-4:6:1.summary: “In the fear of the Lord is hope” pairs “fear” and “hope” as Eliphaz does of Job's piety.
job-4:6:1.why: Fear of God as ground of hope.

job-4:6:2.summary: Job is introduced as “blameless” and “God-fearing,” the fear and innocence of way Eliphaz names.

job-4:6:3.summary: Job asks “where … is my hope,” sharing the word “hope” but answering a later context.

job-4:6:4.summary: Job claims he “guarded His ways,” loosely related to the innocence of his way.

job-4:6:5.summary: Job affirms “nothing unjust in my hands” and pure prayer, a general claim of innocence.

job-4:6:6.summary: The Greek-based text speaks of pleading before God, lacking the hope the English label assumes.

job-4:6:7.summary: Hezekiah appeals to having walked “in truth” before God, a general parallel to innocence of way.

job-4:6:8.summary: Job recounts his righteous deeds, background to his innocence but not a specific echo.

job-4:6:9.summary: Setting hope on grace at Christ's revelation shares only the word “hope.”

job-4:6:10.summary: God calls Job “blameless” and “God-fearing,” and the devil questions his piety; the fear Eliphaz names.

job-4:6:12.summary: Peter urges conduct “in fear,” a general link to godly fear.

job-4:6:13.summary: Job's oath of innocence (shown portion) says “the Lord knows my innocence” and God sees “my way.”
job-4:6:13.why: Job's fullest defense of his way.

job-4:7:0.summary: The psalmist has “not seen a righteous person abandoned,” the same retribution claim as Eliphaz.
job-4:7:0.why: Same doctrine of the righteous preserved.

job-4:7:1.summary: The Lord rescues the godly from trial; a general theme of protection.

job-4:7:2.summary: Elihu says God will not take His eyes from the righteous, a similar but general doctrine.

job-4:7:3.summary: Islanders assume “Justice” punished Paul, the same popular retribution logic Eliphaz uses.

job-4:7:4.summary: Bildad says the Lord “will certainly not reject the innocent,” the same argument Eliphaz makes.

job-4:7:5.summary: Ecclesiastes has seen “a righteous person perishing in his righteousness,” directly contradicting Eliphaz's claim.

job-4:7:6.summary: Job says “the righteous are mocked,” disputing retribution, though the Greek lacks the Hebrew's destroyed blameless.
