job-4:7:7.summary: “One event comes to the righteous and the ungodly” contradicts Eliphaz's claim that the pure never perish.

job-4:8:0.summary: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” states Eliphaz's sowing-and-reaping principle.
job-4:8:0.why: Same principle in the New Testament.

job-4:8:2.summary: Israel “sowed wind-blasted things” and their overthrow receives them; same sowing-to-ruin image.

job-4:8:3.summary: Eliphaz again says the wicked “conceive pains,” matching his claim that they reap “pains.”

job-4:8:4.summary: Sowing and reaping is applied to generosity, sharing the image but not the moral warning.

job-4:8:5.summary: Hosea contrasts sowing righteousness with reaping “injustices,” the same agricultural retribution image.

job-4:8:6.summary: “Your ways … have done these things to you” expresses self-caused ruin in general terms.

job-4:8:7.summary: The wicked “conceived trouble” and it returns “upon his head,” the same self-recoiling evil.

job-4:8:8.summary: “Do not sow in the furrows of injustice” and you will not “reap them” echoes plowing and reaping evil.

job-4:9:0.summary: Eliphaz wishes “wind” to wither the wicked's shoot, close to but not the same as God's breath.

job-4:9:1.summary: “With breath through his lips he will slay the ungodly” parallels the wicked perishing by God's breath.

job-4:9:2.summary: The Lord's “wrath” like burning sulfur; the Greek lacks the breath image of the Hebrew.

job-4:9:4.summary: “The blast of the spirit of Thine anger” closely matches “the breath of His anger.”

job-4:9:5.summary: Christ wages war with “the sword of My mouth,” a related but different judgment image.

job-4:9:6.summary: God sent forth His wind and enemies sank, a related image of destruction by divine wind.

job-4:9:7.summary: “By the breath of Thy wrath” matches “by the breath of His anger” as an agent of divine action.
job-4:9:7.why: Same expression in the Song of the Sea.

job-4:9:8.summary: A great wind killed Job's children; Eliphaz's words may unwittingly recall it, but no verbal link.

job-4:9:9.summary: God's challenge to humble the proud shares only the general theme of the wicked's end.

job-4:9:10.summary: God puts “a spirit” in Sennacherib leading to his death; only loosely related.

job-4:10:0.summary: “The Lord crushed the lions’ grinders” parallels the lion's strength being extinguished as image of the wicked.
job-4:10:0.why: Same lion image of the wicked.

job-4:10:1.summary: Enemies as young lions with weapon teeth; lion imagery for the wicked, but no defeat stated.

job-4:10:2.summary: Evil offspring with sword-teeth; the Greek source mentions no teeth, so the link is lost.

job-4:10:3.summary: God crushes “sinners’ teeth”; the Greek source speaks of extinguished strength, not teeth.

job-4:10:4.summary: Job “crushed the molars of unjust people”; related image of breaking the wicked's power.

job-4:10:5.summary: A wish that some perish in war shares no specific link to the lion imagery.

job-4:11:0.summary: The Greek reads “rich people became poor and hungry,” losing the Hebrew lions but keeping hunger.

job-4:11:1.summary: A lion destroying nations shares only lion imagery.

job-4:11:2.summary: Job's children died together; scattered lion cubs may obliquely evoke this, but only by inference.

job-4:11:3.summary: Paul rescued from “a lion’s mouth” shares only the word lion.

job-4:11:5.summary: The Lord roaring like a lion has no link to the perishing ant-lion and cubs.

job-4:11:6.summary: Israel resting like a “lion cub” shares only the animal image.

job-4:11:7.summary: The wicked's sons “will beg” and die, loosely like starving, scattered cubs.

job-4:11:8.summary: Bildad implies Job's sons perished for sin, related to the image of lost cubs.

job-4:11:9.summary: Israel rising “like a lion cub” is unrelated lion imagery.

job-4:11:10.summary: Judah as “a lion’s cub” is an unrelated blessing.

job-4:11:11.summary: An enemy seizing the soul like a lion has no link to perishing lions.

job-4:12:0.summary: Hearing “a mere drop of speech concerning Him” loosely parallels the ear receiving things from God.

job-4:12:1.summary: “God spoke once; these two things I heard” shares the idea of hearing divine speech.

job-4:12:2.summary: Knowing “in part” is only a general parallel to partial revelation.

job-4:13:0.summary: Elihu speaks of nighttime visions when “terrible fear falls upon people,” nearly Eliphaz's wording.

job-4:13:1.summary: God casts deep sleep on Adam; the Greek source has no sleep, only nocturnal terror.

job-4:13:2.summary: God comes to Balaam at night, a general parallel of nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:3.summary: God comes to Abimelech “by night” in sleep, general nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:4.summary: Daniel falls face down at a vision, a general parallel to overwhelming revelation.

job-4:13:5.summary: Daniel falls asleep face down during a vision, loosely like Eliphaz's terror.

job-4:13:6.summary: Jacob's dream of the ladder shares only nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:7.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's dream made him apprehensive and “fear fell upon me,” matching “fear falling upon people.”

job-4:13:8.summary: “A great dark fear fell upon” Abram in a trance, close to Eliphaz's falling fear.

job-4:13:9.summary: A vision upon a bed revealing mysteries; general night revelation.

job-4:13:10.summary: God speaks to Laban “in a dream by night,” general nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:11.summary: God speaks “in a vision of the night,” general nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:12.summary: God speaks to prophets in visions and “in sleep,” a general principle.

job-4:13:13.summary: A mystery revealed “in a vision that very night,” general nocturnal revelation.

job-4:13:14.summary: A person “troubled by his heart’s vision” in sleep, loosely like night terrors.

job-4:14:0.summary: John falls as dead at a vision; general fear at revelation.

job-4:14:1.summary: Elihu mentions “his bones” growing numb, a loose bodily parallel.

job-4:14:2.summary: Job says God frightens him “with dreams” and “visions,” generally like Eliphaz's terrifying vision.

job-4:14:3.summary: Daniel “stood trembling” at an angelic message, matching the trembling at a night apparition.

job-4:14:4.summary: Flesh nailed down by “fear of Thee,” a general bodily fear of God.

job-4:14:6.summary: Isaiah's “Woe is me” at a vision is a general parallel of dread.

job-4:14:7.summary: Mary “greatly troubled” at an angel's greeting; general parallel.

job-4:14:8.summary: Zechariah troubled and “fear fell upon him” at an angel; similar but general.

job-4:15:0.summary: Angels as “spirits” may illuminate the “spirit” passing Eliphaz, but the link is inferential.

job-4:15:1.summary: Belshazzar's “fears and apprehensions” at the supernatural writing; general terror.

job-4:15:2.summary: God makes His angels “winds,” possibly explaining the spirit/breeze, but only inferentially.

job-4:15:3.summary: Disciples are terrified thinking they see “a spirit,” with “flesh” mentioned, like Eliphaz's shuddering at a spirit.

job-4:15:4.summary: People troubled and changing face in terror; general fear, no spirit.

job-4:15:5.summary: Isaiah's body seized by terror at a vision; general bodily dread.

job-4:15:6.summary: Angels as “ministering spirits” shares only the word spirit.

job-4:15:7.summary: Disciples cry in fear at an “apparition,” a general parallel of terror at a supposed spirit.

job-4:16:0.summary: Elijah hears “the sound of a gentle breeze” where the Lord is, like Eliphaz's “breeze and a voice.”

job-4:17:0.summary: Job asks “how can a mortal be righteous before the Lord?”, echoing the spirit's question.
job-4:17:0.why: Job takes up the same question.

job-4:17:1.summary: Bildad asks “how will a mortal be righteous before the Lord?”, repeating the same question.

job-4:17:2.summary: “No righteous person on earth who will … not sin” states the same human impurity.

job-4:17:4.summary: Praise of God's unsearchable wisdom does not address human purity before God.

job-4:17:5.summary: The deep human heart is a general theme of human unreliability.

job-4:17:6.summary: Paul contrasts God's truth with human lying, a general theme of divine versus human righteousness.

job-4:17:7.summary: “The Lord is righteous in all His ways” is a general statement of divine righteousness.

job-4:17:8.summary: “Where is God who made me” relies on the Hebrew maker link absent from the Greek source.

job-4:17:9.summary: God says He acts so Job may be “shown righteous,” loosely answering the purity question.

job-4:17:10.summary: “What mortal can be blameless?” repeats the spirit's question nearly verbatim, again from Eliphaz.

job-4:17:11.summary: Heavenly “Holy, holy, holy” praise does not address human purity before God.

job-4:17:12.summary: Evil coming from the human heart is a general statement of human impurity.

job-4:17:13.summary: Storing up wrath by a hard heart does not address whether a mortal is pure before God.

job-4:17:14.summary: Jeremiah affirms “Thou art righteous, Lord” while disputing with God; general divine-human justice theme.

job-4:17:15.summary: “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” shares the theme of human standing before God.

job-4:17:16.summary: Elihu asks who can say “I am righteous before the Lord,” the same question of mortal righteousness.

job-4:17:17.summary: Job's washing with snow yet being dipped in filth shows human inability to be pure, generally.

job-4:17:18.summary: Bildad asks whether the Lord does wrong in judging; related to divine justice, not human purity.

job-4:17:19.summary: “Who will be clean from filth? No one” states the same impossibility of human purity.

job-4:17:20.summary: Abraham appeals to the Judge of all to do justice; general theme of divine justice.

job-4:18:0.summary: God “did not spare angels when they sinned,” illustrating faults found in His angels.

job-4:18:2.summary: Angels who “abandoned their proper dwelling” are kept for judgment, showing angelic fallibility.

job-4:18:4.summary: Angels “doing His word” and will presents faithful angels, a contrast rather than parallel.

job-4:18:5.summary: God makes His angels and ministers winds and fire; it names angels and ministers but not their faults.

job-4:18:6.summary: Seraphim cover their faces before the Holy One, loosely suggesting even angels fall short of His holiness.

job-4:19:0.summary: Job says God molded him “as clay” and returns him to earth, the same clay-made frailty.

job-4:19:2.summary: “Earth you are, and unto earth you shall return” grounds the image of humans made from earth.

job-4:19:3.summary: “Fashioned from clay … from the same material” closely echoes “of the same clay.”

job-4:19:4.summary: God melts a person's soul “like a spider” (Hebrew moth); fragile human image, different creature in Greek.

job-4:19:5.summary: Abraham calls himself “earth and ashes,” a general image of human lowliness.

job-4:19:6.summary: “Our earthly house, this tent” matches the image of the body as a house of clay.

job-4:19:7.summary: “This treasure in clay jars” uses the same clay image for frail human bodies.

job-4:19:8.summary: “Your body will be clay” shares the image of the human body as clay.

job-4:19:9.summary: A “moth-eaten garment” shares the moth image, though here the moth destroys rather than is crushed.

job-4:19:10.summary: The wicked “seized before their time” with failing foundations; the Greek lacks the dust foundation.

job-4:19:11.summary: Man falls like a flower and flees like a shadow, a general image of transience.

job-4:19:12.summary: Life passes like grass from morning to evening, a general transience image.

job-4:19:13.summary: “The dust returns to the earth” is a general image of mortal origin and end.

job-4:19:14.summary: Man's days are like grass and he will not exist, general human frailty.

job-4:19:15.summary: “All flesh is like grass” is a general statement of human frailty.

job-4:19:16.summary: Man “will return to his earth,” a general mortality image.

job-4:19:17.summary: “Why are earth and ashes proud?” shares the theme of earthy human frailty.

job-4:20:0.summary: The wicked “will perish utterly” and be gone; general theme of sudden end.

job-4:20:1.summary: Hezekiah's life cut off “until morning” and “from day to night” echoes perishing “from morning until evening.”

job-4:20:2.summary: Sinners spring up like grass to be “utterly destroyed,” a general theme.

job-4:20:3.summary: Nations fighting and God terrifying them with affliction has no specific link to mortals perishing daily.

job-4:20:4.summary: Job will travel a way of no return; general mortality.

job-4:20:5.summary: The name of the impious “is extinguished,” a general theme of vanishing.

job-4:20:6.summary: Man falls like a flower and will not remain; general transience.

job-4:20:7.summary: The wicked's memorial perishes from the earth; general disappearance theme.

job-4:20:8.summary: “He was gone … his place could not be found,” a general image of vanishing.

job-4:20:9.summary: “Before I depart and no longer exist” shares the idea of being no more.

job-4:20:11.summary: God thrusts man away and he departs; a general mortality theme.

job-4:20:12.summary: The Greek speaks of a person living again after death, not of perishing helplessly.

job-4:20:13.summary: Jehoram departing “without praise” relies on the Hebrew's unnoticed death, absent from the Greek source.

job-4:21:0.summary: God does not preserve the ungodly who refuse to know Him, loosely like perishing without wisdom.

job-4:21:1.summary: The rich man and Lazarus dying shares only general mortality.

job-4:21:2.summary: God disciplines and melts a person's soul; general human frailty.

job-4:21:3.summary: The ungodly's dwelling “will be no more”; general ruin, the Greek source lacks the tent image.

job-4:21:4.summary: Grass and flower dry up and the rich “wither” and perish, matching “they withered; they perished.”

job-4:21:6.summary: The fate of those “who do not know the Lord” loosely parallels perishing without wisdom.

job-4:21:7.summary: Onlookers marveling at the fallen king of Babylon has no specific link.

job-4:21:8.summary: Human existence “as nothing” before God; general frailty.

job-4:21:9.summary: The “Fool” dies suddenly, loosely parallel to perishing for lack of wisdom.

job-4:21:10.summary: A person who “did not understand” is like beasts; related to dying without wisdom.

job-4:21:11.summary: Man's spirit goes out and “reasonings will perish”; general mortality.

job-4:21:12.summary: The foolish are placed in Hades like sheep; general fate of the unwise.

job-4:21:5.summary: Isaiah 2:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-4:21:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-4:21:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-5:1:1.summary: Eliphaz again appeals to superior knowledge, only loosely related to his challenge here.

job-5:1:3.summary: God challenges idols to answer and announce; a loose parallel to Eliphaz’s “whether anyone will answer you.”
job-5:1:3.why: Challenge to find an answering power.

job-5:1:4.summary: God summoning the islands to judgment has no specific link to calling on holy angels.

job-5:1:5.summary: The “cloud of witnesses” are human examples, not the holy angels named here.

job-5:1:6.summary: Paul’s greeting to “saints” relies on a Hebrew “holy ones” link; the Greek verse names holy angels.
job-5:1:6.why: Link depends on wording absent here.
job-5:1:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-5:1:7.summary: The psalm’s “holy ones… in His land” are people, while this Greek verse speaks of holy angels.
job-5:1:7.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-5:1:8.summary: Aaron as “the Lord’s holy one” has no real link to holy angels here.

job-5:1:9.summary: Deuteronomy describes angels at God’s right hand; a general link to “holy angels.”

job-5:2:0.summary: “Anger will rest in the bosom of fools,” closely matching “anger kills a fool.”
job-5:2:0.why: Same wisdom about anger and folly.

job-5:2:1.summary: Ephraim as a senseless dove shares only the idea of folly; no real link.

job-5:2:2.summary: The fool denies God; only a general fool motif.

job-5:2:3.summary: Rachel’s envy leads her to say “I shall die,” loosely like jealousy bringing death.

job-5:2:4.summary: Saul’s jealousy of David is a general illustration of destructive jealousy.

job-5:2:5.summary: People humbled for lawless deeds; only a general link to folly bringing ruin.

job-5:2:6.summary: Paul speaks of God’s wrath on the disobedient, not anger destroying the fool himself.

job-5:2:7.summary: “A fool announces his anger,” sharing the fool-and-anger pairing.
job-5:2:7.why: Same wisdom about anger and folly.

job-5:2:8.summary: A warning to the lawless not to raise a horn has no specific link to anger killing fools.

job-5:2:9.summary: Bildad says “Wrath has dealt with you,” loosely echoing anger’s destructive effect.

job-5:2:10.summary: The senseless man does not understand; only a general fool motif.

job-5:2:11.summary: The senseless became ungodly and liable to reproof; a general fool motif.

job-5:2:12.summary: Deceivers taking captive weak women has no specific link to anger and jealousy.

job-5:2:13.summary: Jonah is “grieved, even to death” over the gourd; the Greek lacks anger, so only a loose link.

job-5:2:14.summary: Wisdom’s call to the innocent has no specific link to anger killing fools.

job-5:3:0.summary: The lawless are lifted up then made “desolate suddenly,” like fools taking root and immediately devoured.
job-5:3:0.why: Sudden ruin of the prospering wicked.

job-5:3:1.summary: Sinners “spring up like grass” only to be destroyed, matching fools taking root then being devoured.

job-5:3:2.summary: Job asks what hope the ungodly have; only a general theme of their ruin.

job-5:3:3.summary: A prayer that the enemies’ homestead become deserted; loosely like the fool’s life being devoured.

job-5:3:4.summary: The psalmist envies the prosperous lawless; covers only the flourishing, not the sudden ruin.

job-5:3:5.summary: Jeremiah says the wicked “took root” and prospered, then asks for their slaughter, as Eliphaz describes fools.
job-5:3:5.why: Same image of the wicked taking root.

job-5:3:6.summary: Job wishes the portion of the wicked be cursed; a general parallel.

job-5:3:7.summary: Peter quotes a curse that Judas’s dwelling be deserted; only a loose link.

job-5:3:9.summary: Deuteronomy’s list of curses (truncated) shares no specific element with this verse.

job-5:4:0.summary: Blessed sons are not shamed at the gate, contrasting the fool’s sons battered at doors.

job-5:4:1.summary: “Salvation is far from sinners,” closely matching “may their sons be far from deliverance.”
job-5:4:1.why: Same idea of deliverance far off.

job-5:4:2.summary: Bildad says the wicked man’s roots dry up and his house is not preserved, like the fool’s sons here.
job-5:4:2.why: Friends’ shared doctrine of the wicked’s ruin.

job-5:4:4.summary: Job asks “who is there to rescue,” sharing the phrase of no rescuer.

job-5:4:5.summary: Bildad hints Job’s sons died for sin; Eliphaz likewise wishes ruin on the fool’s sons.
job-5:4:5.why: Friends’ veiled accusation about Job’s children.

job-5:4:6.summary: “With no one to redeem or save” echoes “with no one to rescue them.”

job-5:4:7.summary: The poor are turned aside “at the gates”; only a general link to oppression at doors.

job-5:4:8.summary: The psalm curses the wicked man’s sons with ruin and no helper, closely like Eliphaz’s words.
job-5:4:8.why: Parallel curse on the wicked’s children.

job-5:4:9.summary: God repays fathers’ sins on children; a general basis for the children suffering.

job-5:4:10.summary: Jesus denies that disaster victims were worse sinners, countering the friends’ logic.

job-5:4:11.summary: Eliphaz’s lion cubs abandoning one another loosely parallel the wicked’s offspring scattered.

job-5:4:12.summary: Job’s children died when the house fell; Eliphaz’s words about fools’ sons may implicitly allude to this.

job-5:5:0.summary: Enemies swallowing Jerusalem has no specific link to the righteous eating what fools gathered.

job-5:5:1.summary: Foreigners devour the harvest, loosely like others eating what the fool gathered.

job-5:5:2.summary: Babylon forced to disgorge what she swallowed has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:5:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar devouring Jerusalem has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:5:4.summary: A foreign nation consumes the yield of your land, loosely like others eating what was gathered.

job-5:5:5.summary: Raiders carry off Job’s camels; a loose link to the fool losing his goods.

job-5:5:6.summary: Gideon hides his threshing from Midian; only a loose harvest-loss link.

job-5:5:7.summary: Manasseh’s captivity to Babylon has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:5:8.summary: Midian ruins Israel’s produce; a loose link to losing what was gathered.

job-5:5:9.summary: Bildad’s traps and the “thirsty” rely on Hebrew Job 5:5 wording absent from this Greek verse.
job-5:5:9.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-5:5:10.summary: Zophar’s warning that the wicked will be examined has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:5:11.summary: An invader consumes the produce of the land; a loose parallel to others eating what was gathered.

job-5:5:12.summary: God promises enemies will no longer eat Israel’s grain, reversing the loss described here.

job-5:5:13.summary: Zophar says unjustly “gathered” wealth will be vomited up and taken, like the fool losing what he gathered.
job-5:5:13.why: Friends’ shared doctrine on the wicked’s gains.

job-5:5:14.summary: Raiders carry off Job’s oxen; a loose link to the fool losing his goods.

job-5:5:15.summary: God’s praise of Job’s innocence shares no specific element with this verse.

job-5:5:16.summary: The Lord destroying Judah’s strongholds has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:6:0.summary: God says He “create[s] calamities,” loosely supporting Eliphaz’s point that pain does not just sprout from the earth.
job-5:6:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-5:6:1.summary: The Philistines ask whether harm came from God or “by chance,” loosely related to trouble’s source.

job-5:6:2.summary: Elihu on God giving quiet or hiding His face has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:6:3.summary: Failing under God’s anger shares no specific element with trouble not sprouting from earth.

job-5:6:4.summary: Amos asks whether calamity comes that the Lord has not done; a general link on trouble’s source.

job-5:6:5.summary: A “root of bitterness” growing up uses a sprouting image for trouble, loosely like pain sprouting.
job-5:6:5.why: Trouble pictured as a growing plant.

job-5:6:6.summary: Judgment springs up “like wild grass”; a loose sprouting image for trouble.
job-5:6:6.why: Trouble pictured as a growing plant.

job-5:6:7.summary: “Calamities and good come from the mouth of the Most High”; loosely related to trouble’s source.

job-5:6:8.summary: Enemies boasting the Lord has not acted has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:7:0.summary: “A mortal born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath” matches “a human being is born to toil.”
job-5:7:0.why: Same view of human life as trouble.

job-5:7:2.summary: Ecclesiastes describes man from his mother’s womb toiling in darkness and wrath, like humans born to toil.
job-5:7:2.why: Toil as human lot from birth.

job-5:7:3.summary: Temptation “common to humanity” is only a general link to universal toil.
job-5:7:3.why: Trouble is the common human lot.

job-5:7:4.summary: Our days fail under God’s anger; a general theme of human frailty.

job-5:7:5.summary: “All words are wearisome” is only loosely related to human toil.

job-5:7:6.summary: Ecclesiastes asks what comes to a person “from all his toil,” sharing the theme of human toil.

job-5:7:7.summary: A “heavy yoke” lies on Adam’s sons from the womb, closely like humans born to toil.
job-5:7:7.why: Toil as human lot from birth.

job-5:8:0.summary: God says “Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you,” matching Eliphaz’s counsel to call on the Lord.

job-5:8:1.summary: Eliphaz later urges Job to endure for good fruit; a general link to his counsel here.

job-5:8:2.summary: “Reveal your way to the Lord; hope in Him” is a general parallel to entrusting oneself to God.

job-5:8:3.summary: Afflicted Manasseh sought the Lord and was heard; a general illustration of calling on God.

job-5:8:4.summary: Sufferers “entrust their souls to a faithful Creator”; a general parallel.
job-5:8:4.why: Entrusting oneself to God in suffering.

job-5:8:5.summary: Jesus “entrusted His cause” to God; the Greek verse speaks of calling on the Lord, so the link is loose.

job-5:8:6.summary: Paul trusts God to guard his deposit in suffering; only a general link.

job-5:8:7.summary: Eliphaz later again tells Job “when you pray to Him, He will hear you,” repeating this counsel.

job-5:8:8.summary: Bildad likewise urges Job to “rise early to the Lord Almighty in supplication.”

job-5:8:9.summary: Jacob prays for deliverance in fear (shown text truncated); a general example of entreating God.

job-5:8:10.summary: The psalmist cried to the Lord in the day of affliction; a general parallel.

job-5:8:11.summary: Jonah cries to the Lord in affliction (shown text truncated); a general example.

job-5:9:0.summary: God’s wonders “multiplied beyond number,” matching “extraordinary things beyond numbering.”

job-5:9:2.summary: “Thou art great and dost wondrous things,” matching God who does great and extraordinary things.

job-5:9:3.summary: God “who alone does wonders,” paralleling the praise of His extraordinary deeds.

job-5:9:4.summary: Zophar asks whether one can find a trace of the Almighty’s works, echoing their unsearchable nature.

job-5:9:5.summary: Elihu says God “did great things that we did not know,” close to “great and unsearchable things.”
job-5:9:5.why: Same praise of God’s unknowable deeds.

job-5:9:6.summary: Job lists God’s mighty works in creation (shown text truncated), illustrating His great deeds.

job-5:9:7.summary: God’s “understanding cannot be discovered,” matching His unsearchable deeds.

job-5:9:8.summary: Paul exclaims how “unsearchable His judgments” are, echoing “unsearchable things.”

job-5:9:9.summary: God’s thoughts multiply “beyond the sand”; a loose link to things beyond numbering.

job-5:9:10.summary: Job finally confesses “great and wonderful things I did not understand,” echoing Eliphaz’s words here.
job-5:9:10.why: Job later affirms the same truth.

job-5:10:0.summary: God gives “rains from heaven” as witness to His goodness, as here He gives rain upon the earth.
job-5:10:0.why: Rain as evidence of God’s care.

job-5:10:1.summary: The Lord “gives us early and late rain,” matching God “who gives rain upon the earth.”

job-5:10:2.summary: God “prepares rain for the earth,” closely matching this verse.

job-5:10:3.summary: God visits the earth and waters its furrows, a parallel picture of God watering the land.

job-5:10:4.summary: Only God, not idols, brings rain, affirming that rain is His work.

job-5:10:5.summary: God asks who sends rain on uninhabited land and is “father of rain,” echoing God’s gift of rain.

job-5:10:6.summary: God “counted rain” in ordering creation, affirming His control of rain.

job-5:10:7.summary: God brings clouds and makes lightning for rain, paralleling Him sending water on the earth.

job-5:10:8.summary: God withholds or gives rain city by city, showing rain is in His control.

job-5:10:9.summary: Elihu says God shades clouds over mortals; only a loose weather link.

job-5:11:0.summary: God “raises the poor from the ground,” matching God who raises the lowly to a height.

job-5:11:1.summary: God “helped the poor out of poverty,” paralleling raising the lowly.

job-5:11:2.summary: Jesus promises the hungry will be filled; a general theme of reversal.

job-5:11:4.summary: God “raised up the lowly,” matching “raises the lowly to a height.”

job-5:11:5.summary: “Humble yourselves… and He will exalt you,” matching God raising the lowly.

job-5:11:6.summary: The Lord “raises a low tree,” an image of God exalting the lowly.

job-5:11:7.summary: God rescues the one who hoped in Him; a general deliverance theme.

job-5:11:8.summary: Everlasting arms shelter God’s people; a general protection theme.

job-5:11:9.summary: “Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation,” matching God raising the lowly.

job-5:11:10.summary: God will restore after suffering; a general restoration theme.

job-5:11:11.summary: New birth through resurrection loosely echoes God rousing “those who have perished.”

job-5:11:12.summary: The Lord looked on the poor and “raised him from his low estate,” matching this verse.

job-5:12:0.summary: Enemies “devised a counsel they will certainly be unable to establish,” like God frustrating schemers’ counsels.

job-5:12:2.summary: “Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter,” matching God changing the counsels of the unscrupulous.

job-5:12:3.summary: “There is no counsel with the impious,” affirming wicked counsel fails.

job-5:12:4.summary: Sinners’ arms will be shattered; loosely like their hands doing nothing.

job-5:12:5.summary: God destroys Assyria’s army; a general example of thwarting enemies.

job-5:12:6.summary: God rescues Peter from Herod’s expectation; a general example of foiled plans.

job-5:12:7.summary: “God had scattered their counsel,” a concrete instance of this verse.

job-5:12:8.summary: God leads counselors away captive and confuses judges, matching Eliphaz’s point.

job-5:12:9.summary: A conspiracy to kill Paul is foiled (shown text truncated); a general illustration.

job-5:12:10.summary: God says “I will scatter their counsel” of Egypt, paralleling this verse.

job-5:13:1.summary: The sinner is “caught in the works of his own hands,” like the wise caught in their own cunning.
job-5:13:1.why: The schemer trapped by his own scheme.

job-5:13:2.summary: He falls into the pit he dug, illustrating schemers caught by their own devices.
job-5:13:2.why: The schemer trapped by his own scheme.

job-5:13:3.summary: Paul cites God destroying “the wisdom of the wise,” the same theme; Paul quotes this Job verse nearby.

job-5:13:4.summary: God “scattered the proud in the thought of their heart,” matching confusion of devious counsel.

job-5:13:5.summary: Haman’s evils against the Jews came upon him, a vivid example of the devious caught.

job-5:13:6.summary: The snare they hid catches them, like the wise caught in their understanding.
job-5:13:6.why: The schemer trapped by his own scheme.

job-5:13:7.summary: “With a twisted one Thou wilt twist,” matching God’s confounding of the devious.

job-5:13:8.summary: Haman hung on the tree he prepared for Mordecai, an example of the schemer caught.

job-5:13:9.summary: David prays “scatter Ahithophel’s counsel,” a concrete case of God confounding wise counsel.

job-5:13:10.summary: The lawless do not sit in council with the righteous; only a loose counsel link.

job-5:13:11.summary: Haman’s plot to hang Mordecai turns to honoring Mordecai (shown text truncated), illustrating schemes reversed.

job-5:13:12.summary: Ahithophel’s counsel was not followed and he hanged himself, illustrating wise counsel confounded.

job-5:13:13.summary: David sends Hushai to “scatter Ahithophel’s counsel,” a concrete case of devious counsel confused.

job-5:14:0.summary: “May they grope in darkness and not light,” closely matching groping at noon as at night.

job-5:14:2.summary: They “grope” and “fall at noon as at midnight,” closely matching this verse.

job-5:14:3.summary: The ways of the ungodly are dark and they stumble, like schemers meeting darkness by day.

job-5:14:4.summary: The sun sets at midday and light grows dark in daytime, matching darkness meeting them by day.

job-5:15:1.summary: The Lord acts for “the poor person’s judgment,” paralleling the powerless escaping the ruler.

job-5:15:2.summary: God stands at a poor person’s right hand to save from pursuers, like the powerless escaping.

job-5:15:3.summary: The king saves the needy and humbles the false accuser, matching this verse.

job-5:15:4.summary: The lion’s strength extinguished loosely parallels the powerful perishing.

job-5:15:5.summary: God helps the poor out of poverty; a general parallel.

job-5:15:6.summary: The Lord hears the needy’s desire; a general parallel.

job-5:15:7.summary: The poor are left to God who helps the orphan; a general parallel.

job-5:15:8.summary: He “rescued a poor person from a powerful man’s hand,” closely matching escape from a ruler’s hand.

job-5:16:1.summary: “The mouth of those speaking unjust things was stopped,” closely matching this verse.

job-5:16:2.summary: God raises the needy and seats them with rulers, matching hope for the powerless.

job-5:16:3.summary: The humble will be saved through the Lord; a general parallel.

job-5:16:4.summary: “Every mouth may be stopped” before God, echoing the stopped mouth of the unjust.

job-5:16:5.summary: “The endurance of the needy will not perish,” matching hope for the powerless.

job-5:16:6.summary: The Greek “prisoners of the gathering” lacks the Hebrew “hope” that the label assumes.
job-5:16:6.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-5:16:7.summary: Not even a dog growls with its tongue against Israel; loosely like the unjust mouth being stopped.

job-5:17:0.summary: “Blessed is the man who endures a trial,” paralleling the happiness of one the Lord reproves.

job-5:17:1.summary: “Happy the person Thou disciplinest, Lord,” closely matching “happy is the person whom the Lord reproved.”

job-5:17:3.summary: Christ says “As many as I love, I reprove and discipline,” the same view of God’s reproof.
job-5:17:3.why: Reproof as a sign of love.

job-5:17:4.summary: James calls those who endured “blessed” and cites Job, matching Eliphaz’s beatitude on Job’s suffering.
job-5:17:4.why: Job as model of blessed endurance.

job-5:17:5.summary: Hebrews urges “do not make light of the Lord’s discipline… when reproved,” the same counsel (shown text truncated).

job-5:17:6.summary: Ephraim says “Thou didst discipline me” and returns; a general theme of accepting discipline.

job-5:18:0.summary: The Lord “will strike and dress our wounds,” matching “He struck, and His hands healed.”

job-5:18:2.summary: The Lord heals His people’s fracture and the pain of their wound, matching God restoring after pain.
job-5:18:2.why: God heals the wounds He allows.

job-5:18:3.summary: God “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their fractures,” paralleling His healing hands.

job-5:18:4.summary: “The Lord puts to death and gives life,” the same pattern of God bringing low and restoring.
job-5:18:4.why: God brings down and raises up.

job-5:19:1.summary: God provides a way out of temptation; a general theme of deliverance in trials.

job-5:19:2.summary: God rescues from the trap and evils will not come near (shown text truncated), like “no evil will touch you.”

job-5:19:3.summary: “The righteous will fall seven times and rise,” using the same sevenfold pattern of deliverance.

job-5:19:4.summary: “The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial,” matching God’s repeated rescue from distress.

job-5:19:5.summary: Paul’s affliction beyond strength is only a general link to distress.

job-5:20:1.summary: God says “redeem them from death,” matching “He will rescue you from death.”

job-5:20:2.summary: God sent Joseph to preserve a remnant through famine, an example of rescue in famine.

job-5:20:3.summary: “In days of famine they will be filled,” matching rescue in famine.

job-5:20:4.summary: “The Lord will not starve a righteous life,” paralleling rescue from death in famine.

job-5:20:5.summary: Ravens feed Elijah; the shown text does not mention famine, so only a general provision link.

job-5:20:6.summary: Habakkuk describes failed crops; a loose famine link without the rescue.

job-5:20:7.summary: “Even if war rises against me… in this I hope,” matching deliverance in war.

job-5:20:8.summary: God “redeems David His servant from an evil sword,” matching release from the hand of iron.

job-5:20:9.summary: Jesus’ warning about wars has no promise of rescue; only the word war is shared.

job-5:20:10.summary: The righteous have bread given and water sure; a general provision theme.

job-5:20:11.summary: No one can redeem another from death; this does not carry the link to God rescuing in famine and war.

job-5:21:1.summary: “You will not fear terror by night” and calamity will not come near, matching not fearing coming evils.

job-5:21:2.summary: Some wound “with a sword as they speak”; a general link to the tongue’s lash.

job-5:21:3.summary: Jeremiah’s foes say “let us strike him with the tongue,” the very danger from which God hides here.
job-5:21:3.why: Example of the tongue as weapon.

job-5:21:4.summary: Soft words that are missiles; a general image of harmful speech.

job-5:21:5.summary: Every voice rising in judgment will be defeated; a loose parallel to protection from slander.

job-5:21:6.summary: Men’s tongue is “a sharp sword”; a general image of harmful speech.

job-5:21:7.summary: James describes the tongue as fire and deadly poison; a general link.

job-5:21:8.summary: “Happy is the one sheltered from” the tongue, matching God hiding you from the tongue’s lash.

job-5:21:9.summary: Sirach contrasts “a lash’s blow” with “a tongue’s blow,” the same image as “the lash of the tongue.”

job-5:22:0.summary: God will “remove harmful beasts” so people dwell safely, matching not fearing wild beasts.

job-5:22:1.summary: “No… evil wild beast” will be on the redeemed’s way, matching not fearing wild beasts.

job-5:22:2.summary: “You will… trample a lion and a dragon,” paralleling fearlessness toward wild beasts.

job-5:22:3.summary: God makes “a covenant… with the field’s beasts,” paralleling security from wild beasts.

job-5:22:4.summary: Wolves and lambs graze together and do no harm, a picture of beasts made harmless.

job-5:22:5.summary: Zion “sneers at” Sennacherib; loosely like laughing at the lawless.

job-5:23:0.summary: God gives peace and destroys “harmful animals from your land,” matching beasts at peace with you.

job-5:23:1.summary: God saved Daniel from the lions; a general example of safety from beasts.

job-5:23:2.summary: Wolf, lion and asp do no harm in Isaiah’s vision, matching wild beasts at peace.

job-5:23:3.summary: Treading on lion and asp loosely parallels peace with beasts; the “stone” link relies on Hebrew Job.

job-5:23:5.summary: Nothing separating us from God’s love has no specific link to peace with wild beasts.

job-5:23:6.summary: God sends “evil beasts” in judgment, contrasting with beasts at peace with the righteous.

job-5:24:0.summary: The Lord guards your coming and going; a general security theme.

job-5:24:2.summary: Bildad promises God will “restore to you a righteous way of life,” like Eliphaz’s promise of secure livelihood.

job-5:24:3.summary: Blessing on coming in and going out is a general security parallel.

job-5:24:4.summary: God’s cloud gives shelter over Zion; a general protection link.

job-5:24:5.summary: Bildad describes “the houses of the unjust” in ruin, contrasting the peaceful house promised here.

job-5:24:6.summary: Wanderers finding no city has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:24:7.summary: The wicked man’s dwelling is dark, contrasting with the peaceful house promised.

job-5:24:8.summary: His soul lodges among good things and his seed inherits land; a general blessing theme.

job-5:24:9.summary: Rulers made to wander has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:24:10.summary: Ruin lodges in the wicked man’s tent, contrasting the secure tent promised here.

job-5:24:11.summary: Job retorts that the ungodly’s “houses flourish, and fear is nowhere,” challenging Eliphaz’s promise.

job-5:24:12.summary: Ziklag burned and families taken has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:25:0.summary: “His seed will be powerful in the land,” matching the promise of many offspring.

job-5:25:1.summary: They “blossom… like the earth’s grass,” matching children like the field’s vegetation.

job-5:25:2.summary: “Blessed are the offspring of your womb,” matching promised abundant children.

job-5:25:3.summary: Abraham’s seed will be countless as stars, paralleling many offspring.

job-5:25:5.summary: God will “increase you, multiply you,” a general fertility blessing.

job-5:25:6.summary: Sons are like newly planted olive trees, a plant image for children like this verse.

job-5:25:7.summary: “Sons are the Lord’s inheritance,” and happy is the one with many, matching this promise.

job-5:25:8.summary: God’s blessing on offspring makes them “spring up like grass,” matching children like the field’s vegetation.

job-5:26:0.summary: “Years of your life will be added,” paralleling a full life before burial.

job-5:26:2.summary: “With length of days I will fill him,” matching coming to the grave at the proper time.

job-5:26:3.summary: Abraham buried “at a good old age,” matching death in ripe season.

job-5:26:4.summary: The fear of the Lord adds days; a general link to long life.

job-5:26:5.summary: Abraham died “in a good old age… full of days,” a model of the ripe death promised.

job-5:27:0.summary: The Lord’s works are “searched out,” sharing only the idea of searching.

job-5:27:1.summary: “If you become wise for yourself” loosely parallels “know for yourself.”

job-5:27:2.summary: Elihu notes no one refuted Job, indirectly judging the friends’ searched-out conclusions.

job-5:27:3.summary: Searching out wisdom like treasure is a general link to “we have searched these things out.”

job-5:27:4.summary: Keeping the commandments for one’s good has no specific link to this verse.

job-5:27:5.summary: Job mocks “wisdom will die with you,” answering the friends’ confident claims like this one.
job-5:27:5.why: Job’s sarcastic reply to the friends.

job-5:27:6.summary: Eliphaz again says “what I have seen I will report,” the same appeal to his own investigation.

job-5:27:7.summary: Bildad urges Job to “search out the family of the fathers,” the same appeal to researched tradition.

job-5:27:8.summary: Eliphaz asks whether the Lord teaches understanding; only a loose link.

job-5:27:9.summary: Eliphaz claims “what do you know that we do not know?”, the same confident appeal to the friends’ knowledge.

job-6:1:0.summary: “Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied” uses the same speech-introduction formula; Job now answers him.

job-6:2:0.summary: Job says God’s hand is “heavy upon my groaning”; a general link to weighing his pains.

job-6:2:1.summary: Eliphaz said “pain has come upon you… you have become agitated”; Job now asks that his pain be weighed.

job-6:3:1.summary: The psalmist was troubled and could not speak; a loose link to Job’s words.

job-6:3:2.summary: Jesus invites those who are burdened; a general link to Job’s heavy pains.

job-6:3:3.summary: Elihu’s call to stop speaking has no specific link to Job’s heavy pains.

job-6:3:4.summary: Job says God’s hand “has become heavy upon my groaning,” echoing his pain being “heavier than the sand.”
job-6:3:4.why: Job’s recurring image of heavy suffering.

job-6:3:5.summary: The psalm’s wonders “beyond number” has no real link to Job’s pains heavier than sand.

job-6:4:1.summary: Both are Job's laments of returning pain and lost hope, but Job 30:15 lacks the image of the Lord's arrows.
job-6:4:1.why: Shows Job's suffering as a recurring complaint.

job-6:4:2.summary: The psalmist says God's “wraths passed over me,” loosely matching the “fury” Job feels from the Lord's arrows.
job-6:4:2.why: Another sufferer attributing affliction to divine wrath.

job-6:4:3.summary: The Greek proverb asks “who will bear a fainthearted man?”, only loosely touching Job's crushed spirit; no arrows or wounds.
job-6:4:3.why: Loose echo of an unbearable inner affliction.

job-6:4:4.summary: The psalmist's “spirit is spent” parallels Job's anguish only in general terms of overwhelming distress.
job-6:4:4.why: General lament of a spirit near collapse.

job-6:4:5.summary: Christ's cry of being forsaken shares only the general theme of a righteous sufferer afflicted by God.
job-6:4:5.why: Typological link of the suffering righteous one.

job-6:4:6.summary: Job again describes God setting him “up like a target,” surrounding him with spears and pouring out his gall.
job-6:4:6.why: Develops Job's image of being shot at by God.

job-6:4:7.summary: Lamentations has God drawing His bow and driving “the arrows of His quiver into my kidneys,” matching the Lord's arrows in Job's body.
job-6:4:7.why: Same distinctive image of God's arrows piercing the sufferer.

job-6:4:8.summary: Job says God “multiplied my injuries without cause,” a general parallel to the wounds of the Lord's arrows.
job-6:4:8.why: Job's repeated complaint of undeserved wounds.

job-6:4:9.summary: Paul's “fear of the Lord” does not connect to Job's arrows; the Saints text of Job 6:4 has no “terrors of God.”
job-6:4:9.why: Link depends on wording absent from the Greek-based text.
job-6:4:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-6:4:10.summary: Sharpened arrows in the enemies' heart share only the arrow image; the king's arrows strike enemies, not a righteous sufferer.

job-6:4:11.summary: Jesus' soul “deeply grieved, to the point of death” shares only the general theme of extreme anguish.

job-6:4:12.summary: God fashions “His arrows” for the wicked here, sharing the image of divine arrows but aimed at sinners, not at Job.
job-6:4:12.why: Background for God's arrows as judgment.

job-6:4:13.summary: God says “I will make My arrows drunk with blood,” closely echoing Job's arrows whose fury “drinks up my blood.”
job-6:4:13.why: Distinctive image of blood-drinking divine arrows.

job-6:4:14.summary: God threatens to “spend My arrows upon them” with evils and wasting, matching Job's sense of being hit by the Lord's arrows.
job-6:4:14.why: Covenant curse imagery behind Job's complaint.

job-6:4:15.summary: God “sent out arrows and scattered them” against enemies; the divine-arrow image is shared but the context is deliverance.
job-6:4:15.why: Shared image of God as archer.

job-6:4:16.summary: The Saints Job 21:20 has no drinking of wrath, only seeing one's slaughter, so the expected link to Job 6:4 is absent.
job-6:4:16.why: Greek wording drops the shared image.

job-6:4:17.summary: The Greek Psalm mentions turning backs and preparing faces but no arrows, so the arrow link does not carry.
job-6:4:17.why: No shared image in this wording.

job-6:4:18.summary: “Fear of the Lord gripped me” touches on dread before God, but Job 6:4 here speaks of arrows rather than terrors.
job-6:4:18.why: General theme of Job's dread of God.

job-6:5:0.summary: The deer longing for water and Job's animals crying for food share only the image of creatures longing for what they lack.
job-6:5:0.why: Animal longing as a picture of need.

job-6:5:1.summary: Cattle “wept because they had no pasture” and animals look up for water, matching Job's animals crying out when lacking food.
job-6:5:1.why: Same picture of animals crying from want.

job-6:5:2.summary: God makes grass for livestock, a general background to Job's point that fed animals do not cry out.

job-6:5:3.summary: “Wild donkeys” gasp “because there was no grass,” matching Job's wild donkey crying out when seeking food.
job-6:5:3.why: Same animal and same lack of food.

job-6:6:0.summary: Elihu's “an ear tests words, and a throat tastes food” matches Job's comparison of tasting food with weighing words.
job-6:6:0.why: Same proverb linking taste and words.

job-6:6:1.summary: In the same speech Job asks if his “throat” does not ponder understanding, continuing the taste-and-words image of 6:6.
job-6:6:1.why: Closes the taste metaphor within Job's speech.

job-6:6:2.summary: Jesus speaks of salt becoming “tasteless,” sharing Job's question about food without salt having no taste.

job-6:6:3.summary: The law requiring sacrifices “seasoned with salt” shares only the word salt with Job's proverb about bland food.
job-6:6:3.why: Background on salt as necessary seasoning.

job-6:6:4.summary: “The ear discerns words, and the throat tastes food” directly pairs tasting food with judging words, like Job 6:6.

job-6:6:6.summary: Later in the same speech Job calls words “worthless,” echoing his complaint about “empty words.”

job-6:6:7.summary: God's sayings are sweet to the “throat,” contrasting with Job's question whether empty words have any taste.
job-6:6:7.why: Contrasts tasteless words with God's sweet words.

job-6:6:8.summary: Hebrews speaks of having “tasted God's good word,” sharing the image of tasting words only loosely.
job-6:6:8.why: Tasting words as a spiritual image.

job-6:6:9.summary: Job calls his friends “comforters of evils,” a general parallel to his charge that their words are empty.
job-6:6:9.why: Job's verdict on his friends' speech.

job-6:7:0.summary: Eating bread “with pain” and torment shares only a general picture of food joined to distress.
job-6:7:0.why: Food as a sign of affliction.

job-6:7:1.summary: The psalmist “ate ashes like bread,” a general parallel to Job finding his food a stench.

job-6:7:3.summary: “Bread of affliction” is a prisoner's ration, only loosely related to Job's loathing of his food.

job-6:7:4.summary: Ezekiel's refusal of unclean and “stale meat” shares only the idea of revolting food.

job-6:7:5.summary: The widow's last meal before death has no real link to Job finding his food a stench.

job-6:7:6.summary: Bread rationed by weight in a siege is about famine, not Job's revulsion at his food.

job-6:7:7.summary: Daniel ate “no desirable bread” while mourning, loosely like Job's aversion to food in grief.

job-6:8:0.summary: The psalmist's soul fails with longing and places “hope” in God's word, generally like Job's wish for his hope to be granted.
job-6:8:0.why: Longing for God to grant hope.

job-6:8:1.summary: Job asks “Where, then, is my hope?” tied to Hades and decay, clarifying the death-linked hope he asks God to grant in 6:8.
job-6:8:1.why: Shows Job's hope is bound up with death.

job-6:8:2.summary: The following verses in the same speech explain Job's request: he has no strength or time left to endure.

job-6:9:0.summary: Elijah asks God to take his life; the Greek Job 6:9 asks God not to destroy him completely, so the death-wish link is only partial.
job-6:9:0.why: Prophet's despair compared with Job's plea.

job-6:9:1.summary: Jonah asks God to take his life, but the Greek Job 6:9 asks “let Him not destroy me completely,” weakening the parallel.
job-6:9:1.why: Despairing plea to God, differently framed.

job-6:9:2.summary: Job says “leave me alone, for my life is empty,” a related lament though the Greek 6:9 asks to be spared complete destruction.
job-6:9:2.why: Job's wavering between death and relief.

job-6:9:3.summary: God's refining and rescuing Israel from a furnace has no specific link to Job asking not to be destroyed.

job-6:9:4.summary: Jonah says “It is better for me to die than to live”; the Greek Job 6:9 asks not to be destroyed completely, so the link is loose.

job-6:9:5.summary: Job's earlier lament about those who “long for death” relates generally, though 6:9 in Greek asks to be spared total destruction.

job-6:9:6.summary: People seeking death and not finding it shares only a general theme with Job's plea about God's wounding.

job-6:9:7.summary: Job wishes to be hidden in Hades “until Thy wrath ceased,” loosely like asking God to wound but not destroy completely.

job-6:9:8.summary: Job says “the Lord's hand is the one that touched me,” matching his request that the Lord wound him.
job-6:9:8.why: Job names God as the one striking him.

job-7:5:0.why: Job's repeated image of bodily decay.

job-7:5:1.why: Same image of worms and decay.

job-7:5:3.summary: “My bruises stank and rotted” and “no healing in my flesh” parallel Job's festering, discharging body.

job-7:5:4.summary: “Their worm will not die” shares the worm image, but concerns the punished dead, not a living sufferer.

job-7:5:5.summary: The Saints Job 24:20 lacks any worm image, so the expected link to Job's worm-fouled body is absent.
job-7:5:5.why: Greek wording drops the shared image.

job-7:5:6.summary: Herod “was eaten by worms,” sharing the worm image but as judgment on pride.

job-7:5:7.summary: Job's hope that God will “raise my skin” relates loosely to his diseased skin here.

job-7:5:8.summary: Untreated wounds and bruises “from feet to head” loosely parallel Job's sores.

job-7:5:9.summary: Job “dipped in filth” loosely parallels his fouled body.
job-7:5:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:5:10.summary: Israel's remembering its defiling practices has no specific link to Job's physical decay.

job-7:5:11.summary: Job regarded “as clay” in “earth and ashes” loosely relates to his body among clods of earth.

job-7:6:1.summary: “Where, then, is my hope any longer?” parallels Job's life having “perished in empty hope.”

job-7:6:2.summary: “My days passed in a stench” relates generally to Job's wasted life.

job-7:6:3.summary: Hezekiah's life cut off like a weaver's web relates to life ending, but the Greek Job 7:6 has “chatter,” not a weaver's shuttle.
job-7:6:3.why: Brevity of life, weaver link lost.

job-7:6:4.summary: Days passing “like a shadow” relate generally to Job's fleeting life.

job-7:6:5.summary: Job's “numbered years have come” relates generally to his life ending.

job-7:6:6.summary: The proverb on the impious and the pious has no specific link to Job's empty hope.

job-7:6:7.summary: “All flesh is grass” relates generally to Job's transient life.

job-7:6:8.summary: Peter's “All flesh is like grass” relates generally to Job's fleeting life.

job-7:6:9.summary: Man's days “like grass” relates generally to Job's life passing.

job-7:6:10.summary: Life as “a vapor” relates generally to Job's life being lighter than chatter.

job-7:6:11.summary: “My days bent like a shadow” relates generally to Job's vanishing life.

job-7:6:12.summary: Grass withering and beauty perishing relates generally to Job's life perishing.

job-7:6:13.summary: The Saints Job 13:15 speaks of pleading before God, not hope, so it does not connect to “empty hope.”
job-7:6:13.why: Hope link absent in Greek wording.

job-7:6:14.summary: “Having no hope” shares only the general idea of hopelessness.

job-7:6:15.summary: Job's earlier question “What time remains to me?” relates generally to his life perishing.

job-7:6:16.summary: Years passing like grass relates generally to Job's fleeting life.

job-7:6:17.summary: The Saints Jeremiah 2:25 has no “no hope” wording, so the link to Job's empty hope is absent.
job-7:6:17.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:6:18.summary: Setting hope on grace shares only the word hope; no real link to Job's lament.

job-7:7:0.summary: “You are a vapor” closely parallels Job's “my life is a breath.”
job-7:7:0.why: Same image of life as breath or vapor.

job-7:7:2.summary: “Remember what my existence is” closely echoes Job's “Remember, then, that my life is a breath.”
job-7:7:2.why: Same plea for God to remember human frailty.

job-7:7:3.summary: “Lord, remember me” shares the plea to remember but concerns vindication, not frailty.

job-7:7:4.summary: Job's journey “where I will not return” to a land with “no seeing” parallels his eye no longer seeing good.
job-7:7:4.why: Death as no return and no sight.

job-7:7:5.summary: “Remember this” about enemies reproaching the Lord shares only the verb remember.

job-7:7:6.summary: Asking God to remember His servants' reproach shares only the verb remember.

job-7:7:7.summary: Job's “Remember that Thou didst mold me as clay” is the same plea for God to remember his frailty.

job-7:7:8.summary: Job's life “swifter than a runner” whose days “did not see” parallels his eye no longer seeing good.

job-7:7:9.summary: Asking God to remember a fool's reproaches shares only the verb remember.

job-7:7:10.summary: Jacob's lament over lost sons has no specific link to Job's plea that God remember his brief life.

job-7:7:11.summary: Nehemiah's “Remember” about the covenant shares only the verb with Job's verse.

job-7:8:2.summary: The place disowning one who is swallowed up relates loosely to Job's disappearance from others' sight.

job-7:8:3.summary: God taking account of frail man relates generally to “Thine eyes will be upon me.”

job-7:8:4.summary: God watching “all my works” parallels Job's complaint “Thine eyes will be upon me.”
job-7:8:4.why: Job's sense of God's constant watch.

job-7:8:5.summary: Our age “in the light of Thy face” relates generally to God's eyes on fleeting man.

job-7:8:6.summary: God disciplining and melting a person's soul relates generally to Job vanishing under God's eye.

job-7:9:0.summary: “My salvation like a cloud” passing away shares Job's image of a vanishing cloud.

job-7:9:1.summary: The dead are “like water poured onto the ground that will not be gathered again,” matching no return from Hades.

job-7:9:2.summary: Job speaks of going “where I will not return,” matching one who goes to Hades and never comes up.
job-7:9:2.why: Job's repeated theme of no return.

job-7:9:3.summary: David's “he will not return to me” expresses the same finality of death.

job-7:9:5.summary: “Before I depart and no longer exist” parallels Job's departure to Hades without return.

job-7:9:6.summary: “A way on which I will not return” matches Job's statement that one going to Hades never comes up.

job-7:9:7.summary: Hezekiah's “I will certainly no longer see” relates generally to death ending life's vision.

job-7:9:8.summary: A cloud scattering light shares only the word cloud with Job's vanishing-cloud image.

job-7:9:9.summary: Zophar mentions “Hades” for depth of knowledge, sharing only the word with Job's verse.

job-7:9:10.summary: “There is no return” states the same finality of death as Job's “he will never come up again.”

job-7:10:0.summary: “The place will disown him” parallels “nor will his place recognize him any longer.”
job-7:10:0.why: Same image of one's place forgetting him.

job-7:10:2.summary: “His place will no longer perceive him” closely echoes Job's “nor will his place recognize him.”

job-7:10:3.summary: Being hissed “out of his place” relates loosely to losing one's place.

job-7:10:4.summary: Winnowed “from his place” relates loosely to Job's image of the departed.

job-7:10:5.summary: Those with “no remembrance” who perished as never born relates generally to being forgotten after death.

job-7:11:0.summary: Hannah's “anguish of soul” in prayer relates generally to Job's bitterness of soul.

job-7:11:1.summary: “I will certainly not restrain my lips” closely echoes Job's “I will not restrain my mouth.”
job-7:11:1.why: Same resolve not to keep silent.
job-7:11:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:11:3.summary: “Bitterness of soul” appears in both, describing life lived in anguish.

job-7:11:4.summary: Hezekiah's “soul's pain” relates generally to Job's bitterness of soul.

job-7:11:5.summary: God choosing Hezekiah's soul so it would not perish has no specific link to Job's resolve to speak.

job-7:11:6.summary: Job's refusal to be stopped by reproof relates loosely to his resolve to speak.

job-7:11:7.summary: Jesus' agony in prayer relates only generally to Job's anguished speech.

job-7:11:8.summary: Job's dishonour whether righteous or not relates generally to his distress.

job-7:11:9.summary: “Be silent, so that I may speak” relates to Job's resolve to speak, though addressed to friends.
job-7:11:9.why: Job insisting on his right to speak.

job-7:11:10.summary: The Shunammite's “soul is in pain” relates generally to Job's bitterness of soul.

job-7:11:11.summary: “Lift me up, and I will speak” relates generally to Job's insistence on speaking.

job-7:11:12.summary: Job weighing speech against silence relates generally to his decision not to restrain his mouth.

job-7:11:13.summary: Paul writing from “anguish of heart” relates only generally to Job's speaking in distress.

job-7:11:14.summary: Jesus' soul “deeply grieved” relates only generally to Job's bitterness of soul.

job-7:11:15.summary: Joseph's “affliction of his soul” ignored relates generally to anguish of soul.

job-7:11:16.summary: Inner fire breaks out: “I spoke with my tongue,” paralleling Job's decision to stop restraining his mouth.

job-7:12:1.summary: Pharaoh as “the dragon in the sea” caught with nets and hook shares Job's sea-and-dragon image.
job-7:12:1.why: Same sea dragon subdued by God.

job-7:12:2.summary: Job asks why God gives His mind to man, related to his complaint of being guarded.

job-7:12:3.summary: “He built against me, and I will not go out” parallels God posting a guard over Job.

job-7:12:4.summary: God describes bringing “a dragon with a hook” (shown text truncated), the creature Job says he is not.
job-7:12:4.why: God's own description of the dragon.

job-7:13:0.summary: The psalmist's bed is wet with tears, matching Job's bed bringing no comfort.

job-7:13:1.summary: Sleepless watches and troubled silence relate generally to Job's comfortless bed.

job-7:13:3.summary: Job's groaning and shaking relate loosely to his failed hope of comfort.

job-7:13:4.summary: “At the time of rest upon a bed, night's sleep alters his awareness,” matching Job's bed bringing troubled thoughts.

job-7:14:0.summary: Pharaoh's soul troubled by a dream relates generally to Job frightened by dreams.

job-7:14:1.summary: The prisoners troubled after their dreams relates generally to frightening dreams.

job-7:14:2.summary: The king “fell into visions and dreams and was disturbed,” sharing Job's paired dreams and visions that terrify.

job-7:14:3.summary: Pilate's wife “suffered many things … in a dream,” a general parallel.

job-7:14:4.summary: The Midianite's dream of a barley cake is a favourable omen, not a link to Job's terror.

job-7:14:5.summary: In sleep one “is troubled by his heart's vision,” matching Job frightened with dreams and visions.

job-7:15:0.summary: Ahithophel's hanging depends on a “strangling” reading absent from the Saints Job 7:15.
job-7:15:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:15:1.summary: Judas' hanging depends on a “strangling” reading absent from the Saints Job 7:15.
job-7:15:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:16:0.summary: Elijah's “Let it be enough now!” parallels Job's refusal to keep enduring a life he calls empty.

job-7:16:1.summary: “Weary in my soul” relates generally to Job's weariness of enduring.

job-7:16:2.summary: “Leave him alone” echoes Job's “leave me alone” in the same plea for respite.
job-7:16:2.why: Same plea for God to let him be.

job-7:16:3.summary: “My life is being taken away” relates generally to Job's sense of life ending.

job-7:16:4.summary: Jonah's preference for death relates generally to Job's weariness of life.

job-7:16:5.summary: Job's earlier plea about God's wounding relates loosely to his plea to be left alone.

job-7:16:6.summary: “Is not the time of my life short? Let me rest a little” parallels “I will not live for ever … leave me alone.”
job-7:16:6.why: Same plea for respite in a short life.

job-7:16:7.summary: “The sons of men are vain” relates loosely to Job's “my life is empty.”

job-7:16:9.summary: “Remove Thy scourges from me” relates generally to Job's plea to be left alone.
job-7:16:9.why: Plea for relief from God's hand.

job-7:16:10.summary: Man “likened to futility” relates generally to Job's empty life.

job-7:16:11.summary: Rebekah's “I am weary of my life” shares only general weariness of life.

job-7:16:12.summary: Jonah's “take my life from me” relates generally to Job's refusal to keep enduring.

job-7:16:13.summary: Days that “failed in futility” relate generally to Job's empty life.

job-7:16:14.summary: A “life of futility” spent in a shadow relates generally to Job's empty life.

job-7:16:15.summary: Those who “long for death” relate generally to Job's weariness of life.

job-7:17:0.summary: “What is a human being, that Thou rememberest him” shares Job's question about God's attention to man.

job-7:17:2.summary: “Lord, what is man, that Thou … takest account of him?” closely parallels Job's question.

job-7:17:3.summary: All flesh dying if God withdrew His spirit relates generally to man's dependence on God's attention.

job-7:17:4.summary: Job's complaint of God's guard over him relates generally to God's attention to man.

job-7:17:5.summary: “What is my soul in the immeasurable creation?” asks whether God notices man, inverting Job's complaint of too much notice.

job-7:17:6.summary: “What is a human being, and what is his use?” echoes Job's “what is a human being.”

job-7:18:0.summary: God testing His people through fire relates generally to God's scrutiny, though Saints Job speaks of judging, not testing.

job-7:18:1.summary: Hezekiah “handed over until morning” shares the phrase until morning with God's visits to man.

job-7:18:2.summary: Faith “tested by fire” relates only generally to God visiting and judging man.

job-7:18:3.summary: The Saints Exodus 20:5 says “repaying,” not visiting, so it does not connect to God visiting man.

job-7:18:4.summary: God testing Abraham relates generally to God's scrutiny of man.

job-7:18:5.summary: God bringing calamity on the dead has no specific link to visiting and judging man in Job 7:18.
job-7:18:5.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:18:6.summary: Many “tested and made holy” relates generally to God's scrutiny.

job-7:18:7.summary: Job asks if God will “bring him into judgment,” matching his complaint that God judges frail man.
job-7:18:7.why: Job's repeated complaint of God's judging.

job-7:18:8.summary: God afflicting and testing Israel in the wilderness relates generally to God's scrutiny.

job-7:18:9.summary: Refining and testing as gold relates generally to God's scrutiny of man.

job-7:18:10.summary: “On the day I visit” shares the verb visit, but concerns punishing Israel's sin.

job-7:19:0.summary: “He does not let me breathe” parallels God not letting Job go long enough to swallow his saliva.

job-7:19:1.summary: “Leave him alone” echoes Job's question how long God will not leave him alone.

job-7:19:2.summary: Repeated “How long” with “pains within my heart” parallels Job's “How long wilt Thou not leave me alone.”

job-7:19:3.summary: “How long” about boasting sinners shares only the lament formula.

job-7:19:4.summary: “Lord—how long?” with a troubled soul shares the lament formula with Job.

job-7:19:5.summary: The martyrs' “How long” cry shares only the lament formula.

job-7:20:0.summary: Being fixed “as a target” relates loosely; the Saints Job 7:20 speaks of being made God's accuser, not a target.

job-7:20:1.summary: Job's complaint of a guard posted over him leads directly into his question why he is a burden to God.

job-7:20:2.summary: God saving humans and beasts depends on a “preserver of men” reading absent from the Saints Job 7:20.
job-7:20:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-7:20:3.summary: Job's sighing before food has no specific link to his question about sin and burden.

job-7:20:4.summary: A man confessing God did not punish as his sins deserved relates loosely to Job's “If I sinned.”

job-7:20:5.summary: The Lord's arrows in Job relate loosely to his complaint of being God's burden.

job-7:20:6.summary: Eliphaz's charge of countless sins contrasts loosely with Job's hypothetical “If I sinned.”

job-7:20:7.summary: Job's “having sinned unintentionally” relates generally to his conditional admission of sin.

job-7:20:9.summary: The Greek Psalm about turning backs has no link to Job 7:20.

job-7:20:10.summary: Elihu quotes Job claiming “I am clean, having not sinned,” loosely related to “If I sinned.”

job-7:20:11.summary: Praise of God as Creator has no specific link to Job's question about sin and burden.

job-7:20:12.summary: Job's futile self-cleansing relates generally to his complaint of God's treatment.

job-7:20:13.summary: “How long art Thou angry” relates generally to Job's protest.

job-7:20:14.summary: God numbering Job's practices relates generally to God's scrutiny of his sins.

job-7:20:15.summary: God recording evils against Job relates generally to his complaint.

job-7:20:16.summary: Job set “up like a target” relates loosely; the Saints Job 7:20 has no target image.

job-7:21:0.summary: Those “sleeping in the breadth of the earth” relate generally to Job departing into the earth.
job-7:21:0.why: Death as sleep in the earth.

job-7:21:1.summary: “Thou hast not acquitted me of lawlessness” parallels Job's question why God has not forgotten his lawlessness.
job-7:21:1.why: Job's parallel complaint of unforgiven sin.

job-7:21:2.summary: Asking why God forgets and rejects relates generally to Job's plea.

job-7:21:3.summary: “The dust returns to the earth” relates generally to Job's departure into the earth.

job-7:21:4.summary: God's promise “to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” answers Job's question about cleansing of sin only generally.

job-7:21:5.summary: Asking God not to “remember our sins” relates generally to Job's wish for forgetfulness of lawlessness.
job-7:21:5.why: Plea for God to forget sins.

job-7:21:6.summary: God “turning me back again into earth” matches Job's “I will depart into the earth.”

job-7:21:7.summary: God “removing injustices” relates generally to Job's question why his sin is not cleansed.

job-7:21:8.summary: David's “take away Thy servant's lawlessness” shares the plea for removal of lawlessness.

job-7:21:9.summary: Job asks “How many are my sins and lawless deeds?”, continuing his questioning of God about his sin.

job-7:21:10.summary: Christ ransoming from “lawlessness” and purifying relates generally to Job's wish for cleansing.
job-7:21:10.why: Answer to the need for cleansing.

job-7:21:11.summary: Man's days like grass relate generally to Job's imminent end.

job-7:21:12.summary: Job calling decay his mother relates generally to his departure into the earth.

job-7:21:13.summary: Christ manifested “to take away sins” relates generally to Job's wish for his sin's removal.

job-7:21:14.summary: The Lamb who “takes away the sin of the world” relates generally to Job's plea.

job-7:21:15.summary: “Thou wast not propitiated” relates generally to Job's unforgiven sin.

job-7:21:16.summary: “I will be no more” in 7:8 matches “at daybreak I am no more” in 7:21.

job-7:21:17.summary: “The dead will rise” contrasts with Job's expectation that he will be no more.

job-7:21:18.summary: “I sought him, but his place could not be found” relates generally to Job being no more.

job-7:21:19.summary: The man carried to tombs relates generally to Job's departure into the earth.

job-7:21:20.summary: Hosea's call to return with words has no specific link to Job's verse.

job-7:21:21.summary: Job's wish to have “slept and rested” in death relates generally to his departure into the earth.

job-8:2:0.summary: Eliphaz's rebuke of Job's answers relates generally to Bildad's complaint about Job's words.

job-8:2:1.summary: Job's rejection of the friends' words relates loosely to Bildad's retort.

job-8:2:2.summary: Elijah's strong wind depends on a “strong wind” reading absent from the Saints Job 8:2.

job-8:2:3.summary: Job's resolve “I will not restrain my mouth” is the speech Bildad complains about.
job-8:2:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-8:2:4.summary: Pharaoh's attendants' “How long” shares only the formula with Bildad's question.

job-8:2:5.summary: Job's plea not to be destroyed has no specific link to Bildad's complaint.

job-8:2:6.summary: Job's “words of wind” retort mirrors Bildad's complaint about Job's mouth “full of words.”
job-8:2:6.why: Exchange of charges of windy words.

job-8:2:7.summary: Zophar's “Do not speak at such length” parallels Bildad's “How long will you speak these things?”
job-8:2:7.why: Friends' shared impatience with Job's words.

job-8:2:8.summary: The Greek proverb on the innocent and senseless has no specific link to Bildad's question.

job-8:2:10.summary: Moses' “How long” to Pharaoh shares only the formula.

job-8:2:11.summary: Job's “How long will you … tear me down with words?” turns Bildad's “How long” back on the friends.

job-8:3:0.summary: “With the Lord our God there is no injustice” affirms what Bildad's question assumes.

job-8:3:1.summary: “Thou who judgest all the earth, wilt Thou not do justice?” asks the same question as Bildad.

job-8:3:3.summary: Answering “The Lord's way is not straight,” God defends His judging, the issue Bildad raises.

job-8:3:4.summary: “The Lord our God is righteous in everything He may do” affirms Bildad's point about God's judgment.

job-8:3:5.summary: Elihu asks whether “the Almighty disturb judgment,” closely echoing Bildad's “disturb what is right.”

job-8:3:6.summary: “Is God unrighteous when He brings wrath? … May it never be!” addresses Bildad's question.

job-8:3:7.summary: Job's reported claim “the Lord removed my judgment” is what Bildad's question rebuts.

job-8:3:8.summary: God's challenge to one reproving Him relates generally to the question of God's justice.

job-8:3:9.summary: Job questioning God's favour to the ungodly relates generally to Bildad's defence of God's justice.

job-8:3:10.summary: Job's “judgment is nowhere” contrasts with Bildad's insistence that God does not do wrong in judging.

job-8:3:11.summary: Israel's charge “The Lord's way is not straight” is refuted, as Bildad denies God perverts what is right.

job-8:3:12.summary: The wicked seeing their slaughter has no specific link to Bildad's question about God's justice.

job-8:3:13.summary: The wicked asking what the Mighty One is has no specific link to Bildad's question.

job-8:3:14.summary: God's “Do not reject My judgment” relates generally to the defence of divine justice.

job-8:3:15.summary: Righteousness and judgment as God's throne relate generally to God's just judging.

job-8:3:16.summary: “Righteous and true are Thy ways” relates generally to Bildad's point.

job-8:3:17.summary: The King who “loves judgment” relates generally to God's justice.

job-8:3:18.summary: “The Lord does not wish to see improper things” relates generally to God not doing wrong.

job-8:3:19.summary: “God's righteous judgment” relates generally to Bildad's defence of God's judging.

job-8:3:20.summary: Elihu calls God “eternally righteous” and impartial, developing Bildad's claim that God does not judge wrongly.

job-8:3:21.summary: “Surely My way does not fail to run straight?” refutes the charge Bildad denies.

job-8:3:22.summary: Eliphaz's “Can a mortal be pure before the Lord?” relates generally to God's justice.

job-8:3:23.summary: “True and righteous are Thy judgments” relates generally to Bildad's point.

job-8:3:24.summary: Job's reply “Truly I know that it is so” directly responds to Bildad's claim about God's justice.

job-8:4:0.summary: Job sacrificed for his sons, saying “Perhaps my sons have conceived evil,” the sons Bildad says sinned.

job-8:4:1.summary: Eliphaz's “May their sons be far from deliverance” relates generally to the fate of the wicked's sons.

job-8:4:3.summary: Sodom destroyed for its “lawless deeds” (shown text truncated) relates generally to punishment for sin.

job-8:4:4.summary: Bildad's later picture of the wicked whose house is not preserved relates generally to Job's lost children.

job-8:4:5.summary: Sodom's men “sinful before God” share only the general idea of sinning before God.

job-8:5:0.summary: “Draw near to God … humble yourselves” relates generally to Bildad's call to supplication.

job-8:5:1.summary: “Ask, and it will be given” relates generally to seeking God in supplication.

job-8:5:2.summary: “Do not harden your hearts” has no specific link to rising early in supplication.

job-8:5:3.summary: Zophar urges Job to “turn your hands upward toward Him,” the same counsel to supplication as Bildad's.

job-8:5:4.summary: “Seek God … call upon Him” relates generally to Bildad's call to supplication.

job-8:5:5.summary: Manasseh in affliction sought the Lord and was restored, a general example of Bildad's counsel.

job-8:5:6.summary: Eliphaz's “I will entreat the Lord” parallels Bildad's advice to seek the Lord in supplication.

job-8:5:7.summary: Eliphaz promises “When you pray to Him, He will hear you” (shown text truncated), the same counsel as Bildad.

job-8:6:0.summary: “Awake, awake, Jerusalem” depends on an “awake” reading absent from the Saints Job 8:6.

job-8:6:2.summary: The Greek Isaiah 3:10 about binding the righteous has no link to Bildad's promise.

job-8:6:3.summary: “Awake, Lord” depends on an “awake” reading absent from the Saints Job 8:6.

job-8:6:4.summary: “The prayers of those going straight are acceptable” matches Bildad's claim that God hears the pure.

job-8:6:5.summary: Job insists “my prayer is pure,” answering Bildad's condition “If you are pure.”

job-8:6:6.summary: Eliphaz asks “who perished while pure” or when “true people” were uprooted, matching Bildad's “pure and true.”

job-8:6:7.summary: The Psalm's “Awake” depends on a reading absent from the Saints Job 8:6.

job-8:6:8.summary: God calls Job “blameless, true,” the very qualities Bildad questions with “If you are pure and true.”
