job-12:2:0.summary: Woe to those wise in their own view, generally matching Job’s sarcasm about the friends’ wisdom.

job-12:2:1.summary: Job says God hid the friends’ heart from understanding, implicitly denying the wisdom he mocks here.
job-12:2:1.why: Job’s ongoing dismissal of the friends’ insight.

job-12:2:2.summary: Eliphaz retorts by asking whether a wise person answers this way, continuing the sparring over who is wise.
job-12:2:2.why: Shows the friends’ answer to Job’s sarcasm.

job-12:2:3.summary: Zophar feels shamed and answers from understanding, part of the same quarrel over wisdom.

job-12:2:4.summary: Paul asks whether there is “no wise person among you,” only a general shared irony about wisdom.

job-12:2:5.summary: Paul’s ironic “you are wise” resembles Job’s sarcastic concession to his friends’ wisdom.
job-12:2:5.why: Parallel use of irony against self-assured hearers.

job-12:2:6.summary: Bildad appeals to the fathers’ wisdom, the kind of claim Job mocks with “wisdom will die with you.”
job-12:2:6.why: Shows the friends’ claims Job ridicules.

job-12:2:7.summary: Job’s “teach me” challenges the friends to show their wisdom, related to his sarcasm here.
job-12:2:7.why: Same quarrel over the friends’ counsel.

job-12:2:8.summary: Zophar’s jab about a person swimming in words and like a wild donkey provokes Job’s sarcastic reply.
job-12:2:8.why: Identifies the insult Job is answering.

job-12:2:9.summary: Job finds “nothing true among you,” the same dismissal of the friends’ supposed wisdom.
job-12:2:9.why: Job’s consistent verdict on his friends.

job-12:2:10.summary: A rich man is wise in his own estimation, a general parallel to self-assessed wisdom.

job-12:2:11.summary: Zophar opens his speech rebuking Job’s many words, the speech Job now answers.

job-12:2:12.summary: Elihu says the long-lived are not wise and no one refuted Job, touching the same dispute over wisdom.
job-12:2:12.why: Later voice on who truly has wisdom.

job-12:2:13.summary: Zophar claims God would show the power of wisdom, the kind of claim Job mocks.

job-12:3:1.summary: Paul’s “So am I” claims equality with rivals, like Job’s “I too have a heart like yours.”

job-12:3:2.summary: Avoid becoming like a fool by answering him; only a loose link to Job claiming likeness with his friends.

job-12:3:3.summary: Job sarcastically asks whom Bildad has helped or advised, similar tone to his reply here.
job-12:3:3.why: Same sarcastic stance toward the friends.

job-12:3:4.summary: Paul has fallen short in nothing of the great apostles; Saints Job lacks an explicit not-inferior clause.

job-12:3:5.summary: Job’s images of tasteless food have no real link to claiming a heart like his friends’.

job-12:4:0.summary: “They laughed at me,” the least now mocking Job, matches the righteous man becoming an object of mockery.
job-12:4:0.why: Develops Job’s complaint of being mocked.

job-12:4:1.summary: God answering one who calls upon Him is absent from Saints Job 12:4, which speaks only of mockery.
job-12:4:1.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording not present.

job-12:4:2.summary: Job asks that his friends no longer “laugh at me,” matching his complaint of mockery.

job-12:4:3.summary: Job became a “laughingstock,” directly paralleling the blameless man made an object of mockery.
job-12:4:3.why: Job’s repeated lament of public scorn.

job-12:4:4.summary: Calling on God and being answered does not appear in Saints Job 12:4.

job-12:4:5.summary: Attackers rush upon Job, a general picture of hostility rather than mockery.

job-12:4:6.summary: The righteous sufferer is sneered at by onlookers who taunt his trust, like the blameless man mocked.
job-12:4:6.why: Psalm parallel of the mocked righteous one.

job-12:4:7.summary: Saints Job 17:2 speaks of weary pleading, without the mockers the label assumes.

job-12:4:8.summary: “Mocked me with mockery” directly echoes the righteous man becoming an object of mockery.
job-12:4:8.why: Shared experience of the mocked righteous.

job-12:4:9.summary: Saints Job 11:3 urges brevity and lacks any mockery to connect with 12:4.

job-12:4:10.summary: Waiting for God who listens has no link to the Saints wording about mockery.
job-12:4:10.why: No shared element in this reading.

job-12:4:11.summary: Some “mocked” Paul’s preaching of resurrection, sharing only the act of mockery.
job-12:4:11.why: Loose example of mocking the faithful.

job-12:4:12.summary: The faithful “experienced mockery,” generally like the righteous man mocked.

job-12:4:13.summary: Job’s supplication and tears contain no reference to mockery in the Saints text.

job-12:4:14.summary: Soldiers mocked Jesus, the supremely righteous one, a typological echo of the blameless man mocked.
job-12:4:14.why: Christological reading of the mocked righteous.

job-12:4:15.summary: The Pharisees “sneered at Him,” sharing only the general act of scorn.
job-12:4:15.why: Loose parallel of the just one derided.

job-12:4:16.summary: One who walks uprightly fears the Lord, sharing only uprightness with the blameless man.

job-12:4:17.summary: Job calls himself the righteous person to be associated with, echoing his self-description as righteous.

job-12:4:18.summary: They “laughed at Him,” sharing only the act of ridicule.
job-12:4:18.why: Loose example of the righteous ridiculed.

job-12:5:0.summary: Light of the impious extinguished; the Saints Job 12:5 has no lamp image.

job-12:5:1.summary: Lamps going out does not connect to the Saints text about falling and plunder.

job-12:5:2.summary: Prayer that steps not be shaken loosely relates to being prepared to fall.

job-12:5:3.summary: Job imagines changed places with his friends, loosely tied to his being set to fall beneath others.
job-12:5:3.why: Reversal of fortunes between sufferer and comforters.

job-12:5:4.summary: The rich man and Lazarus share nothing specific with falling and plundered houses in the Saints text.

job-12:5:5.summary: “In the season when their foot shall slip” and things “prepared” echo the appointed time to fall.
job-12:5:5.why: Similar language of fixed time for downfall.

job-12:5:6.summary: A shaken foot sustained by mercy loosely relates to falling.

job-12:5:7.summary: The rich fool’s ease has no link to the Saints wording about falling and plunder.

job-12:5:8.summary: The ungodly’s light extinguished has no counterpart in Saints Job 12:5.

job-12:5:10.summary: Feet stumbling before darkness comes loosely relates to being prepared to fall.

job-12:5:11.summary: Saints Amos 6 speaks of those who despise Zion; the at-ease link is absent from Saints Job 12:5; range truncated.

job-12:5:12.summary: Wild donkey and ox crying for food have no link to falling and plunder.

job-12:5:13.summary: Contempt from those who prosper is not in Saints Job 12:5, which speaks of falling and plunder.

job-12:6:0.summary: The earth handed to the ungodly loosely relates to the wicked and God’s judgment.

job-12:6:1.summary: Sinners ask “How did God know?”, like those who suppose there will be no examination of them.

job-12:6:2.summary: Worldly people filled and satisfied in life, a general picture of the prospering wicked.
job-12:6:2.why: Broad theme of the wicked’s prosperity.

job-12:6:3.summary: Do not envy evildoers, loosely related to warning the wicked of judgment.

job-12:6:4.summary: Job describes the ungodly prospering and dismissing God, whereas Saints 12:6 warns them of examination; range truncated.
job-12:6:4.why: Shows Job’s tension over the wicked’s fate.

job-12:6:5.summary: An ungodly person raised high like cedars, a general picture of the wicked’s confidence.
job-12:6:5.why: Image of the wicked’s false security.

job-12:6:6.summary: Eliphaz says God filled the ungodly’s houses yet their counsel is far from Him, loosely related.
job-12:6:6.why: Friends’ treatment of the prospering wicked.

job-12:6:7.summary: Houses full of deceit made rich, a general parallel on the wicked’s gains.

job-12:7:0.summary: The ox and donkey know their owner, like asking the animals what they know of God.
job-12:7:0.why: Animals as witnesses rebuking human ignorance.

job-12:7:2.summary: The stork and birds of heaven know their times, matching appeal to the birds of heaven as teachers.

job-12:7:3.summary: Job again tells the friends to “ask” others for evidence, the same rhetorical appeal.
job-12:7:3.why: Job’s recurring call to consult wider witness.

job-12:9:0.summary: “Know … that the Lord’s hand did all these things” nearly matches “the Lord’s hand made these things.”
job-12:9:0.why: Close verbal parallel on God’s creative hand.

job-12:9:1.summary: God made the earth and gives its beasts as He wills, broadly matching God’s hand making creatures.

job-12:9:2.summary: All things are from Him, a general statement of God as creator.

job-12:9:3.summary: God making poor and rich has no specific link to creatures knowing the Lord’s hand made them.

job-12:9:4.summary: Only the rhetorical “who … does not know” is shared; the Ephesian Artemis claim is unrelated.

job-12:9:5.summary: Daniel’s prayer for the desolate mountain has no link to creation knowing God’s hand.

job-12:9:7.summary: Rich oppressing the poor is unrelated to creatures knowing the Lord made them.

job-12:9:8.summary: “The might of my hand” versus the Lord who gives strength loosely contrasts with the Lord’s hand.
job-12:9:8.why: Distant reminder of God’s hand as source.

job-12:9:9.summary: Saints Job 12:3 only says “I too have a heart like yours,” lacking the who-does-not-know link.

job-12:9:10.summary: God filling the ungodly’s houses does not connect to creatures acknowledging His hand.

job-12:10:1.summary: “The Almighty’s breath” made and teaches Elihu, matching every human’s breath in God’s hand.
job-12:10:1.why: Human life derives from God’s breath.

job-12:10:3.summary: Job’s breath and divine spirit in his nostrils, loosely echoing breath held by God.

job-12:10:4.summary: “God of the spirits and of all flesh” parallels life of all and every human’s breath in His hand.
job-12:10:4.why: God as sovereign over all life.

job-12:10:5.summary: “Your breath is in His hand” closely echoes “the breath of every human being” in His hand.
job-12:10:5.why: Close verbal parallel on God holding life.

job-12:10:6.summary: Human spirit departing and returning to earth loosely relates to life held by God.

job-12:10:7.summary: Born of flesh and Spirit is about new birth, not God holding all creatures’ breath.

job-12:10:8.summary: If God retained His spirit all flesh would die, matching all life and breath in His hand.
job-12:10:8.why: Shows dependence of life on God.

job-12:10:9.summary: God takes back “their breath” and creatures return to dust, matching breath in His hand.
job-12:10:9.why: Psalm parallel on God controlling life.

job-12:10:10.summary: God breathed “the breath of life” into man, grounding human breath in God’s act.

job-12:10:11.summary: All flesh “in which is the breath of life” shares wording but concerns the flood’s destruction.
job-12:10:11.why: Same phrase in a judgment context.

job-12:11:6.summary: “The throat tastes food” repeated, applied to discerning words as in Job.
job-12:11:6.why: Sirach reuses Job’s proverb on discernment.

job-12:11:1.summary: Trained faculties distinguish good and evil, broadly like the ear discerning words.

job-12:11:2.summary: Having “tasted” the Lord’s goodness shares only the tasting metaphor.

job-12:11:3.summary: Approving what matters is a general parallel to discernment.

job-12:11:4.summary: Job asks whether his “throat” does not ponder understanding, the same throat-as-discerner image.
job-12:11:4.why: Job’s own use of the image.

job-12:11:5.summary: “Judge for yourselves what I say” matches testing words, only generally.

job-12:12:1.summary: Eliphaz appeals to elders weightier in days, the age-equals-wisdom idea in Job 12:12.
job-12:12:1.why: Friends’ claim to wisdom of age.

job-12:12:2.summary: Bildad urges inquiring of former generations, the same appeal to long experience as wisdom.
job-12:12:2.why: Tradition of wisdom from the aged.

job-12:13:0.summary: God is “wise in understanding, mighty,” matching wisdom and power with Him.
job-12:13:0.why: Job’s consistent confession of God’s wisdom and might.

job-12:13:1.summary: The Lord is “mighty in strength of heart,” sharing might but not wisdom or counsel in Saints.

job-12:13:2.summary: The Lord gives wisdom, knowledge and “understanding,” locating these in God as Job does.

job-12:13:3.summary: God gives wisdom to those who ask, broadly assuming wisdom belongs to Him.

job-12:13:4.summary: Only God knows wisdom’s place and understanding, matching wisdom and understanding with Him; range truncated.
job-12:13:4.why: Job’s great poem on divine wisdom.

job-12:13:5.summary: God works all things by “the counsel of His will,” sharing the counsel attribute.

job-12:13:6.summary: God’s “strength” and limitless “understanding” match power and understanding with Him.
job-12:13:6.why: Psalm praise of the same attributes.

job-12:13:8.summary: Wisdom claims “counsel,” “understanding” and “strength,” the same cluster ascribed to God.
job-12:13:8.why: Same attribute list in personified Wisdom.

job-12:13:9.summary: Treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ, broadly locating wisdom in God.

job-12:13:10.summary: Zophar speaks of God’s “power of wisdom,” which Job affirms here in his own way.

job-12:13:11.summary: No one became the Lord’s counselor, implying counsel is His alone.

job-12:13:12.summary: God made the earth by His “strength,” “wisdom” and “understanding,” the same divine attributes.

job-12:13:13.summary: God lavishes grace “in all wisdom and understanding,” sharing two words only generally.

job-12:13:14.summary: “With Him are might and strength; to Him belong knowledge and understanding” nearly repeats 12:13.

job-12:13:15.summary: “All My counsel will stand” shares divine counsel only.

job-12:13:16.summary: Christ gives disciples irresistible wisdom, loosely reflecting wisdom from God.

job-12:13:17.summary: Christ is “God’s power and God’s wisdom,” pairing the same two attributes Job ascribes to God.
job-12:13:17.why: Christological echo of divine wisdom and power.

job-12:13:18.summary: God gives skill in weaving, a narrow instance of wisdom coming from Him.

job-12:13:19.summary: None instructed the Lord in counsel or understanding, affirming these belong to Him.
job-12:13:19.why: Prophetic parallel on God’s self-sufficient wisdom.

job-12:13:20.summary: Elihu weighs whether years bring wisdom, which fits Job 12:12 more than God’s wisdom in 12:13.

job-12:13:21.summary: Seek the wise among elders relates to human age-wisdom (12:12) rather than God’s wisdom.

job-12:13:22.summary: Learn understanding from the old fits 12:12’s age-wisdom, not the divine attributes of 12:13.

job-12:13:23.summary: Counsel befits elders, sharing “counsel” but about humans, closer to 12:12.

job-12:13:24.summary: Wisdom and counsel befit the old, echoing 12:12 more than God’s wisdom in 12:13.

job-12:14:0.summary: Christ “shutteth and no one openeth,” the same sovereign shut-and-open claim as Job 12:14.

job-12:14:1.summary: Saints Isaiah 22:22 lacks the key opening and shutting that links to Job 12:14.

job-12:14:2.summary: If God “overturns everything,” none can challenge Him, like none rebuilding what He throws down.
job-12:14:2.why: Zophar and Job share this view of sovereignty.

job-12:14:3.summary: “They will build, but I will overthrow” matches God throwing down so none can build.
job-12:14:3.why: Concrete prophetic instance of the principle.

job-12:14:4.summary: God handed Job over to the ungodly, loosely like God shutting people in.

job-12:14:5.summary: “The Lord will shut you into my hand” shares the shutting verb in a battle context.
job-12:14:5.why: God’s power to deliver into hands.

job-12:14:6.summary: “The Lord has shut your enemy into your hands” shares only the shutting verb.

job-12:14:7.summary: Babylon’s wall utterly demolished, an instance of God throwing down.

job-12:14:8.summary: God seals every human hand, loosely like God shutting people in.

job-12:14:9.summary: God tore Job down and cut off his hope, an instance of divine overthrow.
job-12:14:9.why: Job’s personal experience of being thrown down.

job-12:14:10.summary: “If He takes away, who will turn Him back?” parallels “If He throws down, who will build?”
job-12:14:10.why: Same rhetorical form for God’s irresistibility.

job-12:14:11.summary: Babylonia made desolate is an instance of God’s destruction.

job-12:14:12.summary: Babylon will sink and not rise, loosely like what God throws down none rebuilds.

job-12:14:13.summary: “The Lord shut me into your hands” shares only the shutting idiom.

job-12:14:14.summary: God “confined all” in disobedience, loosely matching God shutting people in.

job-12:14:15.summary: The ungodly city “will certainly never be rebuilt,” matching who will build what God throws down.

job-12:15:0.summary: Elijah announces no rain, an instance of God restraining water to dry the earth.
job-12:15:0.why: Historical example of drought by God’s word.

job-12:15:1.summary: God calls the sea’s water and pours it upon the earth, like letting waters loose.

job-12:15:2.summary: Neighboring verse on all life in God’s hand, broadly the same sovereignty theme.

job-12:15:3.summary: Witnesses can shut heaven against rain and control waters, loosely like restraining water.

job-12:15:4.summary: Elijah prays and rain stops then returns, illustrating restrained and released water.

job-12:15:5.summary: God resolves to destroy the earth, the flood implied but not stated here.

job-12:15:6.summary: God sets a boundary for waters so they do not cover the earth, matching His control of floods.

job-12:15:7.summary: God dries up the sea and rivers, like restraining water to dry the earth.
job-12:15:7.why: Prophetic image of God drying waters.

job-12:15:9.summary: Heaven was shut and famine came in Elijah’s days, an example of restrained water.

job-12:15:10.summary: Heaven shut with no rain because of sin, loosely matching God restraining water.

job-12:15:11.summary: God brings a flood of water to destroy the earth, matching waters loosed to overturn it.

job-12:15:12.summary: Only God brings rain, broadly affirming His control of water.

job-12:15:13.summary: The Lord “shut up heaven, so that there is no rain” and the land fails, like restraining water.

job-12:16:0.summary: God examining the friends has no link to might, strength and understanding in the Saints text.

job-12:16:2.summary: The lying spirit depends on the Hebrew “deceived and deceiver,” absent from Saints Job 12:16.
job-12:16:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-12:16:3.summary: A prophet led astray by the Lord relates to Hebrew wording not in Saints Job 12:16.

job-12:16:4.summary: Uttering deceit before the Lord has no counterpart in the Saints wording of 12:16.

job-12:16:5.summary: The prayer against temptation has no link to God’s might and understanding.

job-12:17:0.summary: God will destroy the wise people’s wisdom, as He leads counselors away and confounds judges.

job-12:17:1.summary: God destroys “the wisdom of the wise” and makes the world’s wisdom foolish, matching confounded counselors.

job-12:17:2.summary: Ahithophel, whose counsel failed, ends in ruin, a narrative example of a counselor brought down.

job-12:17:3.summary: “Counselors of the earth” in Job 3:14 matches the counselors and earth’s judges of 12:17.

job-12:17:5.summary: God “covers the faces of its judges,” like throwing the earth’s judges into confusion.
job-12:17:5.why: Job’s earlier statement of the same idea.

job-12:17:6.summary: David prays the Lord scatter Ahithophel’s counsel, an example of God undoing counselors.

job-12:17:7.summary: The Lord commanded Ahithophel’s good counsel be scattered, a clear case of God confusing counselors.

job-12:18:1.summary: God tears apart bonds, loosely related to binding with a belt.

job-12:18:2.summary: Manasseh is bound in fetters and then restored to his kingdom, God both binding and seating a king; range truncated.
job-12:18:2.why: Historical example of God over kings.

job-12:18:3.summary: Babylon’s king places captive Ioakim’s throne above others, a king seated on a throne by reversal.
job-12:18:3.why: Example of God’s ordering of kings.

job-12:18:4.summary: Christ as King of kings broadly relates to God ruling over kings.

job-12:18:5.summary: The Lord pulled down rulers’ thrones and “seated” others, like God seating kings on thrones.
job-12:18:5.why: Sirach states the same sovereign reversal.

job-12:19:0.summary: God will “shatter kings’ strength” through Cyrus, matching God overthrowing the earth’s rulers.

job-12:19:1.summary: The Assyrian king is defeated and killed, an example of a ruler overthrown.
job-12:19:1.why: Historical example of a ruler’s fall.

job-12:19:2.summary: God hearing the poor’s cry has no specific link to captive priests and overthrown rulers.
job-12:19:2.why: No shared element in this verse.

job-12:19:3.summary: The kings of the earth are defeated by the rider, a general picture of rulers overthrown.

job-12:19:4.summary: Joshua struck all their kings as the Lord fought, an instance of rulers overthrown.

job-12:19:5.summary: Feet on the necks of kings pictures humbled rulers, only an example of the theme.

job-12:19:6.summary: David defeats the Philistine champion, only loosely related to God overthrowing rulers.
job-12:19:6.why: Distant example of God humbling the mighty.

job-12:19:7.summary: The oppressed crying out has no specific link to captive priests or overthrown rulers.

job-12:19:8.summary: The Lamb conquers the kings, a general picture of rulers overthrown.

job-12:19:9.summary: “Overthrew” appears, but of a wicked man overthrowing the powerless, not God overthrowing rulers.

job-12:20:0.summary: Elihu says elders do not know judgment, touching the elders’ understanding mentioned here.

job-12:20:1.summary: God hid hearts from understanding, loosely related to God’s control over human understanding.

job-12:20:3.summary: God withheld understanding from the ostrich, a loose parallel to God controlling understanding.

job-12:20:4.summary: “The lips of the righteous” shares the lips image only in general.

job-12:20:5.summary: The Lord removes elder and counselor from Judea; Saints Job 12:20 says He knows rather than removes.

job-12:20:6.summary: “Lips” and “faithful” both appear, but as a moral maxim rather than God changing speech.

job-12:20:7.summary: “Truthful lips” shares the lips image without the idea of God changing them.

job-12:21:1.summary: The Lord plans to “dishonor everything glorious,” matching pouring dishonor upon rulers.
job-12:21:1.why: Prophetic example of God humbling the proud.

job-12:21:2.summary: Jezebel and Ahab’s house devoured by dogs is an extreme example of rulers dishonored.

job-12:21:3.summary: Girding with righteousness depends on the Hebrew belt image, absent from Saints Job 12:21.

job-12:21:4.summary: Frogs on Egypt’s borders has no link to dishonoring rulers or healing the lowly.

job-12:21:5.summary: Queen Jezebel’s carcass becomes like dung, an example of dishonor on a ruler.

job-12:21:6.summary: Fastening truth around the waist relies on a belt image not in Saints Job 12:21.

job-12:21:7.summary: Belts not loosened from waists depends on Hebrew wording absent from Saints Job 12:21.

job-12:21:8.summary: God punishes the earth’s kings and imprisons them, a general case of rulers humbled.

job-12:21:9.summary: Herod is struck for not giving God glory, an example of a ruler dishonored.
job-12:21:9.why: New Testament example of a proud ruler’s fall.

job-12:21:10.summary: Nebuchadnezzar loses his glory and kingdom by God’s decree, a clear case of dishonor on a ruler.
job-12:21:10.why: Classic example of a king humbled.

job-12:21:11.summary: God “transfers kings and appoints them,” the sovereign control of rulers Job describes.

job-12:21:12.summary: The magi avoiding Herod and the flight to Egypt do not show a ruler dishonored.

job-12:21:13.summary: Manna not breeding worms has no link to Job 12:21.

job-12:21:14.summary: The Assyrian king is killed by his sons, an example of a ruler brought low.

job-12:21:15.summary: Judgment on Ahab’s house for Naboth’s blood is a broad example of rulers punished.

job-12:21:16.summary: Being strengthened in the Lord has no link to dishonoring rulers in the Saints text.

job-12:21:17.summary: Shebna’s robe and power are given to another, loosely a ruler displaced.

job-12:22:1.summary: The Lord will “bring to light the hidden things of darkness,” matching uncovering deep things from darkness.

job-12:22:2.summary: The Spirit searches and reveals “the depths,” like God uncovering deep things.

job-12:22:3.summary: Job wishes “darkness and death’s shadow” to seize his birth day, the opposite of God bringing it to light.

job-12:22:4.summary: Light shines on those in “darkness and death’s shadow,” matching death’s shadow brought into light.

job-12:22:5.summary: God turns “death’s shadow into morning,” closely echoing bringing death’s shadow into light.

job-12:22:6.summary: Nothing covered will not be revealed, matching God uncovering hidden things.

job-12:22:7.summary: No hiding place for evildoers loosely matches God exposing what is hidden; the darkness image is absent.

job-12:22:8.summary: Wisdom hidden from all but known to God, loosely matching God uncovering deep things.

job-12:22:9.summary: God searches out and “knows the heart’s hidden things,” like uncovering what is hidden.

job-12:22:10.summary: Elisha reveals the king’s bedroom words, a narrative example of hidden things exposed.

job-12:22:11.summary: “Darkness will not be dark from Thee,” matching God bringing darkness into light.

job-12:22:12.summary: “Death’s shadow” appears, but for wrongdoers who love darkness, not God revealing it.

job-12:22:13.summary: God telling the power of wisdom loosely relates to revealing deep things; Saints lacks secrets wording.

job-12:23:0.summary: A multitude brought down then rejoicing loosely echoes nations laid low and guided.
job-12:23:0.why: Partial overlap on God humbling peoples.

job-12:23:1.summary: Prayer to add evils to the earth’s glorious people loosely matches God destroying nations.

job-12:23:2.summary: Nations multiplying is absent from Saints Job 12:23, which speaks of leading astray and destroying.

job-12:23:4.summary: Blessing and multiplying people does not match Saints Job 12:23’s leading astray and destroying.

job-12:23:5.summary: Redeemed people multiplying has no counterpart in the Saints wording of 12:23.

job-12:23:6.summary: Israel multiplying in Egypt does not match nations led astray and destroyed.

job-12:23:7.summary: Israel flowering and filling the world is absent from Saints Job 12:23’s theme.

job-12:23:8.summary: God increasing His people does not match nations led astray and destroyed.

job-12:23:9.summary: Abraham multiplied has no link to the Saints wording of Job 12:23.

job-12:23:10.summary: Israel multiplying in Egypt does not correspond to Saints Job 12:23.

job-12:24:1.summary: “He changes the lips” parallels “He changes the hearts,” the same formula in Job’s speech.
job-12:24:1.why: Immediate parallel in the same poem.

job-12:24:2.summary: Ephraim senseless and wandering between nations loosely illustrates rulers led astray.

job-12:24:3.summary: Egypt’s heart overcome before the Lord loosely matches God changing hearts.

job-12:24:4.summary: The fulfillment of Nebuchadnezzar’s judgment, without the changed heart itself shown.

job-12:24:5.summary: God “didst hide their heart from understanding,” like God changing rulers’ hearts and misleading them.
job-12:24:5.why: Job’s own statement of God darkening hearts.

job-12:24:6.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s “body” is changed, sharing the change idea but not the heart in Saints.
job-12:24:6.why: Partial echo of a ruler altered.

job-12:24:7.summary: The people’s heart grown dull loosely parallels God changing hearts.

job-12:24:8.summary: They “wandered” and “did not find a road,” like rulers led astray on a road they did not know.

job-12:25:0.summary: “May they grope” in darkness at noon matches groping in darkness without light.

job-12:25:1.summary: “Shaken like a drunken man” with wisdom swallowed up matches wandering like one drunk.

job-12:25:2.summary: The earth reels “like someone drunk,” the same drunkard simile for divine disorder.

job-12:25:4.summary: Men struck with blindness cannot find the door, loosely like groping without light.

job-12:25:5.summary: One walking in darkness “does not know where he is going,” matching groping and wandering in darkness.

job-12:25:6.summary: “You shall grope at noonday … in darkness” matches groping in darkness without light.
job-12:25:6.why: Ties Job’s image to the covenant curse.

job-12:25:7.summary: People “grope” like the blind and stumble at noon, the same groping-in-darkness image.
job-12:25:7.why: Prophetic use of the same picture.

job-12:25:8.summary: Darkness falls on Elymas and he seeks someone to lead him, loosely like groping without light.

job-12:5:9.summary: Proverbs 20:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-12:5:9.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-12:5:9.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-12:9:6.summary: Daniel 5:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-12:9:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-12:9:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-12:23:3.summary: Jeremiah 33:22 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-12:23:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-12:23:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-13:1:0.summary: Eliphaz’s list of God’s works, including groping at noon, resembles the things Job says he has seen; range truncated.

job-13:1:1.summary: Bildad appeals to inherited tradition, while Job claims firsthand seeing and hearing.
job-13:1:1.why: Contrasts tradition with Job’s own experience.

job-13:1:2.summary: What “we heard and knew” of God’s mighty acts loosely echoes Job having heard these things.
job-13:1:2.why: Knowledge of God’s works by hearing.

job-13:1:3.summary: Job 12:9–25 is the recital of God’s works that “these things” in 13:1 refers to; range truncated.
job-13:1:3.why: Identifies what Job claims to have seen.

job-13:1:4.summary: Eliphaz speaks of his “ear” receiving things from God, sharing only the hearing motif.

job-13:1:5.summary: Eliphaz answers “what I have seen I will report,” matching Job’s claim to have seen and heard.

job-13:1:6.summary: “What we have seen and heard” shares the seeing-hearing pair in a different context.

job-13:1:7.summary: Eliphaz says “these are the things we have heard,” which Job counters with his own seeing and hearing.

job-13:2:1.summary: Paul reluctantly boasts “I too,” loosely like Job asserting equal knowledge.

job-13:2:2.summary: Paul “fell short in nothing” of the great apostles, like Job not less intelligent than his friends.

job-13:2:3.summary: God judges the friends spoke nothing true unlike Job, later vindicating Job’s claim to understanding.

job-13:2:4.summary: “We all have knowledge” but it puffs up, a general comment on claimed knowledge.

job-13:2:5.summary: Elihu says Job speaks “in ignorance,” opposing Job’s claim to know as much as the friends.

job-13:2:6.summary: Paul has “fallen short in nothing,” a parallel claim of not being inferior to rivals.

job-13:2:7.summary: Hearing the report of God’s wrath has no link to Job’s claim of equal knowledge.

job-13:2:8.summary: Job later admits he is nothing and will add nothing, contrasting his earlier confident claim.

job-13:2:9.summary: Elihu claims Job spoke without knowledge, disputing Job’s self-assessment.

job-13:2:10.summary: Eliphaz retorts “what do you know that we do not know,” turning Job’s claim of equal knowledge back on him.

job-13:3:0.summary: God summons idols to judgment, loosely like a legal contest before God.

job-13:3:1.summary: Job earlier doubts anyone can “enter judgment with Him,” the very contest he now seeks.
job-13:3:1.why: Shows Job’s shift toward arguing his case.

job-13:3:2.summary: Job proposes that God call and he answer, the dialogue he wants when he says he will speak to the Lord.

job-13:3:3.summary: “Come, let us reason together” pictures argument with God, but initiated by God about sin.
job-13:3:3.why: Broad theme of reasoning with God.

job-13:3:4.summary: Job longs for “someone who hears me,” the same desire to plead his case to God.
job-13:3:4.why: Job’s climactic call for a hearing.

job-13:3:6.summary: The Lord will “argue” with Israel, sharing the arguing idea but with God as accuser.

job-13:3:7.summary: Zophar wishes God would speak with Job; Job now seeks to speak to God himself.
job-13:3:7.why: Job takes up Zophar’s wish on his own terms.

job-13:3:8.summary: “I will surely speak and plead before Him” repeats Job’s resolve to argue before God.

job-13:3:9.summary: Jeremiah will “speak judgments with Thee,” arguing his case before God like Job.
job-13:3:9.why: Prophetic parallel of a righteous complaint.

job-13:3:10.summary: Job says “I will plead for His judgment,” the same wish to argue before God.
job-13:3:10.why: Job’s earlier statement of the case.

job-13:3:11.summary: If terror is removed, Job “will speak,” matching his resolve to speak to the Lord.
job-13:3:11.why: Conditions Job sets for his hearing.

job-13:4:0.summary: The arrogant’s “injustice” against the psalmist loosely echoes the friends as unjust physicians.

job-13:4:1.summary: Leaders treat the people’s fracture lightly with false peace, like unjust healers.

job-13:4:2.summary: “Is there no physician” shares the physician image but laments absent healing.

job-13:4:3.summary: Many “physicians” failed the woman, sharing only the image of useless healers.

job-13:4:5.summary: False prophets bring the people no benefit, loosely like worthless comforters.

job-13:4:6.summary: Shepherds failed to heal the sick, a general picture of failed caregivers.

job-13:4:7.summary: “Treated into pain” with no benefit loosely matches harmful healing.

job-13:4:8.summary: Jesus speaks of the sick needing a “physician,” sharing only the image.

job-13:4:9.summary: Assyria “could not heal” Ephraim, a picture of useless helpers.

job-13:4:10.summary: “In vain you multiplied your remedies,” a general image of failed healing.

job-13:4:11.summary: Eliphaz’s harsh moralizing on fools is the kind of counsel Job calls unjust healing.

job-13:4:12.summary: Eliphaz claims none perish while pure, the theology behind what Job calls their unjust treatment.

job-13:4:13.summary: Job says the friends came “without mercy” on seeing his wound, like physicians who harm.
job-13:4:13.why: Job’s earlier charge against his comforters.

job-13:4:14.summary: Job asks “How can you console” him, charging the friends’ comfort is worthless; range truncated.
job-13:4:14.why: Job’s repeated verdict on their help.

job-13:4:15.summary: Eliphaz’s unfounded accusations against Job exemplify the unjust counsel Job condemns; range truncated.

job-13:4:16.summary: Bildad’s portrait of the wicked’s doom, aimed at Job, exemplifies the friends’ harmful counsel; range truncated.

job-13:4:17.summary: The false-witness command depends on a Hebrew lie-smearing image absent from Saints Job 13:4.

job-13:4:18.summary: Bildad blames Job’s sons’ sin, the kind of explanation Job rejects as unjust.

job-13:5:1.summary: “Slow to speak” commends restraint, broadly like silence being wisdom.

job-13:5:2.summary: A fool’s voice comes with many words, implying restraint is wiser.

job-13:5:3.summary: Job again tells the friends “Be silent,” repeating the same demand.

job-13:5:4.summary: Bildad asks Job to stop speaking, the mirror of Job’s request for silence.
job-13:5:4.why: Mutual calls for silence in the debate.

job-13:5:5.summary: Job asks the friends to listen to him, implying they should stop talking.

job-13:5:6.summary: The friends finally ceased contradicting Job, a later fulfillment of his request.

job-13:5:7.summary: “The understanding person will be silent,” matching silence as wisdom.
job-13:5:7.why: Prophetic statement of the same principle.

job-13:5:8.summary: Zophar tells Job not to speak at length, the reverse of Job’s demand.

job-13:5:9.summary: Job dismisses the friends’ “words of wind,” implying they should be silent.

job-13:5:10.summary: Job complains the friends tear him down with words, a reason for wanting them silent.
job-13:5:10.why: Shows the harm of their words.

job-13:6:0.summary: Elihu’s “Hear me” summons is a common call to listen, matching Job’s formula only generally.

job-13:6:1.summary: Job’s “Listen, listen to my words” is the same appeal to hear his speech.

job-13:6:2.summary: Wisdom says “Listen” and speaks from “my lips,” sharing the summons formula.
job-13:6:2.why: Similar call to attend to speech.

job-13:6:3.summary: Elihu’s “hear my words … the understanding of my lips” mirrors Job’s call to hear his mouth and lips.

job-13:6:4.summary: Jotham’s “Listen to me” shares only a general summons to hear.

job-13:7:0.summary: Elihu claims not to speak “unjust words,” loosely touching speaking falsely about God.

job-13:7:1.summary: Job vows his lips will not speak lawless things, contrasting the friends’ deceit.

job-13:7:2.summary: Zophar’s rebuke of Job’s claims is the kind of speech Job calls deceit before God.

job-13:7:3.summary: Announcing evils and wasted eyes has no link to uttering deceit before the Lord in the Saints text.

job-13:7:4.summary: Paul rejects falsehood that supposedly serves God’s glory, loosely like lying on God’s behalf.
job-13:7:4.why: Theme of deceit in God’s cause.

job-13:7:5.summary: Eliphaz’s claim that the pure never perish is an example of what Job calls deceit.
job-13:7:5.why: Shows the friends’ doctrine Job rejects.

job-13:7:6.summary: Not tampering with God’s word but speaking truth “before God” contrasts the friends’ deceit.
job-13:7:6.why: Ideal of honest speech before God.

job-13:7:7.summary: Elihu refuses partiality, a theme closer to 13:8–10 than to deceit before God.

job-13:7:8.summary: Persecutors think they serve God, loosely like wrongdoing done supposedly for God.

job-13:8:1.summary: Laws against perverting judgment loosely relate to the call to become judges.

job-13:8:2.summary: Elihu will not be overawed by a mortal, loosely like the friends shrinking back.

job-13:8:3.summary: Partiality in the law is not in Saints Job 13:8, which speaks of shrinking back and judging.

job-13:8:4.summary: God shows no awe of honored persons, loosely relating to judging without shrinking.

job-13:8:5.summary: “Judge your neighbour in righteousness” loosely relates to Job’s challenge to become judges.

job-13:9:0.summary: God is not mocked and repays, loosely related to God examining the friends.

job-13:9:1.summary: “I, the Lord, examine hearts,” matching God examining the friends.

job-13:9:2.summary: God searches out and knows hidden things, like God examining the friends.

job-13:9:3.summary: Elihu’s call for Job to learn has no link to God examining the friends in the Saints text.

job-13:9:4.summary: “Examine me and know my paths” uses the same examining language.

job-13:9:5.summary: Weary pleading has no specific link to God examining the friends.

job-13:9:6.summary: God’s might and understanding does not carry the Hebrew deceiving link the label assumes.

job-13:9:7.summary: Warning against strengthening bonds has no link to God examining the friends.

job-13:10:1.summary: God says “I will rebuke you,” matching “He will reprove you” to those who think wrongly of Him.

job-13:10:2.summary: Judges who “favor sinners” match those who secretly admire persons and face God’s reproof.

job-13:11:0.summary: “Fear of the Lord gripped me,” matching fear from God falling upon a person.
job-13:11:0.why: Job’s own experience of divine fear.

job-13:11:1.summary: Trembling flesh from fear of God’s judgments, broadly matching fear from Him.

job-13:11:2.summary: “May fear and trembling fall upon them” closely echoes fear from Him falling upon you.
job-13:11:2.why: Same image of fear falling on people.

job-13:11:3.summary: Fear Him who can destroy, a general call to fear God.

job-13:11:4.summary: The Lord will be “your fear,” sharing only the general fear of God.
job-13:11:4.why: God as the one to fear.

job-13:11:5.summary: “Will you not fear Me?” loosely parallels the rhetorical question about His terrors.

job-13:11:7.summary: Job asks God’s “terror” not to overwhelm him, the same divine terror he warns the friends of.

job-13:11:8.summary: “Who shall not fear, Lord,” a general affirmation of fearing God.

job-13:12:0.summary: God’s enduring memorial depends on a Hebrew memorial wording absent from Saints Job 13:12.

job-13:12:1.summary: The dead not rising has no specific link to boasting turning to ashes.
job-13:12:1.why: No shared element in this reading.

job-13:12:2.summary: Destroying the remembrance of evildoers is not in Saints Job 13:12, which speaks of boasting and clay.

job-13:12:3.summary: Man formed from dust of the earth loosely matches the body being clay.

job-13:12:4.summary: The impious name extinguished relies on the memorial idea absent from Saints Job 13:12.

job-13:12:5.summary: A destroyed memorial is not in the Saints wording of Job 13:12.

job-13:12:6.summary: Abraham calls himself “earth and ashes,” sharing the ashes image of human frailty.

job-13:12:7.summary: The earthly tent dismantled loosely relates to the body as clay.

job-13:12:9.summary: A perished memorial does not match boasting like ashes in the Saints text.

job-13:12:10.summary: Blotting out Amalek’s remembrance has no link to the Saints wording of Job 13:12.

job-13:13:0.summary: Job will “not restrain my mouth” but speak, the same resolve to speak out.

job-13:13:1.summary: “May you be silent” repeats the same demand that the friends be quiet.

job-13:13:2.summary: Job will let his words loose and speak in bitterness, matching his resolve to speak.

job-13:13:3.summary: “Lift me up, and I will speak,” the same request for room to speak.
job-13:13:3.why: Job’s repeated plea to be heard.

job-13:13:4.summary: “Leave me alone” loosely relates to Job asking for quiet and rest.

job-13:13:5.summary: Job will not hold back whatever comes, only loosely related to his demand to speak.

job-13:14:0.summary: Jephthah “put my life in my hand,” the same idiom of risking one’s life.

job-13:14:1.summary: “My soul is in my hands continually,” the same life-in-hand idiom.

job-13:14:2.summary: Bildad’s question about the world if Job dies lacks the self-tearing image the label assumes.

job-13:14:3.summary: The medium says “I put my soul in my hand,” the same idiom of risking life.

job-13:14:5.summary: The fool “ate his own flesh,” sharing a flesh image with different meaning.

job-13:14:6.summary: Oppressors “eat their own flesh,” sharing the flesh image in a judgment context.

job-13:14:7.summary: Eating the flesh of one’s own arm shares only the self-consuming flesh image.

job-13:15:0.summary: Fearlessness in death’s shadow loosely relates to Job speaking despite being subdued.

job-13:15:1.summary: Job’s confidence in his everlasting deliverer loosely relates to his determination to plead.

job-13:15:2.summary: God tested Job like gold, loosely relating to being subdued yet maintaining his case.

job-13:15:3.summary: Nothing separates from God’s love; Saints Job 13:15 lacks the trust wording behind this link.

job-13:15:4.summary: God greater than a condemning heart has no specific link to Job pleading his case.

job-13:15:5.summary: Job will “not give up my innocence,” matching his resolve to plead his case though subdued.

job-13:15:7.summary: One trusting in his piety is righteous, loosely matching Job’s confidence in pleading.

job-13:15:8.summary: God answers Job’s challenge to His judgment, a later response to his pleading.

job-13:15:9.summary: Job is near his judgment and will be shown righteous, the goal of his pleading before God.

job-13:15:10.summary: God asks whether one reproving Him will evade judgment with “the Mighty One,” answering Job’s plea.

job-13:15:11.summary: Job wishes a man could “plead” before the Lord, the same desire to argue his case.

job-13:15:12.summary: Job claims clean hands and pure prayer, the innocence behind his pleading.

job-13:15:13.summary: Life perishing in “empty hope” relies on the Hebrew hope wording absent from Saints Job 13:15.

job-13:15:14.summary: Job insists he did not act impiously, the innocence underlying his plea.

job-13:15:15.summary: Job later puts a hand over his mouth, contrasting his vow to speak and plead.

job-13:15:16.summary: Job’s oath of innocence and wish for a hearer continue his resolve to plead; range truncated.

job-13:16:0.summary: The Lord “became my salvation” shares the deliverance theme only generally.

job-13:16:1.summary: God “becamest my salvation” after hearing, a general deliverance parallel.

job-13:16:2.summary: The ungodly tremble in Zion, loosely matching that the deceitful cannot stand before God.

job-13:16:3.summary: God as “my Savior” and salvation, a general deliverance theme.

job-13:16:4.summary: The Lord “has become my salvation,” sharing only the deliverance theme.

job-13:16:5.summary: Bringing salvation to the Gentiles has no specific link to Job’s personal deliverance.

job-13:16:6.summary: The ungodly’s hope perishes, contrasting Job’s expectation of deliverance.
job-13:16:6.why: Fate of the godless versus Job.

job-13:16:7.summary: Hypocrites in heart arrange wrath, loosely matching that deceit cannot stand before God.

job-13:16:8.summary: The ungodly has no hope, no hearing and no freedom before God, the reverse of Job’s confident deliverance.
job-13:16:8.why: Job contrasts himself with the hypocrite.

job-13:16:9.summary: God became a helper “for salvation,” a general deliverance parallel.

job-13:16:10.summary: Salvation comes through the Lord, a general parallel.

job-13:16:11.summary: The Lord as Savior removes fear, a general deliverance theme.

job-13:17:0.summary: “Hear the reproof of my mouth” repeats the call to listen to Job’s words.
job-13:17:0.why: Parallel summons in the same speech.

job-13:17:1.summary: Elihu’s “hear my words and give ear” echoes Job’s “Listen, listen to my words.”

job-13:18:0.summary: Job would “state my own case,” matching his readiness for judgment.

job-13:18:1.summary: Job once asked how a mortal can be righteous before the Lord, contrasting his confidence of being shown righteous.

job-13:18:2.summary: Even if righteous, Job feared he would turn out crooked, the opposite of his confidence here.

job-13:18:3.summary: Job wishes for a hearing before the Lord, loosely tied to being near judgment.

job-13:18:4.summary: “God is the One who justifies,” matching Job’s certainty he will be shown righteous.

job-13:18:5.summary: “Let us be judged … that you may be justified” matches judgment ending in being shown righteous.

job-13:18:7.summary: Paul’s clear conscience loosely matches Job’s confidence in his case.

job-13:19:1.summary: Elihu takes up the challenge, “take your stand against me,” answering Job’s who-will-contend question.

job-13:19:2.summary: Jeremiah cannot stay silent, loosely related to Job’s talk of being silent.

job-13:19:3.summary: Job tells the friends to stop magnifying themselves against him, loosely about contending.

job-13:19:4.summary: Elihu invites Job to answer, loosely like a challenger to contend with him.

job-13:19:5.summary: Job refuses to restrain his mouth, loosely contrasting falling silent.

job-13:19:6.summary: “Be silent” is shared, but there the friends are told to be silent, not Job.

job-13:19:7.summary: God molding and then striking Job has no specific link to who will contend with him.

job-13:19:8.summary: “Who will bring a charge” echoes Job’s challenge “who is there to enter judgment with me.”

job-13:20:0.summary: Remove the rod and let terror not whirl me, the same two conditions Job asks God to grant.

job-13:20:1.summary: Darkness cannot hide from God, loosely related to hiding from God’s face.

job-13:20:2.summary: Adam hid from God’s face, while Job promises not to hide.

job-13:20:3.summary: The mighty hide from the face of the One on the throne, loosely related to hiding from God’s face.

job-13:21:0.summary: Elihu says his fear will not whirl Job nor his hand be heavy, answering Job’s hand-and-terror request.

job-13:21:1.summary: “Remove Thy scourges … the strength of Thy hand,” the same plea for God’s hand to be lifted.

job-13:21:3.summary: Fear of God’s judgments, broadly related to God’s terror.

job-13:21:4.summary: Job asks to rest a little, loosely like asking God to withdraw.

job-13:21:5.summary: “His terrors” and “fear from Him” match Job’s plea that God’s terror not overwhelm him.

job-13:21:6.summary: Eliphaz on unjust men defying God has no specific link to Job’s plea against God’s terror.

job-13:22:0.summary: “Then Thou wilt call, and I will answer Thee” repeats the same wording.

job-13:22:2.summary: Job doubted that if he called God would truly hear, contrasting his proposed exchange here.

job-13:22:3.summary: Job finally asks God to hear him while he speaks and questions, the dialogue he sought.

job-13:22:4.summary: Job laments God is not a human with whom he could contend, the barrier to this exchange.

job-13:22:5.summary: When God speaks, Job finds no answer, contrasting his earlier offer to reply.
job-13:22:5.why: Shows the outcome of Job’s request.

job-13:23:0.summary: “Test me … examine me,” the same plea for God to reveal one’s faults.

job-13:23:1.summary: God would search out sins, loosely related to Job asking to know his sins.

job-13:23:2.summary: God “will announce to them their works and their transgressions,” what Job asks God to teach him.

job-13:23:3.summary: Eliphaz claims Job’s “sins countless,” opposing Job’s demand to know how many they are.

job-13:24:1.summary: “The Lord became like an enemy,” matching Job’s complaint that God regards him as opposed.

job-13:24:2.summary: “How long wilt Thou turn Thy face away,” the same lament of God hiding.

job-13:24:3.summary: “Why dost Thou turn Thy face away,” closely matching “Why dost Thou hide from me.”

job-13:24:4.summary: “Why, Lord … turn Thy face away from me,” the same lament of a hidden God.

job-13:24:5.summary: Elihu quotes Job: God “regards me like an opponent,” echoing this verse.

job-13:24:6.summary: God turns His face from a faithless generation, sharing the hidden-face idea in judgment.

job-13:24:7.summary: God “turned His face away” from Jacob, yet the speaker waits in trust.

job-13:24:8.summary: The psalmist asks if God will reject forever, loosely like Job’s sense of abandonment.

job-13:24:9.summary: Job recalls when God guarded him, contrasting God now hiding.

job-13:24:10.summary: “Why, Lord, hast Thou stood far away,” the same why-lament of God’s distance.

job-13:24:11.summary: “Do not regard him as an enemy” shares the regarding-as-opponent idea in church discipline.

job-13:24:12.summary: The Lord has departed from Saul, loosely like God hiding from Job.

job-13:24:13.summary: Job longs for someone who hears him, related to God’s silence.

job-13:24:14.summary: “Why hast Thou judged me in this way?” matches Job’s why-question about God treating him as opposed.

job-13:24:15.summary: God gnashed His teeth at Job in anger, picturing God treating him as an enemy.
job-13:24:15.why: Job’s image of God as foe.

job-13:24:16.summary: God came upon Job “without mercy” with a mighty hand, as an opponent would.

job-13:25:0.summary: “The sound of a leaf borne along” pursues the fearful, the same windblown-leaf image.

job-13:25:1.summary: “Like straw before the wind,” a parallel image of windblown frailty.

job-13:25:2.summary: Why does God take account of and judge so frail a man, like opposing a windblown leaf.

job-13:25:3.summary: Christ will not break a bruised reed, a gentle contrast to opposing the frail.

job-13:25:4.summary: Chaff-dust before wind shares the windblown image but for fleeing nations.

job-13:25:5.summary: David asks why the king pursues “a dead dog … a single flea,” like God opposing a windblown leaf.

job-13:26:1.summary: Jesus warning a healed man not to sin has no specific link to sins of youth recorded.

job-13:26:2.summary: The psalmist’s soul filled with “evils” under God’s fury loosely matches Job’s lament; range truncated.

job-13:26:3.summary: Bones filled with “his youth” shares youth wording but describes the wicked.

job-13:26:4.summary: “I received reproach from my youth,” matching sins of youth set around Job.

job-13:26:5.summary: Naomi’s bitterness depends on a Hebrew bitter-things wording absent from Saints Job 13:26.

job-13:26:6.summary: Late regret over past folly loosely relates to sins of youth catching up.

job-13:26:7.summary: A man ill for thirty-eight years has no link to Job 13:26.

job-13:26:8.summary: Light given to the bitter does not match the Saints wording of records of evils and youthful sins.

job-13:27:1.summary: Both lines from Job's same speech describe God closely watching his acts: “watch all my works” and “Thou didst number my practices.”
job-13:27:1.why: Shows Job's complaint of God's scrutiny continuing into the next chapter.

job-13:27:2.summary: Both picture God as Job's hostile assailant, but Job 16:9 speaks of anger and arrows, not foot restraint or watching.
job-13:27:2.why: Broad theme of God treating Job as an enemy.

job-13:27:3.summary: Proverbs 7:22 describes a fool led like an ox to slaughter; the only overlap is “bonds,” with no link to Job's foot restraint.

job-13:27:4.summary: Acts 16:24 shows feet “secured…in the stocks,” illustrating the restraint image, but with no further connection to Job's speech.

job-13:27:5.summary: Job complains in both that God searches him out closely: “search out my lawlessness” parallels God watching “all my works.”
job-13:27:5.why: Recurring motif of God's oppressive scrutiny in Job.

job-13:27:6.summary: Asa's prison and foot disease share only words like “prison” and “feet”; no real link to Job's complaint.

job-13:27:7.summary: Job 2:7 has Job struck “from his feet to his head,” loosely echoing feet imagery, but the restraint/watching idea is absent.
job-13:27:7.why: Recalls the bodily affliction behind Job's lament.

job-13:28:0.summary: Psalm 38(39) has a person melted under divine rebuke; in the Greek the image is a spider, not a moth, so only general wasting is shared.
job-13:28:0.why: Shared theme of human frailty under God's discipline.

job-13:28:1.summary: Job 4:19 compares fragile humans to a “moth,” paralleling the “moth-eaten garment” image of decay.
job-13:28:1.why: Same moth image for human fragility within Job.

job-13:28:2.summary: Miriam's flesh being consumed parallels bodily decay loosely, but there is no shared garment or wineskin image.
job-13:28:2.why: Loose picture of flesh wasting away.

job-13:28:3.summary: Greek Hosea 5:12 reads “turmoil” and “goad,” not moth and rot, so the expected moth image is absent.
job-13:28:3.why: Greek wording loses the moth link.

job-13:28:4.summary: Job's darkened skin and scorched bones portray bodily wasting, matching decay only in general theme.

job-13:28:5.summary: Job 30:17-19 describes burned bones and a seized “robe,” loosely touching garment and decay imagery.
job-13:28:5.why: Further lament on Job's wasting body.

job-13:11:6.summary: Jeremiah 10:10 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-13:11:6.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-13:11:6.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-14:1:0.summary: Both state human birth leads to trouble: “born to toil” parallels a mortal born “full of wrath.”
job-14:1:0.why: Same teaching on the troubled human lot.

job-14:1:1.summary: Ecclesiastes says all a person's days are pain and “his distraction is anger,” echoing life “full of wrath.”
job-14:1:1.why: Wisdom parallel on life's trouble and anger.

job-14:1:2.summary: Bildad uses the same phrase “born of woman” for a frail mortal unable to be clean.
job-14:1:2.why: Same formula for human weakness in Job.

job-14:1:3.summary: Jesus uses “born of women” for humanity, but the point is John's greatness, not life's brevity.

job-14:1:4.summary: Job 7:1 calls human life on earth “a trial,” like a day-laborer's, matching life short and troubled.
job-14:1:4.why: Job's earlier statement of the hard human lot.

job-14:1:5.summary: Job 7:6 says his life is “lighter than chatter” and perished, echoing life being “short-lived.”

job-14:1:6.summary: Eliphaz repeats “born of woman” and “mortal,” asking how such a one can be righteous.
job-14:1:6.why: Same phrase reused in the debate.

job-14:1:7.summary: Job 9:25 says his life is “swifter than a runner,” illustrating the short-lived mortal.
job-14:1:7.why: Vivid image of life's swiftness in Job.

job-14:1:8.summary: Psalm 50(51) ties birth to sin through the mother, loosely related to man “born of woman,” but the theme is guilt, not brevity.
job-14:1:8.why: Connects human birth with inherent weakness.

job-14:1:9.summary: Jacob calls his days “few and grievous,” matching the short, troubled life of a mortal.
job-14:1:9.why: Patriarchal witness to life's brevity and hardship.

job-14:1:10.summary: Ecclesiastes hates life because work is “grievous,” sharing only the general theme of life's trouble.

job-14:1:11.summary: Psalm 38(39) says “my days handbreadths” and existence as nothing, paralleling a “short-lived” mortal.

job-14:1:12.summary: The ungodly in Wisdom say “Our life is short and sorrowful,” echoing “short-lived and full of wrath.”
job-14:1:12.why: Close verbal echo, though placed in skeptics' mouths.

job-14:2:0.summary: Isaiah's “flower of grass” that has “fallen” matches the flower that blossomed and fell away.

job-14:2:1.summary: Peter quotes the flower that “fell,” the same transient-flower image for mortal life.
job-14:2:1.why: New Testament use of the fading flower image.

job-14:2:2.summary: Bildad says “our life on earth is a shadow,” matching man fleeing “like a shadow.”

job-14:2:4.summary: David says our days are “as a shadow, and there is no endurance,” echoing a shadow that “will not remain.”
job-14:2:4.why: Close echo of shadow and impermanence.

job-14:2:5.summary: James calls life a vapor appearing briefly then disappearing, paralleling the fleeting shadow.
job-14:2:5.why: New Testament image of life's transience.

job-14:2:6.summary: James pictures the rich passing “like a flower of grass” whose flower fell, echoing Job's falling flower.
job-14:2:6.why: Same flower image applied to the rich.

job-14:2:7.summary: Psalm 143(144) says a man's days “pass like a shadow,” matching Job's fleeing shadow.

job-14:2:8.summary: Psalm 101(102) joins days “like a shadow” with drying “like grass,” combining both of Job's images.

job-14:2:9.summary: Job's days “fled” swiftly like a runner, ship and eagle, echoing he “fled like a shadow.”
job-14:2:9.why: Job's own images of fleeting life.

job-14:2:10.summary: Ecclesiastes mentions days “in a shadow” for the ungodly, but the point is judgment on the wicked rather than universal transience.
job-14:2:10.why: Shadow image applied to the ungodly.

job-14:2:11.summary: The righteous “will blossom like a palm tree” and endure, the reverse of Job's flower that falls; contrast only.
job-14:2:11.why: Only an incidental contrast in blossoming.

job-14:2:12.summary: Psalm 89(90) has grass that may “blossom and pass away,” fall and dry up, closely matching Job's flower.
job-14:2:12.why: Close parallel in Moses' psalm on mortality.

job-14:2:13.summary: Sinners springing up like grass only to be destroyed loosely parallels transience, but it targets the wicked.
job-14:2:13.why: Grass image applied to sinners' downfall.

job-14:2:14.summary: Wisdom says our time is “the passing of a shadow” with no return, echoing Job's fleeing shadow.

job-14:2:15.summary: Sirach likens generations to falling and growing leaves, a plant image of human transience like Job's flower.

job-14:3:2.summary: Both marvel that God attends to a lowly human; “visitest him” parallels taking account of “this one.”
job-14:3:2.why: Job's lament inverts the psalm's wonder.

job-14:3:3.summary: Romans speaks of the world answerable to God, loosely related to bringing man into judgment.
job-14:3:3.why: General theme of accountability before God.

job-14:3:4.summary: Job asks why God opposes a mere leaf or grass, the same protest against God judging a frail man.
job-14:3:4.why: Immediate context of the same complaint.

job-14:3:5.summary: Job 7:17-18 asks why God visits and “judgest him,” closely paralleling bringing “him into judgment.”
job-14:3:5.why: Job's earlier parody of the psalm.

job-14:3:6.summary: Job 13:27, just before, describes God watching all his works, the scrutiny Job questions here.
job-14:3:6.why: Immediate context of God's close scrutiny.

job-14:3:7.summary: Job asks who resists God's “judgment,” sharing his protest at an unequal trial with God.
job-14:3:7.why: Job's sense of hopeless trial before God.

job-14:3:8.summary: Job says he cannot “come together for judgment” with God, matching being brought into judgment before Him.

job-14:4:0.summary: Born of flesh being flesh loosely touches inherited impurity, but John does not speak of filth or cleanness.
job-14:4:0.why: Distant theme of human nature by birth.

job-14:4:1.summary: Eliphaz asks what mortal can be blameless, echoing Job's “who will be clean? No one.”
job-14:4:1.why: Same claim of universal impurity in Job.
job-14:4:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-14:4:2.summary: Paul says all were by nature children of wrath, a doctrinal theme related to universal uncleanness.

job-14:4:3.summary: Those in flesh cannot please God loosely parallels no one being clean, without shared wording.
job-14:4:3.why: General theme of fallen human nature.

job-14:4:5.summary: The holy One born of Mary stands in contrast to no one being clean, a theological contrast only.
job-14:4:5.why: Shows the one exception to human impurity.

job-14:4:6.summary: David's conception “in sins” fits Job's statement that no one is clean from filth.
job-14:4:6.why: Psalm parallel on sin from birth.

job-14:4:7.summary: Sin and death passing to all people loosely parallels universal impurity, with no shared imagery.

job-14:4:8.summary: Psalm 89(90):5 speaks of years passing like grass, unrelated to cleanness from filth.
job-14:4:8.why: No link to the verse's point.

job-14:4:9.summary: Adam begetting Seth in his own likeness only loosely suggests inherited nature; no mention of filth.

job-14:4:10.summary: Sirach asks “What will be cleansed from something unclean?”, a close echo of Job's rhetorical question.
job-14:4:10.why: Near-verbal parallel on cleanness from uncleanness.

job-14:5:1.summary: Paul says God determined “appointed times” for humanity, matching God setting a time man cannot pass.
job-14:5:1.why: God sets the limits of human life.

job-14:5:2.summary: All life being in God's hand loosely supports God fixing life's span, without numbered days.

job-14:5:3.summary: Hebrews says it is “appointed” for people to die once, echoing the set time not to be exceeded.

job-14:5:4.summary: God taking back breath so creatures return to dust touches mortality under God's control, loosely.

job-14:5:5.summary: Job 21:21 speaks of “the numbers of his months,” echoing “his months are numbered.”

job-14:5:6.summary: Belshazzar's kingship “has been numbered,” sharing the numbering idea but about a reign, not a lifespan.

job-14:5:7.summary: The rich fool's life is demanded suddenly, illustrating God's control of life's end in a general way.

job-14:5:8.summary: Job says none contradicts what God wishes, loosely related to an unalterable set time.

job-14:5:9.summary: Psalm 103(104) has a “boundary they will not pass,” echoing the limit but applied to waters.
job-14:5:9.why: Similar image of a God-set limit.

job-14:5:11.summary: Job 7:1 likens life on earth to a hired worker's day, matching a life of one day with fixed span.
job-14:5:11.why: Job's parallel image of limited life.

job-14:5:12.summary: Job 14:14 speaks of “having completed the days of his life,” continuing the theme of an appointed span.
job-14:5:12.why: Same chapter's reflection on life's set days.

job-14:5:13.summary: Christ holding David's key that opens and shuts has no real link to numbered months or a set time.

job-14:5:14.summary: The fall of the Chaldean kingship is unrelated to the limit of an individual's lifespan.

job-14:5:15.summary: The arrogant king prospering until completion shares only a vague idea of set time.

job-14:5:16.summary: Christ's keys of death and Hades imply authority over life's end, a loose theological link.

job-14:5:17.summary: Daniel's seventy weeks concern Israel's history, not an individual's numbered months.
job-14:5:17.why: Only a general idea of determined time.

job-14:5:18.summary: Sirach says God gave humans “numbered days and an appointed time,” closely matching Job's verse.
job-14:5:18.why: Near-verbal parallel on life's appointed span.

job-14:5:19.summary: Sirach calls death the Lord's sentence on all flesh regardless of years, loosely tied to life's set limit.
job-14:5:19.why: Death as divine sentence on all.

job-14:6:0.summary: Job asks how long God will “not leave me alone,” the same plea as “Leave him alone.”
job-14:6:0.why: Repeated plea for relief from God's gaze.

job-14:6:1.summary: The psalmist asks for relief before he departs and no longer exists, matching Job's plea for rest.
job-14:6:1.why: Similar plea for respite before death.

job-14:6:3.summary: Job says his life is short, “Let me rest a little,” the same request for respite.

job-14:6:4.summary: Job says “leave me alone, for my life is empty,” echoing the plea to leave man alone.
job-14:6:4.why: Same plea in Job's earlier speech.

job-14:6:5.summary: The parable of hired laborers shares only the image of a hired day-worker; judged on shown text.

job-14:7:0.summary: Israel will “sprout and flower,” sharing the regrowth image but about a nation's restoration.
job-14:7:0.why: Plant regrowth as hope of renewal.

job-14:7:1.summary: A “shoot” and “blossom” from Jesse's root echo the cut tree that blossoms again with a shoot.

job-14:7:2.summary: Job 14:14 voices hope that a dead person “will live,” applying the tree's renewal to humans.

job-14:7:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's tree is cut down in judgment; the cut-tree image is shared but regrowth is not shown.

job-14:7:5.summary: Leaving “one root” of the felled tree in the earth implies future regrowth, like Job's hopeful tree.

job-14:8:0.summary: Paul's seed that dies and is made alive loosely parallels the dead root reviving, a plant image only.
job-14:8:0.why: Plant death and life as resurrection image.

job-14:8:1.summary: The wheat grain dying in the earth and bearing fruit loosely parallels a root dying in earth yet reviving.

job-14:8:2.summary: Isaiah's dead rising with healing dew contrasts with Job's point, sharing only earth and revival.

job-14:9:0.summary: Paul's grafted olive branches (judged on shown text) concern Israel and Gentiles, not a tree reviving from water.

job-14:9:1.summary: A vine “planted by water” with fruit and shoot from abundant water echoes the tree blossoming from water's scent.

job-14:9:2.summary: Ezekiel's planted vine beside abundant water shares plant-and-water imagery; judged on truncated shown text.

job-14:9:3.summary: God makes “a dry tree flourish,” loosely echoing the revival of a dying tree.

job-14:10:0.summary: Job's hope that his skin be raised contrasts with the dead man being gone, a loose contrast.

job-14:10:3.summary: Jacob's death is described, but only the general fact of dying is shared.

job-14:10:4.summary: Jesus releasing His spirit shares only the event of dying, not Job's despair of finality.

job-14:10:5.summary: Job's hope gone, with Hades as his house, parallels the dead man who is no more.

job-14:10:6.summary: Sapphira's sudden death shares only the act of dying and falling.

job-14:10:7.summary: Lazarus and the rich man continue existing after death, loosely contrasting with “is no more.”

job-14:10:8.summary: Job 14:12 continues: one who lies down “will certainly not rise,” restating death's finality.

job-14:10:9.summary: Zophar says the ungodly's hope is destruction, a loose link to death ending hope.

job-14:10:10.summary: Job wishes he had died at birth; it shares the death theme but not the finality point.

job-14:10:11.summary: Job asks why he did not die from the womb, sharing only the general theme of death.

job-14:11:1.summary: Job likens friends to a failing winter torrent and melting snow, the same image of waters that vanish.

job-14:11:2.summary: Jeremiah's “false water having no faithfulness” evokes failing water, loosely like a drying river.

job-14:12:0.summary: Job speaks of going where he “will not return,” matching the one who will not rise.

job-14:12:2.summary: Ecclesiastes says all return to dust, sharing the view of death's finality in general.

job-14:12:3.summary: Job 3:13 uses “lain down” and “slept” for death, the same sleep image.

job-14:12:5.summary: Job expects death and earth as every mortal's house, a general mortality theme.

job-14:12:6.summary: Present heavens kept for fire touches heaven's end only loosely.

job-14:12:7.summary: Heaven like smoke and earth growing old loosely echo heaven's dissolution.

job-14:12:8.summary: Heavens perishing and changing like a garment loosely echo heaven ceasing.

job-14:12:9.summary: New heaven and new earth loosely relate to the old heaven no longer existing.

job-14:12:12.summary: The first heaven passing away loosely corresponds to “until heaven is no longer.”

job-14:12:19.summary: Those “fallen asleep” whom God will bring contrast with Job's sleepers who will not wake.

job-14:12:20.summary: Job's hope that his skin be raised contrasts with his claim the dead will not rise.

job-14:13:0.summary: The righteous removed into peaceful burial loosely parallels being hidden in Hades from wrath.

job-14:13:4.summary: The dead resting in the grave loosely parallels being hidden in Hades.

job-14:13:9.summary: “Remember us, Lord” shares the plea for remembrance without the Hades context.

job-14:14:16.summary: Job's hope that one will “raise my skin” develops his hope of coming to be again.

job-14:14:17.summary: “The dead in Christ will rise first” answers Job's hope that the dead will live.

job-14:15:4.summary: Entrusting souls to a faithful Creator loosely parallels appealing to God as Maker.

job-14:15:6.summary: Confidence before Christ at His coming loosely relates to answering God's call.

job-14:15:7.summary: God summoning heaven and earth and gathering His holy ones loosely echoes “Thou wilt call.”

job-14:15:8.summary: Being caught up to meet the Lord loosely parallels God calling and Job answering.

job-14:18:0.summary: Mountains moved from their places loosely echoes a rock worn from its place.

job-14:18:10.summary: Heavens growing old like a garment loosely matches the decay of solid creation.

job-14:19:0.summary: “He cut off my hope like a tree” parallels God destroying a person's endurance.

job-14:19:3.summary: The rich fool's plans ended by sudden death loosely parallel God destroying a person's expectations.

job-14:19:4.summary: The flood upon the earth loosely matches waters flooding the earth's surface.

job-14:19:5.summary: The flood's blotting out of life loosely echoes waters overwhelming the earth.

job-14:19:6.summary: Israel says “our hope has perished; we are utterly spent,” echoing destroyed endurance.

job-14:19:7.summary: The psalmist's secure prosperity overturned when God turned His face loosely matches destroyed endurance.

job-14:20:0.summary: Faces darkened and unrecognized loosely relate to a person sent away under God's face.

job-14:20:2.summary: No authority over the day of death matches man powerless as God thrusts him away.

job-14:20:3.summary: Job 14:14 on death and hope of life loosely links to the departing man.

job-14:22:0.summary: Job's skin that “endures these things” loosely parallels flesh feeling pain.

job-14:22:2.summary: Job's “flesh decayed within my skin” parallels flesh feeling pain.

job-14:22:3.summary: Elihu describes flesh decaying while the soul still desires, pairing flesh and soul in suffering.

job-14:22:4.summary: The rich man “in pain in this flame” in Hades loosely parallels pain felt by the dead.

job-14:22:5.summary: Job's “my flesh” pursued by friends shares the flesh motif, not the pain of the dead.

job-15:1:2.summary: Job 22:1 repeats the identical formula “Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied.”

job-22:3:3.summary: One who performs faithful deeds “is acceptable to Him,” loosely countering the claim that blameless works do not matter to God.

job-22:3:4.summary: “The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear Him,” loosely countering the claim that piety brings God no benefit.
job-22:3:4.why: Clarifies what God does delight in.

job-22:3:5.summary: Considering God's ways shares only the word “ways” with the question of what blamelessness means to God.

job-22:3:6.summary: A wish that “my ways were directed” to God's ordinances loosely relates to making one's way sincere.

job-22:3:7.summary: Guarding one's ways against sins of the tongue has no specific link to Eliphaz's question.

job-22:3:8.summary: Job's claim that God “knows my way” and that he guarded His ways answers Eliphaz's dismissal of his blamelessness.
job-22:3:8.why: Job's own defense of his integrity.

job-22:3:9.summary: Paul's “blameless conscience toward God” shares the blameless theme without addressing God's benefit.

job-22:3:10.summary: God “lovest righteousness” and examines hearts, loosely countering the claim that integrity does not matter to Him.

job-22:3:11.summary: Doubting God's justice (“Where is the God of righteousness?”) is loosely related to questioning the value of uprightness to God.

job-22:3:12.summary: “All who are blameless in their ways are acceptable to Him” directly counters asking what blameless ways matter to the Lord.
job-22:3:12.why: Gives the Bible's answer to Eliphaz's question.

job-22:3:13.summary: A gift as an acceptable sacrifice to God has no specific link to this verse.

job-22:4:2.summary: “The Lord Himself will come to judgment with the people’s elders” matches God entering into judgment with someone.
job-22:4:2.why: Same picture of God entering judgment.

job-22:4:3.summary: “As many as I love, I reprove” relates to God's reproof, though with the opposite motive from Eliphaz's question.
job-22:4:3.why: Different view of why God reproves.

job-22:4:4.summary: Perishing at “the rebuke of Thy face” shares only a rebuke idea, not judgment of an individual.

job-22:4:5.summary: If God closely watched lawless deeds, who could stand, loosely relating to God entering judgment.

job-22:4:6.summary: “Who, then, will resist His judgment?” loosely relates to God entering into judgment.

job-22:4:7.summary: Job's warning of wrath on the lawless loosely relates to divine judgment.

job-22:4:8.summary: Job wished he and God “might come together for judgment,” which Eliphaz's question turns against him.

job-22:4:9.summary: The Lord “observes everyone” is only loosely related; the Saints wording lacks entering into judgment.

job-22:4:10.summary: God disciplining a person “with rebukes for lawlessness” loosely parallels God's reproof.

job-22:4:11.summary: Job says “reproof come from Him; may He bring my case to its conclusion,” matching reproof and judgment with God.
