job-22:4:12.summary: Job's complaint about being guarded like a sea or dragon has no specific link to reproof or judgment.

job-22:4:13.summary: Job's wish for “a hearing for a man before the Lord” loosely relates to entering judgment with God.

job-22:4:14.summary: Horsemen growing drowsy at God's rebuke shares only the rebuke idea.

job-22:4:15.summary: God bringing “every deed into judgment” is a general parallel to God entering judgment.

job-22:5:0.summary: “Evils without number” and lawless deeds multiplied match the charge of great wickedness and countless sins.

job-22:5:1.summary: Eliphaz earlier said Job's own mouth condemns him, a lesser form of the same accusation.

job-22:5:2.summary: Eliphaz's first claim that the innocent do not perish underlies his later charge of Job's great wickedness.

job-22:5:3.summary: Zophar's hint of lawlessness in Job's hands loosely anticipates this direct charge.

job-22:5:4.summary: Eliphaz's portrait of the ungodly's fate is a general backdrop to accusing Job of sins.

job-22:5:5.summary: The friends “declared him ungodly,” exactly what Eliphaz does in charging Job with great wickedness.
job-22:5:5.why: Narrative verdict on the friends' accusation.

job-22:5:6.summary: “Who will understand transgressions?” loosely relates to the claim of countless sins.

job-22:5:7.summary: Job's complaint that the friends press on him with insolence anticipates this harsh accusation.

job-22:5:8.summary: Zophar's claim that Job's suffering is “worthy of the sins you committed” parallels Eliphaz's charge.
job-22:5:8.why: Same friends' accusation of hidden sin.

job-22:6:1.summary: The wicked man who “did not return a pledge” and oppressed the poor matches taking pledges unjustly.

job-22:6:2.summary: The righteous man has “not taken a pledge” and “clothed the naked,” the opposite of both charges.

job-22:6:3.summary: The wicked “took a widow’s cow as a pledge,” matching unjust pledge-taking.
job-22:6:3.why: Job describes the very oppression charged.

job-22:6:4.summary: The law on pledges, including restoring a poor man's garment, matches taking pledges and stripping clothing (truncated range).

job-22:6:5.summary: Oppressors “made people lie down naked,” matching removing the clothing of the naked.

job-22:6:6.summary: Job denies disregarding “a naked person” or failing to clothe him, rebutting this charge.
job-22:6:6.why: Job's direct answer to the accusation.

job-22:6:7.summary: The law against taking a millstone “in pledge” matches the charge of oppressive pledges.

job-22:6:8.summary: The righteous man “will return a debtor’s pledge” and “clothe the naked,” the opposite of the charges.

job-22:6:9.summary: Garments and wine “from extortions” loosely relate to oppression, but the Saints text lacks the pledge wording.

job-22:7:1.summary: “I was hungry... thirsty and you did not give Me drink” matches not giving the thirsty water or the hungry food.

job-22:7:2.summary: “Break your bread for the hungry” commands the very duty Job is accused of neglecting.

job-22:7:3.summary: The righteous man “will give his bread to the hungry,” the opposite of depriving the hungry.

job-22:7:4.summary: “He gave his bread to the hungry” describes the righteous act Job is accused of neglecting.

job-22:7:5.summary: The command to open one's hand to a needy brother is a general parallel to feeding the hungry (truncated range).

job-22:7:6.summary: Job's household praised his generosity with food, loosely rebutting the charge of starving the hungry.

job-22:7:7.summary: “Give bread to the hungry from your heart” names the duty Job is accused of neglecting.

job-22:7:8.summary: “If he is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink” matches the duty to the thirsty and hungry.

job-22:7:9.summary: Giving versus gathering loosely relates to generosity, without the hungry or thirsty in view.

job-22:7:10.summary: The righteous man who “gave to the poor” broadly contrasts with depriving the hungry.

job-22:7:11.summary: Mercy on the poor as lending to God is a general parallel to feeding the needy.
job-22:7:11.why: Value of mercy to the poor.

job-22:8:0.summary: Leaders “who show favoritism” match the charge “You showed partiality to certain people.”
job-22:8:0.why: Same sin of partiality in leadership.

job-22:8:1.summary: A ruler and judge acting by desire loosely relates to corrupt favoritism.

job-22:8:2.summary: In the Saints wording Job asks if the friends will “shrink back,” lacking the partiality link of the Hebrew reading.

job-22:8:3.summary: Job denies shrinking before the crowd or sending the powerless away empty, loosely rebutting favoritism.

job-22:8:4.summary: The ungodly walking about while God esteems humans has no specific link to partiality in settling land.

job-22:8:5.summary: Job's account of rescuing the poor from the powerful counters the charge of favoring the mighty (truncated range).
job-22:8:5.why: Job's defense of his past justice.

job-22:8:6.summary: Naboth's vineyard seized for Ahab through corrupt elders loosely illustrates land given by abuse of power (truncated range).
job-22:8:6.why: Example of abused power over land.

job-22:8:7.summary: A list of officials and craftsmen has no specific link to the charge of partiality.

job-22:9:0.summary: The wicked who “had no mercy on a woman” loosely parallels mistreating widows; the Saints wording lacks “widow.”

job-22:9:1.summary: Taking “the orphans’ pack animal” and “a widow’s cow” matches mistreating widows and orphans.

job-22:9:2.summary: “They oppressed the orphan and widow in you” matches the charge exactly.

job-22:9:3.summary: “A widow becomes their prey and an orphan their plunder” matches mistreating widows and orphans.

job-22:9:4.summary: Job denies having “lifted a hand against an orphan,” rebutting this charge.

job-22:9:5.summary: An unjust judge who ignores a widow loosely parallels sending widows away empty.

job-22:9:6.summary: Job says he did not waste away “a widow’s eye” and shared with “an orphan,” rebutting the charge.

job-22:9:7.summary: “You shall not mistreat any widow or orphan” forbids exactly what Job is accused of.

job-22:9:8.summary: Judgment on “those who oppress a widow” and strike orphans matches the charge.

job-22:9:10.summary: Rulers “not judging for orphans and not attending to widows’ judgment” matches neglect of widows and orphans.

job-22:9:11.summary: Crushing the sinner's arm relies on an “arms” wording absent from the Saints verse about widows and orphans.

job-22:9:12.summary: “Give judgment for the orphan and vindicate the widow” commands the opposite of the charge.

job-22:9:13.summary: “The arms of sinners will be shattered” relies on an arms wording absent from the Saints verse.

job-22:9:14.summary: The wicked “killed the widow” and “murdered orphans,” matching abuse of widows and orphans.

job-22:9:15.summary: God shattering Pharaoh's arms has no link to widows and orphans in the Saints wording.

job-22:9:16.summary: A curse on one who perverts the judgment “of the orphan, and of the widow” matches the charge.
job-22:9:16.why: Legal curse on the same sin.

job-22:10:0.summary: The Lord's arrows in Job's body loosely parallel calamities attacking him.
job-22:10:0.why: Job's own view of his affliction.

job-22:10:2.summary: Job's plea that God's “terror” not overwhelm him loosely parallels turmoil seizing him.

job-22:10:3.summary: Sudden destruction from which they “will certainly not escape” loosely parallels traps encircling.

job-22:10:4.summary: “Sudden tumult,” “overthrow,” and “siege” loosely parallel traps and a terrible war throwing one into turmoil.

job-22:10:5.summary: God “will rain traps upon sinners,” matching traps encircling the accused.
job-22:10:5.why: Same image of traps as judgment.

job-22:10:6.summary: The wise will not fear “an approaching fright,” loosely contrasting with being thrown into turmoil.

job-22:10:7.summary: Job says the Lord “disturbed me and raised His stronghold against me,” loosely matching being besieged.

job-22:11:0.summary: “Water overflowed my head” shares the image of water covering the sufferer.

job-22:11:2.summary: Waves passing over Jonah share the image of water covering the sufferer.

job-22:11:3.summary: “His light is darkness in his dwelling” matches “light became darkness for you.”

job-22:11:5.summary: “A day of darkness and gloom” is a general parallel to light turning to darkness.

job-22:11:6.summary: Being cast into “the outer darkness” is only a general parallel to darkness as judgment.

job-22:11:7.summary: “He... led me away into darkness, not light” closely matches light becoming darkness.

job-22:11:8.summary: Calling clouds and water at God's command loosely touches the water image, without covering the sufferer.

job-22:11:9.summary: “The water drowned us; our soul passed through a torrent” shares the water-covering image.

job-22:11:10.summary: “Thrust him from light into darkness” matches light becoming darkness for the wicked.

job-22:11:11.summary: “By day darkness will meet them” parallels light becoming darkness for the wicked.
job-22:11:11.why: Eliphaz's earlier version of the same image.

job-22:11:12.summary: “All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me” shares the water-covering image.

job-22:11:13.summary: “The ways of the ungodly are dark” is a general parallel to darkness for the wicked.

job-22:11:14.summary: Affliction and “darkness so that they cannot see” loosely parallels light turned to darkness.
job-22:11:14.why: Related image of darkness in distress.

job-22:12:0.summary: “Heaven is My throne” loosely relates to the One dwelling on high.

job-22:12:1.summary: “Heaven is high” loosely relates to God's lofty dwelling.
job-22:12:1.why: Zophar's similar appeal to God's height.

job-22:12:2.summary: “God is in heaven and you are on earth” loosely relates to the One dwelling on high.

job-22:12:3.summary: God in the heavens who “visitest” humans loosely relates to the One on high who observes.

job-22:12:4.summary: “Our God is in heaven above” loosely relates to the One dwelling on high.

job-22:12:5.summary: The Most High “who dwells in the heights” yet attends to the lowly closely parallels the One on high who observes and humbles the proud.

job-22:12:6.summary: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” loosely relates to God's lofty dwelling.

job-22:13:0.summary: “The Lord does not see” is the same denial of God's knowledge attributed to Job.

job-22:13:1.summary: “God has forgotten; He turned His face away so as never to see” matches the denial of God's knowledge.

job-22:13:2.summary: “How did God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?” closely matches “What has the Strong One known?”

job-22:13:3.summary: “The Lord does not look upon it” is the same denial of God's oversight.

job-22:13:4.summary: The wicked asking “who has heard?” loosely parallels denying God's knowledge.

job-22:13:6.summary: Deeds “in darkness” and “who will know us” match questioning whether God knows or judges through gloom.

job-22:13:7.summary: The wicked saying “Who will see them?” parallels denying God's knowledge.
job-22:13:7.why: Same hope of escaping God's notice.

job-22:13:8.summary: Those who say “The Lord will certainly do neither good nor harm” share the denial of God's active judgment.

job-22:14:1.summary: “Darkness will not be dark from Thee” directly answers the claim that clouds conceal God's sight.
job-22:14:1.why: Refutes the idea God cannot see.

job-22:14:2.summary: God looking “upon all who inhabit the earth” from His dwelling loosely counters the idea that He cannot see.

job-22:14:4.summary: Nothing hidden that will not be uncovered loosely counters the idea of concealment from God.

job-22:14:5.summary: God knowing every movement “from afar” loosely counters the idea that God does not see.

job-22:14:6.summary: “No place for those doing lawless things to hide” directly counters the notion that God is concealed and cannot see.

job-22:14:7.summary: “Will I not see him? Do I not fill the heaven and the earth?” directly answers the claim of God's concealment.
job-22:14:7.why: God's own rebuttal of the idea.

job-22:14:8.summary: Wisdom “encircled heaven’s circuit,” matching the image of passing around “the circle of heaven.”

job-22:15:0.summary: Noah's generation destroyed by the flood loosely fits the ancient unjust path, made clearer by the next verse.

job-22:15:1.summary: “All flesh had corrupted its way” with unrighteousness fits the “age-old path that unjust men trod.”

job-22:15:2.summary: The wickedness of mankind before the flood loosely fits the ancient path of unjust men.

job-22:16:1.summary: The flood covering the earth fits “seized before their time” with foundations under “a river flowing over” (truncated range).

job-22:16:2.summary: Those taken away suddenly by the flood fits the wicked “seized before their time.”
job-22:16:2.why: Identifies the flood behind the image.

job-22:16:3.summary: Men who “shall certainly not live out half their days” matches being seized before their time.

job-22:16:4.summary: The fountains of the deep bursting open fits foundations swept by a river flowing over.
job-22:16:4.why: Identifies the flood behind the image.

job-22:16:5.summary: Those disobedient in Noah's days loosely fit the ancient wicked swept away.

job-22:16:6.summary: God brought “a flood upon a world of ungodly people,” fitting the unjust seized and overflowed.
job-22:16:6.why: Identifies the flood behind the image.

job-22:16:8.summary: Being taken “at the halfway point of my days” loosely matches being seized before one's time.

job-22:16:9.summary: A house struck when “the rivers came” and fell parallels foundations swept by a river.
job-22:16:9.why: Same image of foundations swept away.

job-22:16:10.summary: Waters flooding the earth's surface loosely parallel the overflowing river image.

job-22:17:1.summary: Many asking “Who will show us good things?” loosely parallels the skeptic's questions about God's action.

job-22:17:2.summary: Refusing to retain God in knowledge broadly relates to the wicked dismissing God's power.

job-22:17:3.summary: The demand to remove the Holy One loosely parallels the wicked's dismissal of God.

job-22:17:4.summary: “What advantage is there” in serving the Lord Almighty parallels the wicked asking what the Almighty will do.

job-22:17:5.summary: Demons asking “What have we to do with Thee” only loosely parallels the defiant questions.

job-22:17:6.summary: Job's description of the wicked's thriving livestock is the prosperity Eliphaz is answering.

job-22:17:7.summary: The city begging Jesus to depart loosely parallels the wicked wanting God away.

job-22:18:1.summary: Job's statement about the wicked and God's examination loosely relates to God's dealings with the wicked.

job-22:18:2.summary: Worldly men whose “belly was filled with Thy hidden things” parallels God filling the wicked's houses with good things.

job-22:18:3.summary: God “filling your hearts with food and gladness” broadly relates to God giving good things to all.

job-22:18:4.summary: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich” broadly relates to God filling houses with good things.

job-22:18:5.summary: God planted the wicked so they bore fruit, though He is “far from their kidneys,” matching God's goods yet distance from the ungodly.

job-22:18:6.summary: “The counsel of the ungodly” is the same phrase the source uses.

job-22:18:7.summary: Rebuilding David's fallen tent has no link to God's gifts to the wicked or their counsel.

job-22:19:0.summary: “A righteous person will rejoice when he sees vengeance upon the ungodly” matches the righteous seeing and laughing.

job-22:19:2.why: Same response of the righteous to judgment.

job-22:19:3.summary: Zion rejoicing at God's judgments loosely parallels the righteous rejoicing at the wicked's fall.

job-22:19:4.summary: Heaven and saints rejoicing over Babylon's judgment loosely parallels the righteous laughing at the wicked's ruin.

job-22:19:6.summary: The multitude's Hallelujah over judgment on the prostitute loosely parallels the righteous rejoicing at judgment.

job-22:19:7.summary: Zion exulting at God's judgments loosely parallels the righteous rejoicing.

job-22:19:8.summary: Job says “the righteous are mocked,” contrasting with Eliphaz's claim that the righteous laugh at the wicked.

job-22:20:0.summary: Sodom reduced to ashes is a general example of fire destroying the wicked.

job-22:20:3.summary: “An unkindled fire will consume him, and may a stranger harm his house” matches fire devouring the wicked's remainder.

job-22:20:4.summary: Wind withering the wicked's shoot loosely relates to their substance being destroyed; the Saints text lacks fire.

job-22:20:5.summary: “Fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all” loosely parallels fire devouring the wicked.

job-22:20:7.summary: Eliphaz's earlier claim that the pure do not perish underlies his assertion that the wicked's substance is destroyed.

job-22:21:0.summary: Serving God wholeheartedly and seeking Him loosely parallels enduring for good fruit; the Saints text lacks “know Him.”

job-22:21:1.summary: “Let us make peace with Him” depends on a peace wording absent from the Saints verse about becoming firm.

job-22:21:2.summary: The peace of God guarding hearts depends on a peace wording absent from this Saints verse.

job-22:21:3.summary: Those who seek the Lord “will not lack any good thing” loosely parallels fruit “among good things.”

job-22:21:5.summary: The appeal “be reconciled to God” depends on a peace wording absent from the Saints verse.

job-22:21:7.summary: Eternal life as knowing God depends on an “acquaint” wording absent from the Saints verse.

job-22:21:8.summary: Settling with an adversary has no specific link to enduring and bearing good fruit.

job-22:21:9.summary: The light of the knowledge of God's glory has no link to the Saints wording.

job-22:21:10.summary: Peace to far and near and no rest for the unjust depends on peace wording absent from the Saints verse.

job-22:22:12.summary: Receiving instructions on how to please God broadly parallels receiving God's utterance.

job-24:23:2.summary: Both describe ruin overtaking those who expect safety; Job says the weakened cannot hope to recover, Paul says they “will certainly not escape.”

job-24:23:3.summary: Psalm’s “eyelids examine the sons of men” matches the Hebrew of Job 24:23, not the Greek about falling by disease.
job-24:23:3.why: Link rests on wording not in the Saints text.

job-24:23:4.summary: Ecclesiastes on officials watching over one another has no real link to a weakened man falling by disease.

job-24:23:5.summary: Jeremiah asks why the impious prosper and asks God to ready them for slaughter; Job describes the wicked’s collapse. Only the general theme is shared.
job-24:23:5.why: Places the wicked’s prosperity and fall side by side.

job-24:23:6.summary: Psalm 72 laments the ease of the lawless; Job 24 likewise treats the fate of the wicked, but the shown text shares no specific image.
job-24:23:6.why: Broad theme of the wicked’s apparent security.

job-24:23:7.summary: The rich fool’s sudden death loosely parallels the wicked man falling without hope of recovery.

job-24:23:8.summary: God swearing never to forget Jacob’s works has no specific tie to the Greek wording of Job 24:23.
job-24:23:8.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-24:23:9.summary: The Assyrian king’s boast of conquests is unrelated to a weakened man falling by disease.
job-24:23:9.why: No shared person, image, or teaching.

job-24:23:10.summary: Delayed punishment emboldening evildoers rests on the Hebrew sense of Job 24:23, not the Greek.
job-24:23:10.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-24:23:11.summary: God watching a man’s ways matches the Hebrew of Job 24:23; the Greek speaks only of weakness and disease.
job-24:23:11.why: Link rests on wording absent here.

job-24:23:12.summary: The ungodly saying God will not call to account fits the Hebrew Job, not the Greek verse about falling by disease.
job-24:23:12.why: No real link in the Saints wording.

job-24:23:14.summary: Both use similar phrasing about the wicked not hoping or trusting for escape (“let him not hope” / “let no wicked person trust”).
job-24:23:14.why: Shows the false hope of the wicked recurring in Job.

job-24:23:15.summary: Feeding one’s enemy and heaping coals has no connection to the verse.

job-24:23:16.summary: The negligent slave who thinks his master is delayed is unrelated to the Greek wording of Job 24:23.
job-24:23:16.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-24:23:17.summary: God pulling sinners from Hades or heaven is not reflected in a verse about falling by disease.

job-24:23:18.summary: Habakkuk’s complaint about God’s pure eye depends on the Hebrew “eyes” of Job 24:23, which the Greek lacks.
job-24:23:18.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-24:23:18.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-24:23:19.summary: God seeing the works of the lawless echoes the Hebrew sense of Job 24:23, not the Greek about disease.
job-24:23:19.why: No real link in the Saints text.

job-24:24:0.summary: Both picture the sinner vanishing; the psalm says his place will not be found, Job says he withers.
job-24:24:0.why: Shares the theme of the wicked’s swift disappearance.

job-24:24:1.summary: Both use plant imagery under “scorching heat” to show the proud or rich withering away.
job-24:24:1.why: A New Testament echo of the withering image.

job-24:24:2.summary: An ungodly man “raised high” then gone parallels Job’s exalted oppressor withering away.
job-24:24:2.why: Same picture of exaltation followed by sudden disappearance.

job-24:24:3.summary: Sinners springing up like grass only to be destroyed matches Job’s withering-plant picture of the wicked.
job-24:24:3.why: Shared plant image for the fleeting wicked.

job-24:24:4.summary: Coming miseries for the rich loosely parallel the fall of one whose exaltation mistreated many.
job-24:24:4.why: General theme of judgment on oppressive prosperity.

job-24:24:5.summary: Reaping the dried harvest shares a grain image with Job’s falling ear of grain, but the judgment scene is broader (shown text truncated).

job-24:24:6.summary: The lawless becoming “desolate suddenly” parallels the quick withering of Job’s oppressor.

job-24:24:7.summary: Both use the image of “ears” of grain and stalks, though Isaiah applies it to gleaning after judgment.

job-24:24:8.summary: A dead man not knowing his sons’ fortunes has no link to the oppressor withering.

job-24:24:9.summary: The ungodly person’s dwelling being no more loosely parallels the oppressor’s ruin.

job-24:24:10.summary: The ungodly’s delight ending in “a terrible fall” matches the theme of exaltation collapsing.

job-24:25:0.summary: Both close with a challenging rhetorical question (“if it is not He, who is it?” / “If it is not so, who…?”).

job-24:25:1.summary: Job asserts he will not lie to his friends, matching his challenge that no one can prove he speaks falsely.
job-24:25:1.why: Job’s repeated claim of truthful speech.

job-24:25:2.summary: Zophar rebukes Job’s many words, the opposite of Job’s claim that his words cannot be reduced to nothing.
job-24:25:2.why: Shows the friends’ challenge to Job’s speech.

job-24:25:3.summary: Job vows his lips will not speak lawless things, related to his claim of not speaking falsely.

job-24:25:4.summary: Eliphaz questions whether Job answers from understanding, the challenge Job dares anyone to make.
job-24:25:4.why: Friends dispute the worth of Job’s words.

job-24:7:5.summary: Proverbs 31:21 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-24:7:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-24:7:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-24:23:13.summary: Isaiah 56:12 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-24:23:13.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.

job-25:2:0.summary: Fear before the face of the One on the throne loosely echoes the “fear” that comes from God.

job-25:2:1.summary: Colossians on making peace in heaven relies on the Hebrew “makes peace”; the Greek Job says He makes the whole in the highest.
job-25:2:1.why: Link not carried by the Saints wording.
job-25:2:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:2:2.summary: Christ proclaiming peace depends on Hebrew wording absent from the Greek Job 25:2.
job-25:2:2.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-25:2:3.summary: Job’s reply describes God’s power over Hades, sky, and sea, expanding Bildad’s claim about the One who makes all in the highest (shown text truncated).
job-25:2:3.why: Job answers Bildad with his own hymn on divine power.

job-25:2:4.summary: David’s prayer says God rules all things in heaven and earth and before Him every nation is shaken, echoing Job’s fear and rule from on high.
job-25:2:4.why: Same praise of God’s universal rule.

job-25:2:6.summary: Authority in heaven and on earth only generally echoes God’s rule in the highest.

job-25:2:7.summary: Christ seated above every rule in the heavenly places loosely echoes God’s dominion on high.

job-25:2:8.summary: Reconciliation in Christ depends on the Hebrew “peace,” which the Greek Job 25:2 lacks.
job-25:2:8.why: No shared element in the Saints text.
job-25:2:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:2:9.summary: A doxology ascribing majesty and authority to God only generally matches Bildad’s praise of God’s rule.

job-25:2:10.summary: “Peace upon peace” relies on the Hebrew of Job 25:2; the Greek speaks of fear and making the whole.
job-25:2:10.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:2:11.summary: Nebuchadnezzar praises the Most High who created heaven and earth, a general echo of God working in the highest.
job-25:2:11.why: General praise of the Creator’s rule.

job-25:2:12.summary: God’s challenge about His arm, glory, and humbling the arrogant loosely relates to His awe-inspiring rule.

job-25:2:13.summary: Job’s hymn on God shaking the world and stretching out heaven parallels Bildad’s awe at the Maker of all on high.
job-25:2:13.why: Shared praise of God’s cosmic power in Job.

job-25:2:14.summary: The Lord exalted, His name “fearsome,” the earth shaken, generally echoes fear coming from God.

job-25:2:15.summary: Peacemakers depend on the Hebrew “makes peace”; the Greek Job 25:2 has no such wording.
job-25:2:15.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:2:16.summary: Isaiah’s Lord Most High “who dwells in the heights” echoes the One working “in the highest.”
job-25:2:16.why: Shared picture of God on high.

job-25:2:17.summary: The Lord’s Prayer petition has no real link to Bildad’s statement.

job-25:3:0.summary: The Father of lights links to the Hebrew “light” of Job 25:3, absent from the Greek about raiders and ambush.
job-25:3:0.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:3:1.summary: The sun rising on all depends on the Hebrew of Job 25:3; the Greek speaks of an ambush from God.
job-25:3:1.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-25:3:2.summary: Countless attendants link to the Hebrew “armies” of Job 25:3, absent from the Greek.
job-25:3:2.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-25:3:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:3:3.summary: Creation of light relies on Hebrew wording; the Greek verse concerns raiders and ambush.

job-25:3:4.summary: Angels blessing the Lord relate to the Hebrew “armies,” not the Greek Job 25:3.
job-25:3:4.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-25:3:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:3:5.summary: Lights in the firmament have no tie to the Greek wording about raiders.

job-25:3:6.summary: Life as the light of humankind depends on the Hebrew “light,” not in the Saints text.

job-25:3:7.summary: Twelve legions of angels relate to the Hebrew “armies,” absent from the Greek verse.
job-25:3:7.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-25:3:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:3:8.summary: God numbering the heavenly array depends on the Hebrew “number of His armies,” absent in the Greek.
job-25:3:8.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-25:3:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-25:3:9.summary: Angels and lights praising God rest on Hebrew wording not in the Saints text.

job-25:3:10.summary: Dawn shaking the ungodly out of the earth loosely matches God’s ambush reaching wrongdoers.

job-25:3:11.summary: Myriads of angels relate to the Hebrew armies, not the Greek Job 25:3.
job-25:3:11.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-25:3:12.summary: The true Light enlightening all depends on the Hebrew “light,” absent here.
job-25:3:12.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:3:13.summary: “No one who will be hidden from his heat” loosely parallels no one escaping God’s ambush.

job-25:4:0.summary: Bildad asks how a mortal can be righteous; Romans answers with justification from faith.

job-25:4:1.summary: “Who will withstand?” if God marks lawless deeds matches Bildad’s point that no mortal is righteous before the Lord.
job-25:4:1.why: Same confession of human guilt before God.

job-25:4:2.summary: Eliphaz asks how one “born of woman” can be righteous, the same question Bildad repeats.

job-25:4:4.summary: Job asked the identical question: “how can a mortal be righteous before the Lord?”

job-25:4:5.summary: “No one living will be justified before Thee” states the same truth as Bildad’s question.

job-25:4:6.summary: Being conceived in lawless deeds parallels the impurity of one “born of woman.”

job-25:4:7.summary: Christ freeing us from sins answers the cleansing no mortal can achieve himself.

job-25:4:8.summary: The Saints text of Zechariah 13:1 lacks the cleansing fountain; it shares nothing with Bildad’s question.
job-25:4:8.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:4:9.summary: “Who will be clean from filth? No one” matches Bildad’s question whether anyone could cleanse himself.
job-25:4:9.why: Job had already said the same.

job-25:4:10.summary: God cleansing those who confess loosely answers the impossibility of self-cleansing.

job-25:4:11.summary: “No flesh will be justified before Him” restates that no mortal is righteous before the Lord.
job-25:4:11.why: Paul’s parallel teaching on universal guilt.

job-25:4:12.summary: Being washed and justified in Christ answers Bildad’s question of cleansing and righteousness.
job-25:4:12.why: New Testament answer to the problem.

job-25:4:13.summary: Being “by nature children of wrath” loosely parallels human impurity from birth.

job-25:5:0.summary: The moon no longer lighting because the Lord is the light loosely echoes the moon not shining before God.

job-25:5:1.summary: Eliphaz says “heaven is not pure before Him,” paralleling Bildad’s stars “not pure before Him.”

job-25:5:2.summary: Both mention the moon failing or diminishing, though Job 31 concerns not worshiping it.
job-25:5:2.why: Shared image of the moon’s waning.

job-25:5:3.summary: The Greek Isaiah 24:23 speaks of brick melting and walls falling, not the moon; the link rests on the Hebrew.
job-25:5:3.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:5:4.summary: Lesser glory losing its glory beside surpassing glory loosely parallels the moon not shining before God.

job-25:5:5.summary: Even the sun “fails,” so flesh and blood is worse; same argument from heavenly lights to human weakness.

job-25:6:0.summary: The Greek Isaiah 41:14 reads “little Israel” without the “worm” the English label assumes.
job-25:6:0.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-25:6:2.summary: Abraham calls himself “earth and ashes,” a parallel confession of human lowliness before God.

job-25:6:3.summary: “What is a human being” that God magnifies him contrasts with Bildad calling humanity a worm.

job-25:6:4.summary: Eliphaz describes humans living in houses of clay and crushed like a moth, matching Bildad’s worm image.
job-25:6:4.why: Friends’ shared view of human frailty.

job-25:6:5.summary: A “son of man is not immortal” echoes Bildad’s “son of humanity” as decay.

job-25:2:5.summary: Jeremiah 10:6–7 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-25:2:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-25:2:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-26:2:0.summary: Eliphaz recalls Job helping the weak; Job now mocks Bildad’s supposed help, but the Greek frames it as helping the mighty One.

job-26:2:1.summary: Strengthening limp hands relies on the Hebrew sense of helping the powerless; the Greek Job asks whether Bildad helps the Mighty One.
job-26:2:1.why: No shared element in the Saints text.

job-26:2:2.summary: Elijah’s mocking question resembles Job’s sarcastic tone, but the subjects differ.

job-26:2:3.summary: Job’s sarcasm “Surely wisdom will die with you!” matches his ironic retort to Bildad here.
job-26:2:3.why: Job’s recurring sarcasm toward his friends.

job-26:2:4.summary: Idol-makers helping one another share only the word “help” with Job’s question.

job-26:2:5.summary: A prayer when strength fails shares only the word “strength.”

job-26:2:6.summary: Job says he is not asking the friends for strength, related to his question about their help.

job-26:2:7.summary: Job’s lament about his strength shares only the strength motif.

job-26:2:8.summary: Job says he could speak as the friends do, related to his ironic challenge of their words.
job-26:2:8.why: Job turning the friends’ rhetoric back.

job-26:2:9.summary: God needs no instructor; this fits Job 26:3 more than 26:2’s question about helping the Mighty One.
job-26:2:9.why: God needs no helper or counselor.

job-26:3:0.summary: The psalmist’s mouth speaking wisdom shares only the wisdom theme.

job-26:3:1.summary: Job claims a heart like his friends’, consistent with his challenge to their wisdom.

job-26:3:2.summary: God asks who hides “counsel,” loosely related to Job’s question whom Bildad has advised.

job-26:3:3.summary: Job says silence would be the friends’ wisdom, matching his scorn for their advice.

job-26:3:4.summary: Paul declaring God’s whole purpose has no real tie to Job’s sarcastic question.

job-26:3:5.summary: Elihu mentions finding “wisdom by attaching ourselves to the Lord,” echoing Job 26:2–3’s attaching and wisdom.
job-26:3:5.why: Echoes the debate over true wisdom.

job-26:3:6.summary: Paul’s public teaching has no specific tie to Job’s question.

job-26:3:7.summary: Elihu’s claim of pure words shares no specific element with the verse.

job-26:3:8.summary: Eliphaz taunted Job about wisdom; Job here returns a similar taunt.

job-26:3:9.summary: Job’s lament that help is far shares no clear link with whom Bildad advised.

job-26:3:10.summary: Wisdom’s noble speech has only a general wisdom theme.

job-26:3:11.summary: Job finds nothing true among the friends, matching his scorn here.

job-26:3:12.summary: The psalmist proclaiming God’s power shares only general words.

job-26:3:13.summary: Elihu offering to teach wisdom relates loosely to the question of whom one advises.

job-26:4:0.summary: Zedekiah asks what spirit “spoke in you,” paralleling Job asking “whose is the breath that came out of you?”
job-26:4:0.why: Same challenge to a speaker’s inspiration.

job-26:4:1.summary: Elihu says a spirit within compels his words, related to Job’s question about the breath behind speech.

job-26:4:2.summary: Speaking by God’s Spirit generally relates to the source of the breath behind words.

job-26:4:3.summary: Testing spirits loosely echoes Job questioning the spirit behind Bildad’s words.

job-26:4:4.summary: Zophar claimed “a spirit from understanding answers me”; Job now challenges whose breath speaks through the friends.
job-26:4:4.why: Job’s retort to the friends’ claim of inspiration.

job-26:4:5.summary: The spirit returning to God shares only the word “spirit,” not the question of inspiration.

job-26:4:6.summary: Unclean spirits from mouths loosely echo breath coming out of a speaker.

job-26:5:0.summary: Both speak of “giants,” the Greek Job referring to ancient giants now beneath the waters.

job-26:5:1.summary: The Greek psalm speaks of the dead not rising, loosely related to giants beneath the water.

job-26:5:2.summary: The dragon of the sea shares only the underwater-creature setting (shown text truncated).

job-26:5:3.summary: Pharaoh as river dragon has no real link to giants beneath water.

job-26:5:4.summary: Creatures and the dragon in the sea share only the deep-water setting.

job-26:6:1.summary: “If I descend into Hades, Thou art present” matches Hades lying open before God.

job-26:6:2.summary: “All things are naked and laid open to His eyes” echoes Hades being “naked before Him.”

job-26:6:3.summary: “Destruction” is personified with Death in both Job passages, as a realm known to God.

job-26:6:4.summary: God’s hand reaching into Hades parallels Hades lying naked before Him.

job-26:6:5.summary: Hades and “giants” appear together as in Job 26:5–6, but Isaiah describes a king’s descent.

job-26:6:6.summary: The dead and God’s wonders loosely relate to the underworld lying open before Him.
job-26:6:6.why: Realm of the dead before God.

job-26:6:7.summary: The shown verse about darkness only hints at nothing being hidden from God.

job-26:6:8.summary: God claiming the whole realm beneath heaven loosely relates to His sight of Hades.

job-26:6:9.summary: Zophar speaks of things “deeper than those in Hades” as known to God, as Job does here.

job-26:7:0.summary: “He alone stretched out heaven” parallels God stretching the north over nothing.

job-26:7:1.summary: God holds the earth’s circuit and “stretched” the heavens, matching Job’s stretched north and hung earth.

job-26:7:3.summary: God made heaven and established the earth, paralleling His spreading the north and hanging the earth.
job-26:7:3.why: Creator’s establishment of heaven and earth.

job-26:7:4.summary: The earth founded upon seas differs from earth hung on nothing, sharing only a creation theme.

job-26:7:5.summary: Wisdom present at the making of earth and heaven shares only a general creation theme.

job-26:7:6.summary: God displaying the heavenly array loosely relates to His ordering of the cosmos.

job-26:7:7.summary: An unformed earth over the deep loosely relates to earth hung upon nothing.

job-26:8:1.summary: Elihu describes God directing clouds and knowing “the division of clouds,” paralleling water bound in clouds.

job-26:8:2.summary: “An abundance of water in heaven” and clouds raised by God match water bound in His clouds.
job-26:8:2.why: God storing water in the sky.

job-26:8:3.summary: God commanding clouds not to rain loosely relates to clouds holding water.

job-26:8:4.summary: God asks who counts clouds with wisdom, matching His mastery of water in clouds.

job-26:8:5.summary: God wraps the sea in cloud and mist, paralleling water held in clouds.

job-26:8:6.summary: “Dark water in clouds of the air” matches water bound in His clouds.
job-26:8:6.why: Shared image of water in clouds.

job-26:8:7.summary: God bringing clouds and rain shares the general theme of control over clouds.

job-26:8:8.summary: Waters divided above the firmament parallel water held aloft in clouds.

job-26:8:9.summary: Elihu speaks of the “extensions of a cloud” and His tent, the same cloud imagery.

job-26:9:1.summary: “Clouds are His concealment” matches God spreading His cloud over His throne.

job-26:9:2.summary: God dwelling in thick darkness parallels His throne covered by cloud.
job-26:9:2.why: God hidden in cloud and darkness.

job-26:9:3.summary: God’s excellence covering the heavens loosely echoes cloud spread over His throne.

job-26:9:4.summary: Instructions to keep people off Sinai have no link to a cloud-covered throne.

job-26:9:5.summary: God covering Moses so His face is unseen loosely relates to God’s throne veiled.

job-26:9:6.summary: Solomon says the Lord spoke of “dwelling in gloom,” matching God’s throne shrouded in cloud.

job-26:9:7.summary: God in unapproachable light shares the theme of hiddenness, but with light rather than cloud.

job-26:10:0.summary: The Greek Proverbs 8:29 shown speaks only of strong foundations, not the sea’s boundary the label assumes.

job-26:10:2.summary: God set the sea’s boundary as “an eternal command,” matching His command circled on the waters.
job-26:10:2.why: God limiting the sea by decree.

job-26:10:3.summary: God gathering the sea’s waters relates generally to His control of the waters.

job-26:10:4.summary: God’s oath after Noah’s flood does not mention a boundary on the waters in the shown text.

job-26:10:5.summary: “Thou didst set a boundary they will not pass” parallels God’s command circling the waters.
job-26:10:5.why: Same limit set on the waters.

job-26:10:6.summary: Day and night continuing loosely relates to the limit of light with darkness.
job-26:10:6.why: Fixed order of day and night.

job-26:11:0.summary: The Greek 1 Samuel 2:8 shown has no pillars of the earth; it speaks of raising the poor.
job-26:11:0.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-26:11:1.summary: God shaking heaven and earth loosely relates to heaven’s pillars trembling.

job-26:11:2.summary: Foundations shaken because God was angry parallel heaven’s pillars astonished at His rebuke.

job-26:11:3.summary: Heaven not being pure shares only the word “heaven” with the verse.

job-26:11:4.summary: God shaking heaven echoes heaven’s pillars trembling, but in an eschatological setting.

job-26:11:5.summary: Heavens passing away on the Lord’s day loosely relates to heaven trembling at God.

job-26:11:6.summary: Heaven fleeing from God’s face loosely parallels heaven’s pillars astonished at His rebuke.

job-26:12:0.summary: God who stirs the sea shares divine power over the sea, though Job speaks of calming it.

job-26:12:1.summary: God making the sea’s waves boom relates generally to His power over the sea.

job-26:12:2.summary: A call to awake with strength of arm; the shown Greek text lacks the sea-monster reference.

job-26:12:3.summary: “Wisdom and power” belong to God, the same pair as strength and knowledge in this verse.

job-26:12:4.summary: The “sea creatures” bending down beneath God parallels His wounding the great sea creature.

job-26:12:5.summary: God quiets the sea’s surge and humbles a proud one “like a wounded man,” echoing calm sea and wounded creature.

job-26:12:6.summary: The Lord mighty above the sea’s surges relates generally to Him calming the sea.

job-26:12:8.summary: The Red Sea parted by God loosely illustrates His power over the sea (shown text truncated).

job-26:12:9.summary: Humbling the insolent depends on the Hebrew “Rahab” (pride); the Greek Job 26:12 speaks of a sea creature.
job-26:12:9.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-26:12:10.summary: God opposing the proud depends on Hebrew wording absent from the Greek verse.

job-26:12:11.summary: Praise of the Creator of seas shares only the general theme of God’s power.

job-26:12:12.summary: A day against the arrogant relies on the Hebrew sense of Rahab, not the Greek sea creature.
job-26:12:12.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.

job-26:12:13.summary: The Lord settling the flood relates loosely to His calming the sea.

job-26:12:14.summary: The sea fleeing before God loosely echoes His mastery over the sea.

job-26:13:1.summary: God sending His Spirit relates to the Hebrew “by His spirit”; the Greek Job 26:13 has “bars of heaven” and a dragon.
job-26:13:1.why: Link not carried by the Saints text.
job-26:13:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-26:13:2.summary: God crushing “the dragon’s heads” parallels His killing the rebellious dragon.

job-29:8:1.summary: Younger submitting to elders loosely echoes young men deferring to Job.

job-29:8:2.summary: Paying honor to whom honor is due is too general for Job's specific scene of deference.

job-29:8:3.summary: Being subject to rulers has no specific link to youths hiding before Job.

job-29:8:4.summary: Old age as a crown in righteousness loosely relates to Job's honored standing.

job-29:8:5.summary: A righteous king on his throne before whom evil cannot stand loosely echoes respect shown to Job.

job-29:8:6.summary: Paul on rulers bearing the sword does not match Job's scene of youths and elders honoring him.

job-29:8:7.summary: “Honor everyone… honor the king” is too general to link to Job 29:8.

job-29:8:8.summary: Sirach's advice to defer among dignitaries loosely reflects the deference shown to Job.

job-29:9:0.summary: “Placing a hand upon your cheek” is a similar gesture of silent amazement to a finger on the mouth.

job-29:9:1.summary: Sparing the lips as intelligence loosely echoes powerful men ceasing to speak.

job-29:9:2.summary: Job himself will “place a hand over my mouth” before God, the same gesture the powerful made before him.

job-29:9:4.summary: Being slow to speak is a general teaching, not tied to deference shown Job.

job-29:9:5.summary: “Put your hand over your mouth” is the same silencing gesture as in Job 29:9.

job-29:9:6.summary: Job refusing to restrain his mouth contrasts with men who stopped speaking before him.

job-29:9:7.summary: Eliphaz's remark about Job's words does not involve silence or the hand-on-mouth gesture.

job-29:9:8.summary: Wisdom of Solomon's hearers “place a hand upon their mouth” when he speaks, closely echoing Job 29:9.

job-29:10:1.summary: God binding Ezekiel's tongue so he is mute echoes tongues clinging to throats.

job-29:11:0.summary: All bore witness and wondered at Jesus' words, loosely like hearers calling Job blessed.

job-29:11:1.summary: Job's oath recalls the powerless who would “bless me,” the same blessing he describes in 29:11.
job-29:11:1.why: Job's own account of being blessed.

job-29:11:2.summary: Peoples rejoice when the righteous are praised, echoing Job's being called blessed.

job-29:11:3.summary: A woman calls Jesus' mother “Blessed,” loosely like hearers calling Job blessed.

job-29:12:0.summary: The psalm says nearly verbatim: “rescued a poor person from a powerful man's hand… who had no helper.”

job-29:12:1.summary: One who ignores the weak will not be heard, the opposite of Job's rescuing the poor.

job-29:12:2.summary: Pure religion cares for orphans, as Job helped the orphan.

job-29:12:3.summary: The law forbids afflicting orphans and widows, the duty Job fulfilled.

job-29:12:4.summary: God executes judgment for the orphan, as Job helped the orphan.

job-29:12:5.summary: God as “Father of orphans” parallels Job's helping the orphan.

job-29:12:6.summary: “Rescue those being led to death” loosely echoes Job rescuing the poor.

job-29:12:7.summary: “Deliver the needy and the poor; rescue them from the hand of a sinner” matches Job's rescue of the poor.
job-29:12:7.why: Same duty of rescue from the powerful.

job-29:12:8.summary: Kings who failed to judge for the poor contrast with Job's help for the poor.
job-29:12:8.why: Contrast in care for the poor.

job-29:12:9.summary: Job swears he never lifted a hand against an orphan, complementing his help to the orphan.

job-29:12:11.summary: Nehemiah intervenes for the oppressed poor against honored men, loosely like Job's rescue (shown part of range).
job-29:12:11.why: Defending the poor against the powerful.

job-29:12:12.summary: Job's oath about sharing his morsel with an orphan parallels his helping the orphan.

job-29:12:13.summary: The wicked divert powerless people, contrasting with Job's rescue of the poor.

job-29:12:14.summary: Sirach urges “be like a father to orphans,” the role Job describes in helping orphans.

job-29:13:0.summary: Job speaks of the “perishing” naked and the powerless who “bless me,” matching 29:13.

job-29:13:1.summary: The “lost” exiles returning to worship share only a word with the perishing blessing Job.

job-29:13:2.summary: Saints' hearts refreshed through Philemon loosely parallels those blessing Job for his help.

job-29:13:4.summary: Paul blesses Onesiphorus for refreshing him, loosely like the perishing blessing Job.

job-29:13:5.summary: The confession of the wandering father does not link to the perishing blessing Job in the Saints text.

job-29:13:6.summary: Recipients of generosity give thanks and pray for the givers, akin to blessing for Job.

job-29:13:7.summary: Servants exulting versus others wailing has no specific link to the widow blessing Job.

job-29:13:8.summary: Widows weeping over Dorcas's garments show gratitude for charity, akin to the widow blessing Job.

job-29:13:9.summary: Including the orphan and widow in rejoicing loosely relates to Job's care for the widow.

job-29:13:10.summary: Sending portions to those who have none loosely echoes benevolence earning blessing.

job-29:13:11.summary: Nations rejoicing in God's judgment has no specific link to Job 29:13.

job-29:13:12.summary: Judging the case of the poor and weak loosely relates to Job's help of the perishing.

job-29:13:13.summary: Returning a poor man's pledge “that he may… bless you” parallels the needy blessing Job.

job-29:14:0.summary: “He clothed me in a garment of salvation” uses the same clothing-in-virtue image as Job.

job-29:14:2.summary: Priests “clothe themselves in righteousness,” the same phrase Job uses of himself.
job-29:14:2.why: Same image of righteousness as clothing.

job-29:14:3.summary: The “breastplate of righteousness” is a related image of wearing righteousness.

job-29:14:4.summary: Fine linen as “righteous acts of the saints” echoes righteousness as clothing.

job-29:14:5.summary: Job's resolve of “holding to righteousness” connects to his claim of being clothed in it.

job-29:14:6.summary: Putting on the breastplate of faith and love is a related clothing-in-virtue image.

job-29:14:7.summary: Zion as a crown in God's hand lacks Job's clothing-in-righteousness image.

job-29:14:8.summary: “Weapons of righteousness” share only the word righteousness with Job's clothing image.

job-29:14:9.summary: Returning a garment pledge does not relate to being clothed in righteousness.

job-29:14:10.summary: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” uses the clothing metaphor for spiritual identity.

job-29:14:11.summary: The Lord as crown of hope does not reflect Job's clothing in righteousness.

job-29:15:0.summary: Moses asks Hobab to guide them in the wilderness; the Saints text reads “elder,” weakening the “eyes” link.
job-29:15:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-29:15:1.summary: Jesus' ministry where “the blind receive sight and the lame walk” echoes Job's help to the blind and lame.
job-29:15:1.why: Help for the blind and lame.

job-29:15:2.summary: Paul's body imagery of eye and foot loosely echoes Job as eye and foot for others (shown part of range).

job-29:16:0.summary: “A righteous person knows how to judge for the needy” fits Job as father to the powerless and investigator of cases.

job-29:16:1.summary: God as “Father of orphans and judge of widows” mirrors Job as a father to the powerless.

job-29:16:2.summary: A king's glory in honoring matters loosely echoes Job tracing out an unknown case.

job-29:16:3.summary: The wicked divert the powerless, contrasting with Job as their father.

job-29:16:4.summary: Mordecai raising orphaned Esther shares only a foster-care idea, not Job's justice for the powerless.

job-29:16:6.summary: Judges handling matters loosely relates to Job's investigating cases.

job-29:16:7.summary: Solomon discerns a disputed case between two women, illustrating tracing out an unknown case (shown part of range).

job-29:16:8.summary: Imitating God as beloved children has no specific link to Job's judicial care.

job-29:16:9.summary: “Inquire and search diligently” echoes Job tracing out an unknown case.

job-29:16:10.summary: Hard cases taken to judges to inquire loosely relates to Job's investigation.

job-29:16:11.summary: Caring for orphans and widows loosely parallels Job as father to the powerless.

job-29:17:0.summary: God “didst crush sinners' teeth,” the same image as Job crushing the molars of the unjust.

job-29:17:1.summary: Evil men with blades for “molars” devouring the poor match Job's unjust whose molars he crushed.

job-29:17:2.summary: The Saints psalm verse speaks of melting wax, not broken teeth, so the link fails.

job-29:17:3.summary: David pulled the sheep from the predator's mouth, as Job tore plunder from between their teeth.

job-29:17:4.summary: The Lord did not give us “as prey to their teeth,” echoing plunder torn from teeth.

job-29:17:5.summary: Enemies who would have swallowed us alive loosely echo the devouring unjust.

job-29:18:0.summary: “I said in my prosperity, ‘I will certainly never be shaken’” parallels Job's “I said” expecting long life.
job-29:18:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-29:18:1.summary: Edom's nest on high depends on the Hebrew “nest”; the Saints Job text has a palm trunk instead.
job-29:18:1.why: Greek wording lacks the nest image.

job-29:18:2.summary: Seed like sand assumes the Hebrew “days as the sand”; Saints Job speaks of a palm trunk.
job-29:18:2.why: Greek wording lacks the sand image.
job-29:18:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-29:18:3.summary: “With length of days I will fill him” matches Job's expectation to live a long time.

job-29:18:4.summary: Obadiah's nest among the stars relies on the Hebrew nest image absent from the Saints text.
job-29:18:4.why: Greek wording lacks the nest image.

job-29:18:5.summary: Eliphaz promises coming to the grave in ripe age, akin to Job's hope of old age.

job-29:18:7.summary: Nesting among cedars depends on the Hebrew nest image not in the Saints Job text.
job-29:18:7.why: Greek wording lacks the nest image.

job-29:18:8.summary: Grain like sand of the sea relies on a Hebrew “sand” image absent from Saints Job 29:18.
job-29:18:8.why: Greek wording lacks the sand image.

job-29:18:9.summary: Setting a nest on high depends on the Hebrew nest image missing from the Saints text.
job-29:18:9.why: Greek wording lacks the nest image.

job-29:19:1.summary: A tree planted by waters that prospers matches Job's root “opened toward water.”

job-29:19:2.summary: Bildad's wicked man: “his roots will dry up… his harvest will fall,” the reverse of Job's watered root and harvest.

job-29:19:3.summary: God “like dew” and roots like Lebanon echo Job's root by water and dew on his harvest.

job-29:20:0.summary: Bows strengthened “by the hand of the Mighty One” loosely echoes Job's bow in His hand.

job-29:20:1.summary: Those enduring for God exchange their strength, loosely like Job's renewed glory.

job-29:20:2.summary: The inner person “renewed day by day” echoes Job's glory being new.

job-29:20:3.summary: God made the psalmist's arms “a bronze bow,” echoing Job's bow strengthened by God's hand.
job-29:20:3.why: God-given strength pictured as a bow.

job-29:20:4.summary: Joseph's glory in Egypt shares only the word glory with Job 29:20.

job-29:20:5.summary: Youth “renewed like an eagle's” echoes Job's glory being new.

job-29:20:6.summary: The Lord as “my glory” loosely echoes Job's glory with him.

job-29:20:7.summary: Job laments God “stripped glory from me,” reversing his former glory that was ever new.

job-29:20:8.summary: Job's righteousness as clothing belongs to the same recollection but does not share the glory-bow image.

job-29:21:0.summary: Job 29:9–10 describes the same scene of powerful men falling silent while hearing Job.

job-29:21:1.summary: Elihu demands attention while he speaks, a contrasting scene of listening to counsel.

job-29:21:2.summary: “When I speak they will pay attention” closely parallels hearers paying attention and keeping silent at Job's counsel.

job-29:22:0.summary: Moses' words descending “as the dew… as a shower” matches Job's speech awaited like rain (29:22–23).

job-29:22:1.summary: No one could answer Jesus a word, loosely like hearers adding nothing to Job's word.

job-29:22:2.summary: The bride's honeyed lips depend on a “dropping” image absent from Job 29:22's Saints text.

job-29:22:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-29:22:3.summary: Kings closing their mouths before the servant loosely echoes hearers adding nothing to Job's word.

job-29:22:4.summary: A prophecy against the southern forest shares nothing with Job's hearers' joy at his speech.

job-29:22:5.summary: Job's friends “answered no more,” a later silencing scene akin to hearers adding nothing.

job-29:22:6.summary: Elihu demanding Job's silence does not match hearers rejoicing at Job's word.

job-29:22:7.summary: Amos's rebuke over forbidding prophecy shares no specific element with Job 29:22.
job-29:22:7.why: Greek text lacks the dropping image.

job-29:22:8.summary: The Saints Micah text speaks of not weeping, lacking the “dropping” speech image.
job-29:22:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-29:23:0.summary: The Lord will come “like rain, early and late upon the land,” matching earth awaiting rain.

job-29:23:1.summary: Asking the Lord for rain in season relates loosely to thirsty earth awaiting rain.

job-29:23:2.summary: The king descending “like drops dripping upon the earth” parallels Job's speech awaited like rain on earth.

job-29:24:0.summary: “The light of Thy face was marked upon us” shares the phrase “light of… face” with Job 29:24.

job-29:24:1.summary: Walking “in the light of Thy face” shares Job's “light of my face” image of favor.

job-29:24:2.summary: Joy at Zion's restoration loosely parallels hearers' incredulous joy at Job's smile.

job-29:24:3.summary: The disciples “still did not believe for joy,” matching hearers who would not believe Job's smile.

job-29:24:4.summary: Jacob did not believe good news of Joseph, loosely like hearers not believing Job's favor.

job-29:25:0.summary: God comforting us to comfort others in affliction echoes Job as one consoling sufferers.

job-29:25:1.summary: Encouraging the fainthearted loosely parallels Job consoling sufferers.

job-29:25:2.summary: Joseph set over Pharaoh's house with all obeying him loosely echoes Job sitting as ruler.

job-29:25:3.summary: Abram's rescue raid shares only a military setting with Job's encamping like a king.

job-29:25:4.summary: Elders make Jephthah their head, loosely like Job choosing their way as ruler.

job-29:25:5.summary: The anointed one sent “to comfort all who mourn” matches Job's role consoling sufferers.

job-29:25:6.summary: Timothy sent to encourage the afflicted loosely echoes Job consoling sufferers.

job-29:25:7.summary: David consulting commanders about the ark does not reflect Job's rule and consolation.

job-29:25:8.summary: God who comforts the lowly, through Titus, loosely echoes consoling sufferers.

job-29:25:9.summary: David appointed shepherd and ruler over Israel loosely echoes Job sitting as ruler.

job-29:25:10.summary: Job 1:3 describes Job's wealth and “noble standing among those from the sunrise,” the status recalled in 29:25.

job-29:25:11.summary: Deuteronomy's ruler in the beloved shares only the word ruler with Job's verse.

job-29:25:12.summary: The Saints text of Job 31:37 concerns returning a bond, not approaching as a prince.

job-29:25:13.summary: Eliphaz recalls Job encouraging the weak and raising them with words, confirming Job's consoling role.

job-29:3:14.summary: Proverbs 20:20 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
job-29:3:14.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
job-29:3:14.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

job-30:1:0.summary: A blameless man “became an object of mockery,” matching “they laughed at me.”

job-30:1:1.summary: Rulers sneering at Jesus parallels a righteous sufferer mocked, generally.

job-30:1:2.summary: Lowly “scourges” gather and mock the psalmist, paralleling the least mocking Job.

job-30:1:3.summary: Gate-sitters and drinkers talking against the psalmist is a general mockery parallel.

job-30:1:4.summary: Small children mock Elisha, loosely like the least mocking an elder.

job-30:1:5.summary: Jesus spat on and mocked parallels the mocked sufferer in general.

job-30:1:6.summary: Soldiers mocking Jesus parallels Job's mockery only generally.

job-30:1:7.summary: Pilate finding no ground for accusations has no mockery or link to Job 30:1.

job-30:1:8.summary: “The child will collide with the elder, the dishonored with the honored,” like the least rising against Job.

job-30:1:10.summary: The crowd choosing Barabbas has no specific link to Job's mockers.

job-30:1:11.summary: Job lists brothers, servants and friends who “speak against me” and abhor him.

job-30:1:12.summary: A saying about Cretans has no real link to Job's mockers.

job-30:1:13.summary: “Wicked men from the marketplace” forming a mob loosely resembles base men rising against Job.

job-30:1:14.summary: A criminal blaspheming Jesus parallels mockery by the lowly, generally.

job-30:3:2.summary: Wandering in deserts and caves loosely parallels outcasts in waterless places.

job-30:4:1.summary: Amos scratching sycamore figs has no real link to hunger-driven root eating.

job-30:4:2.summary: In famine wild fruit is gathered from the field, loosely like foraging plants from hunger.

job-30:5:0.summary: Being sent to a deserted place relies on Hebrew “driven out from among men,” not this Greek “Thieves rose.”

job-30:5:1.summary: Being cast out from homes does not match the Greek “Thieves rose against me.”

job-30:5:3.summary: Cain cast out as a wanderer fits the Hebrew outcasts, not “Thieves rose against me.”

job-30:7:0.summary: The wild donkey that “cries out” for food loosely echoes outcasts who cry out.

job-30:7:1.summary: Ishmael as “a wild man” loosely parallels people living in the wild.

job-30:7:2.summary: A mortal “like a donkey of the wilderness” loosely relates to the wild outcasts.

job-30:8:2.summary: The “senseless” hating perception shares only the theme of folly.

job-30:8:3.summary: Herodias's daughter asking for John's head has no link to Job 30:8.

job-30:8:4.summary: Job calling himself “nothing” does not concern the dishonored outcasts whose name was extinguished.

job-30:8:5.summary: Fear of God as beginning of wisdom has no specific link to these outcasts.

job-30:8:6.summary: “The fool will speak foolish things” shares only the description of fools.

job-30:8:7.summary: The wicked “held in contempt” loosely parallels dishonored people.

job-30:8:8.summary: A king walking in Ahab's way has no link to dishonored outcasts in Job.

job-30:8:9.summary: “The foolish and senseless will perish” and names invoked on lands parallels foolish people whose name was extinguished.

job-30:8:10.summary: Ahaziah walking in Ahab's way is unrelated to Job's outcasts.

job-30:8:11.summary: A king doing evil like Ahab's house is unrelated to Job 30:8.

job-30:9:3.summary: Being mocked with mockery parallels Job's ridicule generally, without the song image.

job-30:9:5.summary: A blameless man “became an object of mockery,” as Job becomes their tale.

job-30:9:6.summary: Made “a parable among the nations” parallels being their repeated tale.

job-30:12:1.summary: The child colliding with the elder loosely parallels young upstarts rising against Job.

job-30:15:10.summary: Job hunted like a lion is a general picture of his torment.

job-30:15:11.summary: Terrifying dreams loosely parallel returning pains.
