job-31:16:10.summary: Sending relief according to one’s means is a general parallel to supplying the needy.

job-31:16:11.summary: Shares the word “powerless” and concern for their hope, but no specific act of provision.
job-31:16:11.why: Same concern for the powerless in Job.

job-31:16:12.summary: Remembering the poor is a general theme shared with Job’s care for the needy.

job-31:16:13.summary: Eyes that “waste away” is shared wording, but Deuteronomy speaks of parents watching captive children.

job-31:17:0.summary: The command to open one’s hands to the poor broadly matches Job’s sharing with the orphan.

job-31:17:1.summary: Sending food portions “to those who have none” loosely parallels sharing one’s morsel, though in a festival setting.
job-31:17:1.why: Example of sharing food with the needy.

job-31:17:2.summary: Sharing in others’ needs is a general parallel to sharing food with an orphan.

job-31:17:3.summary: Giving something to the poor is only a general parallel.

job-31:17:4.summary: Job elsewhere says he “helped an orphan who had no helper” and was “a father to the powerless,” matching this oath.
job-31:17:4.why: Job’s own fuller testimony of care for orphans.

job-31:17:5.summary: The righteous man “gave his bread to the hungry,” the same act Job claims in sharing his morsel.
job-31:17:5.why: Prophetic list of righteous deeds matching Job’s.

job-31:17:6.summary: True religion is to “care for orphans,” the very duty Job says he did not neglect.
job-31:17:6.why: NT definition of piety includes Job’s practice.

job-31:17:7.summary: Giving “his bread to the hungry” is listed as a mark of the righteous, matching Job’s shared morsel.
job-31:17:7.why: Same righteous deed in Ezekiel’s list.

job-31:17:8.summary: John condemns one who has goods and closes his heart to a brother in need, the selfishness Job disowns.

job-31:17:9.summary: Holding possessions in common is only a general parallel to not eating alone.

job-31:17:10.summary: Giving alms is a general parallel to sharing food.

job-31:17:12.summary: Generous provision for a released slave is a loose parallel to sharing with an orphan.

job-31:19:1.summary: Love “in deed and truth” is a general principle, not specific to clothing the naked.

job-31:19:2.summary: Sharing a tunic with “the one who has none” is the same act as clothing a naked person.

job-31:19:3.summary: The men “covered all the naked” and “dressed them,” the act Job claims he never neglected.
job-31:19:3.why: Historical example of clothing the naked.

job-31:19:4.summary: Jesus condemns those who saw Him “naked and you did not clothe Me,” the failure Job disowns.

job-31:19:5.summary: “If you see someone naked, clothe him” is the same duty Job affirms.

job-31:19:6.summary: Job recalls “the blessing of the perishing,” echoing the “perishing” naked person he helped.
job-31:19:6.why: Job’s own memory of the needy blessing him.

job-31:19:7.summary: Dorcas made garments for widows, a general example of clothing the needy.

job-31:19:8.summary: Oppression of “powerless people” is only a loose background to neglecting the naked.
job-31:19:8.why: Shows the opposite of Job’s care.

job-31:19:9.summary: James rebukes saying “be warmed and filled” without giving what the body needs, the neglect Job denies.

job-31:19:10.summary: “Naked and you clothed Me” praises the very act Job claims.

job-31:20:0.summary: Restoring a poor man’s garment so he may sleep in it “and bless you” matches the warmed poor blessing Job.
job-31:20:0.why: Law ties clothing the poor to their blessing.

job-31:20:1.summary: Job recalls being “called … blessed” by those who heard him, matching the blessing of the powerless.
job-31:20:1.why: Job’s own memory of being blessed.

job-31:21:1.summary: Job says he “helped an orphan who had no helper,” the opposite of lifting a hand against one.
job-31:21:1.why: Job’s positive counterpart to this oath.

job-31:21:2.summary: Job accuses friends who would “fall upon an orphan,” the very wrong he denies here.
job-31:21:2.why: Same crime named elsewhere in Job.

job-31:21:3.summary: Hands prepared for evil and a corrupt judge are only loosely related to oppressing an orphan.

job-31:21:4.summary: The wicked “snatched an orphan from the breast,” the violence Job swears he never did.

job-31:21:5.summary: The powerful “plundered orphans” and oppressed houses, the abuse Job disowns.
job-31:21:5.why: Prophetic indictment of the same sin.

job-31:21:6.summary: Jerusalem “oppressed the orphan and widow,” the wrong Job denies.
job-31:21:6.why: Prophetic charge of the same oppression.

job-31:21:7.summary: Do not enter “orphans’ property,” for the Lord will judge their case, matching Job’s refusal to exploit orphans.
job-31:21:7.why: Shows God as the orphan’s defender.

job-31:21:8.summary: Failing to judge “an orphan’s case” relates to injustice toward orphans, but the shown Job text lacks a court setting.

job-31:22:0.summary: A conditional self-curse (“If … may He not deliver us”) shares only the oath form.

job-31:22:1.summary: The psalmist’s “if I repaid … then may” self-imprecation matches Job’s conditional curse on himself.

job-31:22:2.summary: God will “crush the arm of the arrogant,” echoing Job’s wish that his arm be “shattered.”
job-31:22:2.why: Shows the broken arm as divine judgment.

job-31:22:3.summary: Another “may … then” curse in Job’s same oath series concludes his defense.
job-31:22:3.why: Part of the same chain of self-curses.

job-31:22:4.summary: Another self-curse in the same oath chapter, attached to a different sin.

job-31:22:5.summary: “May my tongue cling … if I do not remember you” is a parallel self-curse on a body part.

job-31:23:0.summary: Job warns that “fear from Him” will fall on the friends, matching his own fear of the Lord.

job-31:23:1.summary: “Fear of Thee” and dread of God’s judgments restrain the psalmist as they restrain Job.
job-31:23:1.why: Fear of God as a moral restraint.

job-31:23:2.summary: Paul acts “knowing the fear of the Lord,” the same motive Job gives for his conduct.
job-31:23:2.why: NT echo of fear of the Lord as motive.

job-31:23:3.summary: “Who will withstand Thee?” matches Job’s confession that he could not endure God’s grip.
job-31:23:3.why: Shows no one can withstand God.

job-31:23:4.summary: Isaiah’s “shattering … from God” is only loosely related to Job’s fear of God’s taking hold.

job-31:23:5.summary: Not being “delivered from the Lord” loosely parallels being unable to endure God’s hold.

job-31:23:6.summary: Joseph refuses evil because it would be sin “before God,” the same God-fearing restraint Job claims.
job-31:23:6.why: Example of fear of God restraining sin.

job-31:23:7.summary: Job’s later self-abasement before God relates only generally to his fear of God.
job-31:23:7.why: Shows Job’s final response to God.

job-31:23:8.summary: Joel’s “suffering from suffering” on the Lord’s day does not carry the Hebrew “destruction from God” link to this Greek verse.
job-31:23:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-31:23:9.summary: Having “an arm against the Lord” relates loosely to inability to resist God.

job-31:23:10.summary: God’s “fury of wrath” on the wicked is only a general parallel.

job-31:24:0.summary: Those “trusting in their strength” and wealth parallel making gold one’s strength.
job-31:24:0.why: Psalm warning against trust in wealth.

job-31:24:2.summary: Multiplied “silver and … gold” can lift the heart and make one forget God, the danger Job disowns.
job-31:24:2.why: Law warns of wealth’s pull from God.

job-31:24:3.summary: The man who “hoped in the abundance of his wealth and became strong” is what Job denies being.
job-31:24:3.why: Close portrait of trust in riches.

job-31:24:4.summary: “If wealth flows, do not attach your heart” matches Job’s refusal to trust gold.

job-31:24:5.summary: The rich cannot take wealth at death; a general point about wealth’s futility.
job-31:24:5.why: Shows why wealth is no strength.

job-31:24:6.summary: The rich man’s wealth as “a fortified city” is the false strength Job refuses in gold.

job-31:24:7.summary: The love of money as a root of evils is a general warning on wealth.

job-31:24:8.summary: Life not consisting in possessions is a general warning about wealth.

job-31:24:9.summary: The rich must not “set their hope on the uncertainty of wealth,” the trust Job disowns.
job-31:24:9.why: NT parallel to not trusting riches.

job-31:24:10.summary: Becoming full and denying God loosely relates to trusting wealth.

job-31:24:11.summary: The difficulty of the rich entering the kingdom is a general wealth warning; trust in riches is not in the shown text.

job-31:24:12.summary: Laban’s sons’ complaint about Jacob’s acquired glory has no link to trusting gold.

job-31:24:13.summary: Greed called “idolatry” loosely relates to Job’s treating gold as strength.

job-31:24:14.summary: Blessed is the rich person who “did not go after gold,” matching Job’s refusal to trust gold.

job-31:24:15.summary: Praise for one tested and not transgressing relates only generally to Job’s integrity with wealth.
job-31:24:15.why: Sirach’s context of testing by wealth.

job-31:25:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar boasting in what he built is only a general parallel to rejoicing in wealth.

job-31:25:2.summary: The Assyrian’s boast of seizing by his hand loosely parallels laying hand on countless things.

job-31:25:3.summary: Tyre increased strength by trade and its “heart was exalted,” the pride in wealth Job disowns.

job-31:25:4.summary: “My … hand have gotten me this great wealth” is the self-congratulation Job denies.
job-31:25:4.why: Law forbids boasting in gained wealth.

job-31:25:5.summary: Ephraim says “I have become rich,” the self-satisfied rejoicing in wealth Job refuses.

job-31:25:6.summary: The rich man “received your good things” in life; a general wealth link.

job-31:25:7.summary: The rich man enjoying splendor is only a general picture of rejoicing in wealth.

job-31:25:8.summary: Worshiping the means of one’s wealth loosely relates to rejoicing in gain.

job-31:25:9.summary: The rich fool rejoices over “many goods laid up,” exactly the gladness in wealth Job disowns.

job-31:25:10.summary: Haman displaying “his wealth and the glory” shows the gloating over wealth Job denies.

job-31:25:11.summary: “Let no rich man boast in his wealth” forbids the rejoicing in wealth Job denies.
job-31:25:11.why: Prophetic command on the same point.

job-31:25:12.summary: Wealth flying away like an eagle is a general warning about riches.

job-31:26:0.summary: Men bowing “to the sun” is astral worship, while the Greek Job text only says sun and moon fail and nothing depends on them.
job-31:26:0.why: Background on sun worship implied in Job.

job-31:26:2.summary: Worship of “the sun, or … the moon” is forbidden; the Greek Job verse implies rejecting reliance on them rather than describing worship.
job-31:26:2.why: Law against the astral cult in view.

job-31:26:3.summary: Jerusalem served “the sun and moon”; Job’s Greek text only says they fail and nothing depends on them.
job-31:26:3.why: Shows the astral worship Job rejects.

job-31:26:4.summary: Josiah ended incense to “the sun, the moon”; the Greek Job verse only implicitly rejects trust in them.

job-31:26:5.summary: Horses and chariot dedicated “to the sun” are astral worship; Job shares only the sun.

job-31:26:6.summary: Incense to the “queen of heaven” is astral worship, loosely related to Job’s point about the moon.
job-31:26:6.why: Shows heavenly bodies treated as gods.

job-31:26:7.summary: God made the two great lights; Job’s point that the sun and moon fail implies they are creatures.
job-31:26:7.why: Shows sun and moon as created lights.

job-31:26:8.summary: A warning not to serve other gods is general; nothing specific to sun or moon.

job-31:26:9.summary: The psalmist sees the moon and stars as God’s works; only the heavenly bodies are shared.

job-31:26:10.summary: People supposed “the lights of heaven to be gods,” the error Job rejects by saying nothing depends on sun and moon.
job-31:26:10.why: Wisdom explains the folly Job avoids.

job-31:27:1.summary: Deuteronomy warns lest “your heart be enlarged” and serve other gods; only a general link to a deceived heart.

job-31:27:2.summary: The idolater’s heart “is ashes” and wanders, loosely like Job’s secretly deceived heart.

job-31:27:3.summary: The Greek-based psalm reads “Take hold of instruction,” lacking the “kiss” that the Hebrew link assumes.
job-31:27:3.why: No kissing gesture in this wording.

job-31:27:4.summary: God handing people to an unfit mind relates only generally to a deceived heart.

job-31:27:5.summary: Every mouth that “has not bowed down” to Baal concerns idolatrous worship; the kiss image of the Hebrew is not in this wording.

job-31:27:6.summary: A “senseless heart” darkened by idolatry broadly parallels a secretly deceived heart.

job-31:27:7.summary: The Greek-based Hosea speaks of sacrificing people, not kissing calves, so the gesture link is absent.
job-31:27:7.why: No kissing gesture in this wording.

job-31:28:0.summary: Another verdict on a sin’s gravity in the same oath chapter, though the wording (“fury of wrath”) differs.

job-31:28:1.summary: Deuteronomy condemns worship of “the sun, or … the moon” as transgression before the Lord, the lawlessness Job names.
job-31:28:1.why: Shows why astral worship is grave.

job-31:28:2.summary: “God is judge” fits the Hebrew idea of judges, but the Greek Job verse speaks of lying before the Lord.
job-31:28:2.why: Link rests on wording not in this text.

job-31:28:3.summary: Job’s wish for his case to conclude has no tie to lying before the Lord Most High.

job-31:28:4.summary: “The Lord, who judges” matches the Hebrew judges idea absent from this Greek-based verse.
job-31:28:4.why: Link not carried by this wording.

job-31:28:5.summary: Coming to the judge for judgment relates to Hebrew wording about judges, absent here.
job-31:28:5.why: Link not carried by this wording.

job-31:28:6.summary: Pleading for God’s judgment does not connect to lying before the Lord.

job-31:28:7.summary: The stone witnesses if you “deal falsely with the Lord,” close to Job’s “lied before the Lord.”
job-31:28:7.why: Same idea of falsehood toward God.

job-31:28:8.summary: Removing foreign gods relates generally to the idolatry Job disowns.

job-31:28:9.summary: God as judge of all the earth relates to Hebrew judges wording absent here.

job-31:28:10.summary: Denying the Master is loosely akin to being false toward the Lord Most High.

job-31:28:11.summary: Denying God by deeds broadly parallels being false before the Lord.
job-31:28:11.why: NT parallel on denial by conduct.

job-31:28:12.summary: Denying “our only Master and Lord” is a loose parallel to lying before God.

job-31:28:13.summary: “God the judge of all” relies on the Hebrew judges idea not in this verse.

job-31:28:14.summary: Denying the Son is only a general parallel to falsehood toward God.

job-31:28:15.summary: Becoming “false” toward God through fullness loosely matches lying before the Lord.

job-31:29:1.summary: “One who rejoices over someone perishing will not be acquitted” condemns the gloating Job denies.

job-31:29:2.summary: “Do not rejoice … on the day of their destruction” forbids rejoicing at a foe’s fall.

job-31:29:3.summary: The psalmist mourned and fasted for those who troubled him, the opposite of rejoicing at their fall.

job-31:29:4.summary: Enemies say “Well done! Well done!” and rejoice at troubles, the same gloating words Job disowns.

job-31:29:5.summary: Shimei exults over David’s calamity, an example of the gloating Job rejects.

job-31:29:6.summary: David punished one who brought news of Saul’s death as good news, a loose example of refusing to gloat.
job-31:29:6.why: Example of not celebrating a foe’s fall.

job-31:29:7.summary: David’s people mourned for Saul, a loose example of grieving a former foe’s fall.

job-31:29:8.summary: “Do not rejoice over a dead person” directly forbids rejoicing at another’s fall.
job-31:29:8.why: Wisdom precept on the same point.

job-31:30:0.summary: Not returning reviling concerns cursing others, while the Greek Job verse is a self-curse on his own ear.
job-31:30:0.why: Greek wording lacks the label’s link.

job-31:30:1.summary: “Bless, and do not curse” concerns cursing others; the Greek Job verse invokes a curse on himself.
job-31:30:1.why: Greek wording lacks the label’s link.

job-31:30:2.summary: Blessing and cursing from one mouth concerns speech toward others, not Job’s self-imprecation.
job-31:30:2.why: Greek wording lacks the label’s link.

job-31:30:3.summary: Helping an enemy’s animal does not connect to hearing one’s own curse.

job-31:30:4.summary: Anger and insults toward a brother do not connect to Job’s self-curse.

job-31:30:5.summary: Loving enemies does not appear in the Greek Job verse, which is a self-curse.
job-31:30:5.why: Greek wording lacks the label’s link.

job-31:30:6.summary: Christ not reviling in return is unrelated to Job’s wish to hear his own curse.

job-31:30:7.summary: Accounting for idle words is unrelated to this self-imprecation.

job-31:30:8.summary: The tongue as a fire is unrelated to the Greek Job verse.

job-31:30:9.summary: Not letting the mouth cause sin relates to the Hebrew wording, not this Greek-based self-curse.
job-31:30:9.why: Greek wording lacks the label’s link.

job-31:30:10.summary: Hasty words before God do not connect to Job’s self-curse.

job-31:31:0.summary: David refusing to kill Saul fits only one reading of the obscure Greek line about being “filled with his flesh.”

job-31:31:1.summary: Rulers who “ate the flesh” of the people share the flesh-eating image only.
job-31:31:1.why: Shares the image of eating flesh.

job-31:31:3.summary: Abishai wants to kill Shimei and David restrains him, fitting only one reading of this obscure verse.

job-31:31:4.summary: Abishai urging David to kill Saul fits only one reading of the servants’ words here.

job-31:31:5.summary: Enemies approached “to eat my flesh,” sharing only the flesh-eating image.

job-31:31:6.summary: Abishai urges Shimei’s death and David refuses, fitting only one reading of the Greek line.

job-31:31:7.summary: Jesus healing the slave’s ear does not connect to maidservants wishing to be filled with flesh.

job-31:31:8.summary: Murderers storing up evil does not connect to the shown Job text.

job-31:31:9.summary: Enemies saying “We have swallowed him” is not linked to Job’s maidservants’ words.

job-31:31:10.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of depriving the hungry of a morsel, contrasting the kindness Job claims here.

job-31:31:11.summary: Sinners plotting to swallow a righteous man do not link to this verse.

job-31:31:12.summary: Disciples urging fire on enemies and being rebuked fits only one reading of the obscure Greek line.

job-31:31:13.summary: David’s men urging him against Saul fits only one reading of the servants’ words here.

job-31:31:14.summary: Johanan urging Gedaliah to kill Ishmael fits only one reading of this obscure verse.

job-31:32:0.summary: “Do not forget hospitality” matches Job’s open door to every stranger.

job-31:32:2.summary: The old man insists “do not lodge in the square” and brings the traveler in, as Job did for strangers.

job-31:32:3.summary: “I was a stranger and you welcomed Me” praises the hospitality Job claims.

job-31:32:4.summary: “Bring homeless poor people into your house” matches Job’s open door.
job-31:32:4.why: Prophetic command for the same act.

job-31:32:5.summary: “Pursue hospitality” calls for the welcome Job showed strangers.

job-31:32:6.summary: “Be hospitable” echoes Job’s practice of lodging travelers.

job-31:32:7.summary: In Gibeah “no one took them into a house to lodge,” the opposite of Job’s open door.

job-31:32:8.summary: Service to “the least of these” relates only generally to hospitality.
job-31:32:8.why: Broader principle of serving the needy.

job-31:32:9.summary: Job’s earlier oath about sharing food with orphans is a related but distinct act of generosity.
job-31:32:9.why: Companion oath in the same chapter.

job-31:32:10.summary: Failing to serve “a stranger” is condemned, the very neglect Job denies.

job-31:32:11.summary: A widow “received strangers” as a good work, the hospitality Job practiced.
job-31:32:11.why: NT example of the same virtue.

job-31:33:1.summary: Sapphira’s lie conceals a sin, loosely like hiding one’s sin.

job-31:33:2.summary: “If we confess our sins” contrasts with hiding sin, the concealment Job denies.
job-31:33:2.why: NT teaching on confessing, not hiding, sin.

job-31:33:3.summary: Adam shifts blame after sinning; the Greek Job text lacks the Adam reference the label assumes.

job-31:33:4.summary: “Like a person transgressing a covenant” lacks both the hiding of sin and the Adam wording.

job-31:33:5.summary: Israel stole devoted things and put them among belongings, a loose example of hidden sin.

job-31:33:6.summary: Adam and his wife “hid themselves” after sin, loosely parallel to hiding sin, though Adam is not named in Job’s Greek text.
job-31:33:6.why: Primal example of hiding after sin.

job-31:34:0.summary: “You shall not join the many” warns against yielding to a crowd, as Job refused to shrink before numbers.
job-31:34:0.why: Law against bowing to the multitude.

job-31:34:1.summary: Those who “feared and felt shame before people” fell, the fear of the crowd Job denies.

job-31:34:2.summary: Pilate yields to the crowds despite knowing the truth, the opposite of Job’s refusal to shrink before them.
job-31:34:2.why: Example of yielding to a crowd.

job-31:34:3.summary: Eliasib’s chamber for Tobia has no link to fearing a crowd or turning away the powerless.

job-31:34:4.summary: Nehemiah driving away a priest’s son-in-law does not connect to this verse.

job-31:34:5.summary: Nehemiah confronting leaders before an assembly is unrelated to the shown Job text.

job-31:34:6.summary: The Levites’ slaughter at Sinai has no link to this verse.

job-31:34:7.summary: The names of Zimri and Cozbi have no connection to Job’s text.

job-31:34:8.summary: The law of the king’s inner court has no link to Job’s claim.

job-31:34:9.summary: Rescuing those led to death loosely relates to not turning the powerless away.

job-31:34:10.summary: Mordecai’s challenge to Esther does not connect to this verse.

job-31:34:11.summary: The king could not oppose the officials, a loose example of yielding to pressure.

job-31:34:12.summary: “Turning aside the poor at the gates” loosely parallels sending the powerless away empty.
job-31:34:12.why: Prophetic charge of neglecting the poor.

job-31:34:13.summary: The king fears mockery by Judeans, a loose example of fearing people.

job-31:34:14.summary: The king’s secret oath to Jeremiah has no link to this verse.

job-31:34:15.summary: Eliphaz’s charge of partiality does not connect to the shown Job text.

job-31:34:16.summary: Corrupt rulers and judges do not connect to this verse.

job-31:34:17.summary: Knowing no one according to the flesh is unrelated to this verse.

job-31:34:18.summary: God does not stand in awe of honored persons, loosely like Job not shrinking before the crowd.

job-31:35:0.summary: Job asks God to answer him and keep His “hand” away, the hearing he longs for here.
job-31:35:0.why: Job’s earlier plea for a hearing.

job-31:35:1.summary: Job’s eventual reply when heard relates loosely to his wish for a hearer.
job-31:35:1.why: Shows the outcome of his wish.

job-31:35:2.summary: Job asks why God hides from him, loosely related to wanting someone to hear.

job-31:35:3.summary: Asking someone to “bind himself to my hand” loosely parallels the bond Job mentions.

job-31:35:4.summary: Job wishes his words “be written and placed in a book,” matching his appeal to a written bond.
job-31:35:4.why: Job’s earlier wish for a written record.

job-31:35:5.summary: Job longs to find God and “state my own case,” the hearing he wishes for here.

job-31:35:6.summary: The Lord finally speaks to Job and demands an answer, answering Job’s wish for one who hears.

job-31:35:7.summary: “I will argue before Him” expresses Job’s same desire for a hearing with God.
job-31:35:7.why: Job’s repeated wish to plead his case.

job-31:35:8.summary: Elihu presents himself as a fellow creature to hear Job, loosely answering his wish.

job-31:35:9.summary: Elihu’s call to enter judgment before God loosely relates to Job’s wish for a hearing.

job-31:35:10.summary: Job cries out but “judgment is nowhere,” the lack of a hearer he laments here.
job-31:35:10.why: Job’s earlier complaint of no hearing.

job-31:35:11.summary: “Judge me, Lord, for I walked in my innocence” is a general appeal of the innocent.

job-31:35:12.summary: Elihu quotes Job’s complaint that God treats him as an opponent; only a general link.

job-31:35:13.summary: Job crying out in the assembly loosely relates to seeking a hearer.

job-31:35:14.summary: Settling with an adversary relates to the Hebrew “adversary,” not this Greek wording about a bond.
job-31:35:14.why: Link not carried by this wording.

job-31:35:15.summary: God treating Job as an enemy loosely relates to his longing for a fair hearing.

job-31:35:16.summary: Job’s wish against his enemies loosely relates to his legal challenge.

job-31:36:0.summary: The Greek-based Isaiah gives “David’s glory” with no shoulder or key, so the label’s link to bearing on the shoulder is absent.
job-31:36:0.why: Link not carried by this wording.

job-31:36:1.summary: Aaron bears memorial stones “on his two shoulders,” loosely like Job carrying the bond on his shoulders.
job-31:36:1.why: Shared image of bearing on the shoulders.

job-31:36:2.summary: Job wore righteousness like a cloak, loosely like wearing the bond as a crown.

job-31:36:3.summary: Paul calls believers his “crown”; only the word is shared.

job-31:36:4.summary: Zion as a “crown of beauty” shares only the word crown.

job-41:6:3.summary: Shutting doors in old age shares only the word doors/gates.

job-41:6:4.summary: Enemies' teeth as weapons share the fearsome-teeth image.

job-41:6:5.summary: God shattering teeth shares the teeth image but not the monster.

job-41:7:0.summary: Not boasting in strength relies on the Hebrew “pride” of its scales, absent from the Greek source.

job-41:7:1.summary: Opening a sealed scroll relies on the Hebrew “seal” wording, absent from the Greek source.

job-41:7:2.summary: The Lion opening the seals relies on Hebrew “seal” wording, absent from the Greek source.

job-41:10:0.summary: Job's “morning star rising” shares the dawn-star image used for the creature's eyes.

job-41:10:1.summary: Christ's eyes “like a flame of fire” share a shining-eyes image.

job-41:12:0.summary: A cauldron heated from beneath resembles the furnace image, but the Greek source has no pot.

job-41:13:1.summary: “Coals of fire” before God share coal-fire wording in a theophany.

job-41:13:2.summary: A ravine burning with fire and sulfur shares fiery imagery only.

job-41:13:3.summary: The Greek Habakkuk verse lacks the Hebrew burning coals, so no link remains.

job-41:14:1.summary: God clothes the horse “with power” and puts fear “upon its neck,” matching power lodging in the creature's neck.

job-41:14:2.summary: Death's sting and victory have no link to the creature's neck.

job-41:14:3.summary: Death's punishment and sting have no link to the creature.

job-41:16:0.summary: A stubborn neck of iron and bronze forehead shares hardness imagery.

job-41:16:1.summary: The Greek Zechariah lacks the Hebrew stone-hard heart, so only “heart” remains.

job-41:16:2.summary: People “hardened their faces beyond rock,” a similar hardness-as-stone image.

job-41:17:0.summary: Crying to the Lord in distress has no specific link to fear of the creature.

job-41:17:1.summary: Sailors' fear in a storm shares only general fear.

job-41:20:0.summary: The wild donkey laughing at the city shares a creature scorning human threats.

job-41:20:1.summary: Invaders mock every fortress; similar scorn of defenses.

job-41:21:0.summary: A list of weapons including slings for stones shares only weaponry vocabulary.

job-41:22:0.summary: Saw-toothed threshing wheels resemble the sharp spits, though the Greek source lacks a threshing sledge.

job-41:24:0.summary: Darkness over “the deep” shares only the abyss setting.

job-41:24:1.summary: Old age as a crown relies on the Hebrew “hoary” deep, absent from the Greek source.

job-41:24:2.summary: “Who fixed the face of the abyss?” shares the word abyss in the same divine speeches.

job-41:24:3.summary: Abraham's good old age relies on Hebrew “hoary” wording absent from the Greek source.
job-41:24:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-41:24:5.summary: Gray hair as glory relies on Hebrew wording absent from the Greek source.

job-41:24:6.summary: The personified “abyss” speaks in Job; shares only the abyss.

job-41:24:7.summary: Lights in the firmament have no link to the abyss.

job-41:24:8.summary: Abram's peaceful old age relies on Hebrew “hoary” wording absent from the Greek source.
job-41:24:8.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-41:24:9.summary: Jacob's gray hairs going to Hades rely on Hebrew wording absent from the Greek source.

job-41:26:1.summary: Arrogance seizing the wicked relies on the Hebrew “children of pride”; the Greek source says “king of all things in the waters.”
job-41:26:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

job-41:26:2.summary: God “wounded the great sea creature,” the same king of the waters, showing God's mastery.

job-41:26:3.summary: “Sons of the arrogant” shares a pride term only.

job-41:26:4.summary: The people returning has no link to the sea creature.

job-41:26:5.summary: Pharaoh's defiance has no specific link to the creature's sovereignty over waters.

job-41:26:6.summary: The dragon gives the beast power and a throne; related monster-kingship imagery.

job-41:26:7.summary: The dragon is bound and thrown into the abyss; related monster imagery.

job-41:26:8.summary: A great red dragon with diadems shares crowned-monster imagery only.

job-41:26:9.summary: Ephraim's “crown of insolence” shares only a pride word.

job-42:2:0.summary: Jesus says “with God all things are possible,” echoing Job’s confession that God “canst do all things” and nothing is “impossible.”
job-42:2:0.why: Same confession of God’s unlimited power.

job-42:2:1.summary: Mark’s “all things are possible with God” and “impossible” mirror Job’s confession that nothing is impossible for God.
job-42:2:1.why: Same confession of God’s unlimited power.

job-42:2:3.summary: Hebrews stresses that nothing is hidden from God’s eyes, while Job confesses God’s power; the overlap is general divine greatness.
job-42:2:3.why: Adds God’s all-seeing knowledge to His power.

job-42:2:4.summary: Jeremiah praises God’s “great strength” in making heaven and earth, but the Greek ends with “nothing can be hidden,” not “impossible.”

job-42:2:5.summary: God says “I will do everything I have planned,” a general parallel to Job’s confession that God can do all things.

job-42:2:6.summary: Paul speaks of God who “works all things” by His will, a loose echo of Job’s “all things.”
job-42:2:6.why: God’s sovereign working in all things.

job-42:2:7.summary: The Lord’s counsel “remains for ever”; the Greek Job verse speaks of power, not counsel, so the link is general.

job-42:2:8.summary: The psalm says God knows the heart’s hidden things, while Job’s verse speaks of power; only general divine greatness is shared.

job-42:2:9.summary: Earlier Job says “whatever He Himself wished, He also did,” anticipating his final confession that God can do all things.
job-42:2:9.why: Job’s own earlier grasp of God’s sovereignty.

job-42:2:10.summary: Isaiah asks who can turn back God’s “high hand,” a general parallel to God’s unlimited power.

job-42:2:11.summary: God says “I will act, and who will turn it back?”, loosely matching Job’s confession of God’s power.

job-42:2:13.summary: Ecclesiastes says God’s works endure and nothing can be added or taken; only a general theme of divine sovereignty.

job-42:2:14.summary: John speaks of Jesus knowing human hearts; Job’s Greek verse is about God’s power, so the link is incidental.

job-42:2:15.summary: The psalm concerns God knowing one’s sitting and rising; Job’s verse concerns power, not knowledge.

job-42:2:16.summary: Jeremiah speaks of God testing hearts to repay; Job’s verse confesses God’s power, so no specific link.

job-42:2:17.summary: Jesus prays “all things are possible for Thee,” the same address to God as Job’s “nothing is impossible for Thee.”
job-42:2:17.why: Same prayerful confession of God’s power.

job-42:2:18.summary: Ezekiel describes evil plans rising in Gog’s heart; it has no real link to Job’s confession of God’s power.

job-42:2:19.summary: “The things impossible with people are possible with God” restates Job’s confession that nothing is impossible for God.
job-42:2:19.why: Same confession of God’s unlimited power.

job-42:2:20.summary: Peter’s “Lord, Thou knowest all things” resembles Job’s address “Thou canst do all things,” but concerns knowledge, not power.
job-42:2:20.why: Similar humble confession before the Lord.

job-42:3:0.summary: The psalmist says God’s knowledge is “wondrous beyond me,” as Job confesses wonderful things he did not understand.
job-42:3:0.why: Same humility before God’s incomprehensible wisdom.

job-42:3:1.summary: David did not walk among “wonders beyond me,” paralleling Job’s admission of wonderful things beyond his understanding.
job-42:3:1.why: Humility about matters too great to grasp.

job-42:3:3.summary: The psalm praises God’s many “wonders” beyond number; Job speaks of wonderful things he did not understand.

job-42:3:4.summary: Agur confesses “human understanding is not in me” and asks who went up to heaven, like Job admitting things he did not understand.
job-42:3:4.why: Parallel confession of human ignorance before God.

job-42:4:0.summary: God told Job “I will question you, and you must answer Me”; Job now echoes, “I will question Thee, and Thou, teach me.”
job-42:4:0.why: Job repeats God’s challenge in humility.

job-42:4:2.summary: Abraham repeatedly asks the Lord to “allow me to speak,” loosely like Job’s request “hear me… so that I too may speak.”
job-42:4:2.why: Humble boldness in speaking to God.

job-42:4:3.summary: Abraham ventures “to speak to the Lord, though I am earth and ashes,” a closer match to Job 42:6 than this verse.

job-42:5:0.summary: Paul prays for “eyes of your heart enlightened” in knowing God; Job contrasts hearing with seeing God, a loose theme.

job-42:5:1.summary: Paul says faith comes “from hearing”; Job moves from hearing of God to seeing Him, only a loose association.
job-42:5:1.why: Hearing as the start of knowing God.

job-42:5:2.summary: Jesus says whoever “beholds Me beholds the One who sent Me,” loosely related to Job’s seeing God.

job-42:5:3.summary: Isaiah says “I saw the Lord seated on a throne,” a comparable vision of God like Job’s “my eye has seen Thee.”
job-42:5:3.why: Another person who sees God directly.

job-42:5:4.summary: Isaiah says “my eyes have seen the King” and cries woe over himself, as Job sees God and then abases himself.
job-42:5:4.why: Vision of God leading to self-abasement.

job-42:5:5.summary: John says Isaiah “saw His glory,” only a general link to Job’s seeing God.

job-42:5:6.summary: Job earlier said we “hear a mere drop of speech concerning Him”; now he moves beyond hearing to seeing.
job-42:5:6.why: Shows Job’s growth from hearsay to encounter.

job-42:5:7.summary: Job asks whether his “ear” will receive extraordinary things from God; the link is mainly the ear-hearing motif.

job-42:5:8.summary: John says “No one has ever seen God,” contrasting with Job’s claim that his eye has seen God.

job-42:5:9.summary: Moses saw “the glory of the Lord” in visible appearance, a general parallel to Job seeing God.

job-42:5:10.summary: Earlier Job complained “I will not see” God’s actions; now he says “my eye has seen Thee.”
job-42:5:10.why: Shows Job’s reversal from not seeing to seeing.

job-42:5:11.summary: Elihu speaks of God uncovering minds with fearful forms; there is no specific link to Job hearing and seeing God.

job-42:5:12.summary: Destruction and Death have only “heard” of wisdom’s renown, loosely like Job’s former hearing of God by ear.

job-42:5:13.summary: Stephen “saw the glory of God”; only a general parallel to Job’s seeing God.

job-42:6:0.summary: Ezra is “ashamed and abashed” before God over sins, a general parallel to Job’s self-abasement.

job-42:6:1.summary: Paul calls himself the foremost of sinners; only a general theme of self-humbling.

job-42:6:2.summary: James calls people to mourn and “humble yourselves before the Lord,” a general theme of repentance.

job-42:6:3.summary: In his earlier reply Job says “I am nothing” and covers his mouth, anticipating his full self-abasement here.

job-42:6:4.summary: Job says his portion is “in earth and ashes,” the same phrase he uses of himself here.

job-42:6:5.summary: Daniel prays with fasts, sackcloth and “ashes,” a general penitential parallel.

job-42:6:6.summary: Job sits on a dung heap in his affliction; the Greek has no “ashes,” so only a loose link to his lowliness.

job-42:6:7.summary: Israel will remember their ways and beat their faces over evils, a general theme of remorse.

job-42:6:8.summary: Ephraim says “I repented” and groaned over shame; a general penitential parallel.

job-42:6:9.summary: Jesus speaks of repenting “in sackcloth and ashes,” a general penitential link to Job’s “earth and ashes.”

job-42:6:10.summary: Paul calls himself “the least of the apostles,” a general self-humbling theme.

job-42:6:11.summary: Israel will “feel disgust” at their deeds, loosely like Job despising himself.

job-42:6:12.summary: A “broken and humbled heart” God will not despise; only a general theme of contrition.

job-42:6:13.summary: Israel will “remember and be ashamed” and not open her mouth, a general theme of humbled silence.

job-42:6:14.summary: Jesus speaks of repenting “in sackcloth and ashes,” only a general penitential link.

job-42:6:15.summary: Mordecai puts on sackcloth and ashes in mourning, not self-abasement; the link is the ashes motif.

job-42:6:16.summary: The prodigal says “I am no longer worthy,” a general theme of humbled confession.

job-42:6:17.summary: Nineveh’s king “sat in ashes” in repentance; a general penitential parallel.

job-42:6:18.summary: Isaiah’s vineyard judgment has no real link to Job’s self-abasement.

job-42:6:19.summary: Isaiah mentions spreading “sackcloth and ashes” to humble oneself, a general penitential motif.

job-42:6:20.summary: Job says his robe abhorred him in a complaint; this does not carry the self-abasement of his repentance.

job-42:6:21.summary: Ahab humbles himself with sackcloth and fasting; a general theme of humbling before God.

job-42:7:1.summary: Zophar wished the Lord would speak to rebuke Job; in the end God rebukes the friends instead.
job-42:7:1.why: Ironic reversal of the friends’ expectation.

job-42:7:2.summary: Elihu notes the “three men” had no answer, matching the three friends God now rebukes.

job-42:7:3.summary: Introduces a speech of “Eliphaz the Temanite,” the friend God directly addresses here.

job-42:7:4.summary: Introduces Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar as Job’s three friends, the “two friends” and Eliphaz of this verse.
job-42:7:4.why: Introduces the friends who are rebuked.

job-42:7:5.summary: David’s confession “against Thee alone I sinned” shares only the word sin with God’s rebuke of the friends.

job-42:7:6.summary: Introduces a speech of Bildad, one of the “two friends” rebuked here.

job-42:7:7.summary: Introduces a speech of Zophar, one of the “two friends” rebuked here.

job-42:8:2.summary: Eliphaz said an innocent person would be “saved through your clean hands”; ironically Eliphaz himself is spared through Job.
job-42:8:2.why: Ironic fulfilment of Eliphaz’s own words.

job-42:8:3.summary: God “has not dealt with us according to our sins,” loosely like God sparing the friends.

job-42:8:4.summary: Abraham prayed and God healed Abimelech, as Job is to pray for those who wronged him.

job-42:8:5.summary: The Levites sacrificed “seven calves and seven rams,” the same offering prescribed for the friends.

job-42:8:6.summary: Ezekiel names Job alongside Noah and Daniel as righteous, matching God’s praise of “My servant Job.”

job-42:8:7.summary: Balaam asks for “seven calves and seven rams,” the same offering set.

job-42:8:8.summary: Hezekiah brings seven calves and seven rams “for sin,” matching this atoning offering.

job-42:8:9.summary: The friends do “as the Lord commanded” and their sin is released through Job, fulfilling this command.

job-42:8:10.summary: Elders are to pray over the sick; only a general theme of intercessory prayer.

job-42:8:11.summary: God’s pleasure in His Son shares only a vague idea of divine approval with accepting Job’s person.

job-42:8:12.summary: John urges asking for a sinning brother so he will receive life, like Job praying for his friends’ sin.

job-42:8:13.summary: Balak offers “a calf and a ram” on each of seven altars, the same seven-and-seven offering.

job-42:8:14.summary: Job habitually offered sacrifices for his children’s possible sins; now he offers for his friends.

job-42:8:15.summary: Opponents bowing at the church’s feet has no real link to the friends’ offering through Job.

job-42:8:16.summary: David “favoured your face” for Abigail, an idiom like God accepting Job’s person; only the idiom is shared.

job-42:8:17.summary: Christ coming through water and blood has no real link to Job’s intercessory sacrifice.

job-42:8:18.summary: Jethro, a non-Israelite, offers sacrifices to God; only a general sacrificial link.

job-42:8:19.summary: The prince offers “seven calves and seven unblemished rams,” the same offering set, with a goat for sin.

job-42:8:20.summary: Paul’s note that the Lord will repay Alexander shares no specific element with this verse.

job-42:8:21.summary: God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people, contrasting with God’s command that Job pray for his friends.
job-42:8:21.why: Contrast in God’s acceptance of intercession.

job-42:8:22.summary: Even Moses and Samuel would not prevail for Judah, unlike Job whose intercession God accepts.

job-42:8:23.summary: Hebrews says animal blood cannot remove sins; a general reflection on sacrifices like Job’s.

job-42:8:24.summary: Former oppressors coming to Zion in fear has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:8:25.summary: Hebrews contrasts repeated sacrifices with Christ’s one offering; only a general sacrificial link.

job-42:8:26.summary: Jesus requires reconciliation with a brother before offering, loosely like the friends offering through wronged Job.

job-42:8:27.summary: Being favored in the Beloved shares only a vague idea of acceptance.

job-42:8:28.summary: Christ “always lives to intercede,” a general parallel to Job interceding for his friends.

job-42:8:29.summary: Malachi asks whether God will “accept” and “show favor,” sharing the idea of God accepting a person’s plea.

job-42:8:30.summary: Heliodorus’s companions beg righteous Onias to pray that the offender be spared, like Job praying for his friends.

job-42:9:0.summary: Abraham obeyed God’s call; only a general theme of obedience.

job-42:9:1.summary: Saul being told what to do in Damascus shares no specific element with the friends’ obedience.

job-42:9:2.summary: Proverbs on the Lord’s discipline has no specific link to the friends’ sin being released.

job-42:9:3.summary: Ecclesiastes’ “God has already favored your deeds” is unrelated to this narrative.

job-42:9:4.summary: Hearing and doing Jesus’ words is a general parallel to the friends doing as the Lord commanded.

job-42:9:5.summary: Elihu’s obscure speech about confession shares no specific element with this verse.

job-42:9:6.summary: “Whatever He tells you, do” is a general parallel to doing as the Lord commanded.

job-42:9:7.summary: Isaiah’s oppressors coming to Zion has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:9:8.summary: Cornelius waits to hear what the Lord commanded; only a general theme of obedience.

job-42:9:9.summary: Eliphaz promised Job “when you pray to Him, He will hear you”; it is fulfilled as Job prays for Eliphaz.

job-42:9:10.summary: God’s command to the friends to go to Job for sacrifice and prayer is what they carry out here.

job-42:10:0.summary: The Greek says the Lord will “heal your sins” and restore; loosely parallels forgiveness and restoration here.

job-42:10:1.summary: Bildad predicted God would restore Job and make his last things beyond telling, fulfilled in Job’s doubled goods.

job-42:10:2.summary: Fear of the Lord brings wealth and glory; only a general link to Job’s restored wealth.

job-42:10:3.summary: Jerusalem’s “sin is loosed” and she receives “double,” paralleling forgiveness and Job’s double restoration.

job-42:10:4.summary: Isaiah’s “second time” inheritance is only loosely like Job’s doubling; the Greek lacks “double.”

job-42:10:5.summary: The psalm’s turning back “captivity” relies on the Hebrew Job wording, which this Greek verse lacks.
job-42:10:5.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-42:10:6.summary: Turning back Zion’s captivity relies on the Hebrew Job wording, which this Greek verse lacks.
job-42:10:6.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-42:10:7.summary: God’s hand making all things has no specific link to Job’s restoration.

job-42:10:8.summary: Lists Job’s original livestock and servants, the former wealth the Lord now doubles.

job-42:10:9.summary: Moses prayed for Aaron when God intended to destroy him, a general parallel to Job interceding for his friends.

job-42:10:10.summary: God’s ownership of silver and gold has no specific link to Job’s restoration.

job-42:10:11.summary: Moses prays for Miriam who had wronged him, loosely like Job praying for his friends.

job-42:10:12.summary: Miriam and Aaron’s complaint has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:10:13.summary: Stephen asks the Lord not to hold sin against his killers, loosely like Job praying for friends’ forgiveness.
job-42:10:13.why: Praying for those who wronged you.

job-42:10:14.summary: The Lord “makes poor and makes rich,” a general link to Job’s restored wealth.

job-42:10:15.summary: “The Lord can give you far more than these” is a general parallel to Job’s doubled possessions.

job-42:10:16.summary: God gives strength to gain wealth; only a general link to Job’s restored wealth.

job-42:10:17.summary: Abraham prayed for Abimelech and God healed his house, as Job prays and God forgives his friends.

job-42:10:18.summary: Eliphaz promised Job wealth and divine help if he returned; a loose link to Job’s restoration.

job-42:10:19.summary: The rich man’s request for his father’s house has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:10:20.summary: The congregation’s threat to stone Moses’ companions has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:10:21.summary: Israel’s grumbling and wish to return to Egypt has no specific link to this verse.

job-42:10:22.summary: Moses crying out over a hostile people has no specific link to Job’s restoration.

job-42:10:23.summary: Moses and Aaron intercede for the congregation threatened with destruction; a general intercession theme.

job-42:10:24.summary: The psalm’s turning back “captivity” relies on Hebrew Job wording absent from this Greek verse.
job-42:10:24.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

job-42:10:25.summary: Eliphaz said God “struck, and His hands healed” and restores; Job’s doubled restoration fulfils this pattern.
job-42:10:25.why: Pattern of wounding and healing realised.

job-42:10:26.summary: Moses intercedes to spare the people (shown text truncated), a general parallel to Job’s intercession.

job-42:10:27.summary: Aaron makes atonement and stands between dead and living; only a general mediation theme.

job-42:10:28.summary: Those sowing in tears reap with exultation; a general theme of reversal, though “captivity” is not in this Greek verse.

job-42:10:29.summary: God forgave lawlessness and turned back captivity; loosely matches forgiveness and restoration here.

job-42:11:1.summary: Job’s friends “heard of all the bad things” and came to comfort him, as his family now hears, comes and consoles him.

job-42:11:2.summary: Abraham’s servant gives gold pieces weighed in drachmas; only a general link to gifts of gold.

job-42:11:3.summary: Proverbs on doing righteous things has no specific link to Job’s family visit.

job-42:11:4.summary: “Weep with those who weep” is a general parallel to relatives consoling Job.

job-42:11:5.summary: Strengthening drooping hands has no specific link to Job’s relatives consoling him.

job-42:11:6.summary: Isaiah’s call to strengthen weak knees has no specific link to this family visit.

job-42:11:7.summary: “All his sons and daughters… came to comfort him,” closely like Job’s brothers and sisters coming to console him.
job-42:11:7.why: Family gathering to comfort in grief.

job-42:11:8.summary: Remembering those mistreated is a general parallel to visiting the afflicted Job.

job-42:11:9.summary: Jacob paid “one hundred ewe lambs,” the same distinctive unit Job receives as gifts.
job-42:11:9.why: Explains the ewe lamb as a unit of value.

job-42:11:10.summary: Job’s wish for strength in his mouth has no specific link to his relatives’ visit.

job-42:11:11.summary: Job once strengthened the weak with words; now others console him, a loose reversal.

job-42:11:12.summary: Saul’s critics bringing no gifts shares only the idea of gifts; no real link.

job-42:11:13.summary: Members suffering together is a general parallel to relatives sharing Job’s sorrow.

job-42:11:14.summary: Gifts of silver and gold to Rebekah’s family are only loosely like gifts of gold to Job.

job-42:11:15.summary: Many came to “console” Martha and Mary, a general parallel to Job’s relatives consoling him.

job-42:11:16.summary: Job earlier said he asked his friends for nothing; now relatives freely give him gifts.

job-42:12:0.summary: Bildad foretold “your last things beyond telling,” fulfilled as the Lord blesses Job’s latter things above the former.

job-42:12:1.summary: “The end… is better than their beginning,” matching Job’s latter things being blessed more than the former.

job-42:12:2.summary: The Lord’s blessing “makes rich,” a general parallel to Job’s blessed prosperity.

job-42:12:3.summary: Multiplying sheep and fat oxen describe a blessed people; a general prosperity parallel.

job-42:12:4.summary: “The Lord has greatly blessed my master” with sheep, camels and donkeys, a close parallel to Job’s blessing.

job-42:12:5.summary: The Lord blessed Isaac until he became very great with flocks and herds, like Job’s blessed increase.

job-42:12:7.summary: God tested Israel “to do you good in your latter days,” matching Job’s blessed latter end after testing.
job-42:12:7.why: Testing leading to a good end.

job-42:12:8.summary: God “richly provides,” but Paul warns against trusting wealth; only a general link.

job-42:12:9.summary: “He blessed them… and He did not diminish their livestock,” a general parallel.

job-42:12:10.summary: James recalls Job’s endurance and “the outcome from the Lord,” referring to this final blessing.
job-42:12:10.why: New Testament reading of Job’s ending.

job-42:13:1.summary: Sons lost are restored in abundance; a loose parallel to Job’s new children.

job-42:13:2.summary: “Sons are the Lord’s inheritance,” a general reflection on Job’s new children.

job-42:13:3.summary: God lifts the poor and makes “families like sheep,” loosely like Job’s restored family.

job-42:15:1.summary: The psalm praises beautified daughters, a general parallel to Job’s excellent daughters.

job-42:15:2.summary: Joshua’s survey for dividing land shares no specific element with Job’s daughters’ inheritance.

job-42:15:3.summary: Moses being “beautiful before God” has no real link to Job’s daughters.

job-42:15:4.summary: Caleb gives his daughter land at her request, a parallel case of a father giving a daughter an inheritance.

job-42:16:0.summary: “The crown of elders is children’s children,” matching Job seeing sons’ sons to the fourth generation.
job-42:16:0.why: Grandchildren as crown of old age.

job-42:16:2.summary: “May you see sons of your sons,” the very blessing Job enjoys.

job-42:16:3.summary: Jacob’s total lifespan is recorded in a similar formula; a general patriarchal parallel.

job-42:16:4.summary: Abraham’s lifespan formula is a general patriarchal parallel to Job’s long life.

job-42:16:9.summary: Terah’s 205 years is a general patriarchal parallel.

job-42:17:1.summary: Eliphaz promised Job would come to the grave “like ripe grain… in its season,” fulfilled in Job’s full old age.

job-42:17:2.summary: Abraham is promised burial “at a good old age,” matching Job dying elderly and full of days.

job-42:17:3.summary: Keeping God’s commands to “prolong your days” is a general link.

job-42:17:4.summary: “With length of days I will fill him,” matching Job dying “full of days.”

job-42:17:5.summary: Wisdom holds “length of life,” a general parallel to Job’s long life.
